units.text: In the UAE, the Emirates Drug Establishment (EDE; 'UAE Drug Corporation' in the official English translation) has been the federal authority regulating medical products since Federal Decree-Law 28/2023 (issued 25 Sep 2023, in force 30 Sep 2023), with the power to approve and register medical products.
units.note: no cited source has readable text — nothing can be verified

units.text: In the UAE, since 2 January 2025 (Federal Decree-Law 38/2024, which replaced Federal Law 8/2019), no medical product may be imported, distributed, possessed, sold, displayed, used or manufactured for circulation without an EDE marketing approval.
units.note: no cited source has readable text — nothing can be verified

units.text: In the UAE, physicians may prescribe a medicine for uses not in its leaflet, or a medicine never submitted for marketing approval, only when necessary, when no equivalent alternative is available and with the patient's approval; compassionate use is excluded from this rule (Federal Decree-Law 38/2024, Art. 42(1)).
units.note: no cited source has readable text — nothing can be verified

units.text: In Dubai, the DHA prohibits circulating, prescribing, dispensing, administering or using any peptide product unless it is registered or licensed with the EDE and used within the scope of its licence, and requires registered peptide products to be used strictly within their approved indications (External Circular 0867, 29 July 2026).

assertions.text: In Dubai, the DHA prohibits circulating, prescribing, dispensing, administering or using any peptide product unless it is registered or licensed with the EDE and used within the scope of its licence.
assertions.quote: It is prohibited to circulate, prescribe, dispense, administer, or use any peptide product unless it is duly registered or licensed with the Emirates Drug Establishment, and authorized for use within the scope of its license.
assertions.note: The circular expressly bans circulating, prescribing, dispensing, administering, or using any peptide product unless licensed or registered with the EDE and used within its license scope.

assertions.text: The DHA requires registered peptide products to be used strictly within their approved indications.
assertions.quote: Strict adherence to the approved indications for use of each registered or authorized produ ct is required.
assertions.note: The circular explicitly mandates strict adherence to approved indications for registered or authorized peptide products.

units.text: In the UAE, medical products compounded in licensed compounding pharmacies are exempt from the marketing-approval requirement (Federal Decree-Law 38/2024, Art. 5(2), in force 2 Jan 2025).
units.note: no cited source has readable text — nothing can be verified

units.text: In the UAE, a compounding pharmacy may not compound essential copies of products holding an EDE marketing approval unless no commercially available product can deliver the expected benefit to the patient, and may not formulate products intended for research, development or experimentation (Federal Decree-Law 38/2024, Art. 95).
units.note: no cited source has readable text — nothing can be verified

units.text: In Abu Dhabi, the DoH Standard for Provision of Compounding Pharmacy Services (August 2026) allows compounding only for a genuine, documented clinical need that no suitable licensed product meets, and bars copying commercially available products for convenience or cost or introducing experimental or unverified products.

assertions.text: In Abu Dhabi, the DoH Standard for Provision of Compounding Pharmacy Services (August 2026) allows compounding only for a genuine, documented clinical need where no suitable licensed product meets the patient's needs.
assertions.quote: Compounding shall be performed only to meet a genuine, documented clinical need where a suitable licensed commercial product does not meet the patient’s needs (e.g., required strength, dosage form, excipient restrictions, or verified shortage).
assertions.note: Supported directly by section 3.1.2 of the standard.

assertions.text: The DoH Standard bars copying commercially available products for convenience or cost or introducing experimental or unverified products under a pharmacy license.
assertions.quote: Compounding shall not be used to copy or replicate commercially available products for convenience or cost, to manufacture at scale for general supply, or to introduce experimental or unverified products into the market under a pharmacy license.
assertions.note: Supported directly by section 3.1.2 of the standard.

units.text: In Abu Dhabi, compounding requires a Good Compounding Practice (GCP) certificate issued by the EDE, and compounding from unapproved or unknown-source substances, or from substances not on the DoH Registry for Compounded Substances, is prohibited unless the DoH permits it (DoH compounding standard, August 2026).

assertions.text: In Abu Dhabi, compounding requires a Good Compounding Practice (GCP) certificate issued by the EDE.
assertions.quote: Ensure compliance with this Standard and related DoH regulations, and hold a valid, scope-banded Good Compounding Practice (GCP) certificate from EDE before performing any compounding activity.
assertions.note: The standard requires healthcare facilities to hold a valid GCP certificate issued by the EDE before performing any compounding activity.

assertions.text: Compounding using unapproved or unknown-source substances is prohibited in Abu Dhabi.
assertions.quote: Experimental or unverified compounding, the use of unapproved or unknown-source substances, investigational drugs (except where supplied and used under a DoH-approved clinical trial), and any product containing banned or EDE, MOHAP, DoH-restricted substances are prohibited.
assertions.note: The DoH standard strictly prohibits the use of unapproved or unknown-source substances in compounding.

assertions.text: Substances not on the DoH Registry for Compounded Substances are prohibited from routine compounding unless explicitly permitted by the DoH.
assertions.quote: Substances that are not listed on the DoH Registry for Compounded Substances (as permitted and/or under regulatory evaluation) shall not be used for routine compounding unless explicitly permitted by the DoH.
assertions.note: Substances not listed on the DoH Registry cannot be used for routine compounding without explicit DoH authorization.

units.text: In Abu Dhabi, the DoH treats peptides as emerging, non-monographed, high-risk substances: novel substances of unknown risk may be compounded only if monographed, a component of an approved medicine, or listed on the DoH Registry for Compounded Substances (DoH compounding standard, August 2026).

assertions.text: In Abu Dhabi, the DoH treats peptides as emerging, non-monographed, high-risk substances.
assertions.quote: A substance defined by risk signature rather than chemical name (e.g.,  peptides): no monograph, marketed ahead of approval, thin evidence,  identity or purity risk, or demand-driven uptake. Treated as high-risk and  non-default.
assertions.note: Supported by the DoH standard's definition of emerging and non-monographed substances.

assertions.text: Novel substances of unknown risk may be compounded only if monographed, a component of an approved medicine, or listed on the DoH Registry for Compounded Substances.
assertions.quote: Novel substances of unknown risk are considered experimental and prohibited unless the substance is  monographed, is an approved medicinal product component, or is listed on the DoH Registry for  Compounded Substances following regulatory review.
assertions.note: Supported by Section 3.3.3 of the DoH standard.

units.text: In Abu Dhabi, where emerging substances such as peptides are permitted, prescribing is limited to eligible facilities and credentialed prescribers for accepted indications, office-stock ordering to hospitals and DoH-approved specialty clinics, and compounding pharmacies must dispense only against individual prescriptions (DoH compounding standard, August 2026).

assertions.text: In Abu Dhabi, where emerging substances such as peptides are permitted, prescribing is limited to eligible facilities and credentialed prescribers for accepted indications.
assertions.quote: Where permitted, prescribing and administration shall be restricted to eligible facilities and appropriately credentialed prescribers in approved specialties, commensurate with the product’s risk classification, and limited to accepted indications and eligible populations, with mandatory monitoring, renewal controls, and reporting of adverse effects and quality defects through the DoH pharmacovigilance system, and subject to the availability of quality assurance and control testing.
assertions.note: The DoH compounding standard limits prescribing of permitted emerging substances to eligible facilities, credentialed prescribers, and accepted indications.

assertions.text: Office-stock ordering of permitted emerging substances is restricted to hospitals and DoH-approved specialty clinics, and compounding pharmacies must dispense only against individual prescriptions.
assertions.quote: Bulk (office-stock) ordering is restricted to hospitals and DoH-approved specialty clinics; patient-specific compounding pharmacies shall dispense only against an individual prescription and shall not supply office stock.
assertions.note: Bulk ordering is restricted to hospitals and approved specialty clinics, while compounding pharmacies may dispense only against individual prescriptions.

units.text: In Abu Dhabi, compounded peptide formulations may use only certified active ingredients imported under EDE oversight, clinics must hold technical agreements with licensed compounding pharmacies, and peptide products must be traceable from source to patient (DoH Circular 148/2026, 31 July 2026).

assertions.text: In Abu Dhabi, compounded peptide formulations may use only certified active ingredients imported under EDE oversight.
assertions.quote: Only certified active pharmaceutical ingredients (APIs) imported under EDE oversight shall be used in compounded peptide formulations, subject to DoH verification;
assertions.note: The circular requires that only certified APIs imported under EDE oversight be used in compounded peptide formulations.

assertions.text: Clinics must hold technical agreements with licensed compounding pharmacies.
assertions.quote: Clinics shall establish technical agreements with licensed compounding pharmacies to ensure traceability across the supply chain;
assertions.note: The circular states that clinics must establish technical agreements with licensed compounding pharmacies.

assertions.text: Peptide products must be traceable from source to patient.
assertions.quote: Full traceability of peptide products from source to patient shall be maintained to ensure patient safety and regulatory compliance;
assertions.note: The circular explicitly mandates full traceability of peptide products from source to patient.

units.text: In Dubai, the DHA prohibits using any peptide product intended for research use on humans or for therapeutic purposes outside a study or clinical trial approved by the competent authority (External Circular 0867, 29 July 2026).

assertions.text: In Dubai, the DHA prohibits using any peptide product intended for research use on humans or for therapeutic purposes outside a study or clinical trial approved by the competent authority.
assertions.quote:
It is prohibited to use any peptide product 
intended for research use  on humans or for 
therapeutic purposes, except within a study or 
clinical trial approved by the competent authority, 
and in accordance with its protocol and the 
necessary regulatory approvals applicable in the 
State.
assertions.note: The circular explicitly prohibits using research-use peptide products on humans or therapeutically outside an approved study or clinical trial.

units.text: In Dubai, facilities may not buy, accept or use peptide products from websites, social media, individual accounts or unlicensed or unverifiable suppliers, and products without full identification data (active substance, concentration, batch, expiry) may not be used (DHA External Circular 0867, 29 July 2026).

assertions.text: In Dubai, healthcare facilities may not purchase, accept, or use peptide products from websites, social media, individual accounts, or unlicensed or unverifiable suppliers.
assertions.quote: It is prohibited to purchase, accept, or use peptide products from websit es, social media platforms, individual accounts, or unlicensed or unverifiable suppliers.
assertions.note: DHA Circular 0867 explicitly bans purchasing, accepting, or using peptide products from websites, social media platforms, individual accounts, or unlicensed/unverifiable suppliers.

assertions.text: In Dubai, peptide products lacking full identification data (including active substance, concentration, batch, or expiration date) may not be used in healthcare facilities.
assertions.quote: with incomplete or ambiguous identification data, or that do not indicate the active substance, concentration, dose, batch, or expiration date, are considered high -risk products that may not be used in the facility.
assertions.note: The circular states that products lacking identification data or not indicating active substance, concentration, batch, or expiry are high-risk and cannot be used.

units.text: In the UAE, Federal Decree-Law 38/2024 brings cosmetics with a medical effect on the skin, hair or nails within its definition of medical products regulated by the EDE.
units.note: no cited source has readable text — nothing can be verified

units.text: In the UAE, the EDE registers 'healthcare products' not intended to diagnose, treat or prevent disease, including dietary supplements, herbal products and cosmetics with a medical effect, through a marketing authorisation valid for five years (EDE service page, read 25 Sep 2026).

assertions.text: In the UAE, the EDE registers healthcare products not intended to diagnose, treat, cure, or prevent disease.
assertions.quote: This service enables applicants to register healthcare products, including general pharmaceutical products, which are used for the promotion of general human health and are not intended for the diagnosis, treatment, cure, or prevention of any disease.
assertions.note: The EDE service description confirms healthcare products registered under this service are not intended for diagnosis, treatment, cure, or prevention of disease.

assertions.text: The scope of healthcare products covered includes dietary supplements, herbal products, and cosmetics with a medical effect.
assertions.quote: The scope includes dietary supplements, antiseptics and disinfectants, herbal products, and cosmetics with a medical effect.
assertions.note: The service page explicitly defines the scope to include these product categories.

assertions.text: The marketing authorisation certificate issued for healthcare products is valid for five years.
assertions.quote: Issue the marketing authorization certificate for healthcare products, valid for five years from the date of the committee’s approval.
assertions.note: The service process specifies that the marketing authorization certificate is valid for five years from committee approval.

units.text: In the UAE, whether a borderline product (for example a peptide serum) needs an EDE marketing authorisation, and in which category, is settled by an EDE classification letter based on the product's presentation, composition, use and design (EDE service page, read 25 Sep 2026).

assertions.text: In the UAE, whether a product requires an EDE marketing authorisation, and in which category, is determined by an EDE classification letter.
assertions.quote: The classification letter determines the regulatory category of the product in terms of the requirement for marketing authorization with the Emirates Drug Establishment.
assertions.note: The service page confirms that the classification letter determines the product's regulatory category regarding marketing authorization requirements.

assertions.text: In the UAE, EDE product classification is based on the product's presentation, composition, use, and design.
assertions.quote: This service allows the classification of products of all types and forms based on Presentation /Composition / Use and Design.
assertions.note: The EDE portal confirms that product classification is based on presentation, composition, use, and design.

units.text: In the UAE, ordinary cosmetics and personal-care products are a MoIAT-regulated product category under Cabinet Resolution 18/2014 (the UAE control system for cosmetics and personal care products), needing a conformity certificate backed by accredited test reports, a formula declaration and a product safety report.

assertions.text: In the UAE, ordinary cosmetics and personal-care products are a MoIAT-regulated product category under Cabinet Resolution 18/2014.
assertions.quote:
9النظام الإماراتي للرقابة على مستحضرات التجميل والعناية الشخصيةقرار مجلس الوزراء رقم (18)  لسنة2014Cosmetics and personal care
o	 Valid UAE Industry/Trade License.
assertions.note: MoIAT lists cosmetics and personal care under Cabinet Resolution No. 18 of 2014.

assertions.text: Conformity certification for cosmetics and personal-care products requires accredited test reports and a formula declaration.
assertions.quote:
o	 Test Report from accredited and recognized laboratory according to Gulf standard, UAE.S GSO 1943 
o	 Formula Declaration with ingredients and percentage issued by the manufacturer.
assertions.note: Required documents include test reports from an accredited laboratory and a manufacturer formula declaration.

assertions.text: Conformity certification for cosmetics and personal-care products requires a product safety report.
assertions.quote: o	 Product safety report according to Annex No. 3 of the cabinet resolution No. 18 of 2014
assertions.note: MoIAT requirements include a product safety report according to Annex 3 of Cabinet Resolution 18/2014.

units.text: In Abu Dhabi, the DoH classes topical cosmetic peptides with no systemic effect as low-risk products that stay under existing regulatory pathways, while systemic, regenerative or weakly evidenced peptides face enhanced controls (Circular 148/2026, 31 July 2026).

assertions.text: In Abu Dhabi, the DoH classes topical cosmetic peptides with no systemic effect as low-risk products that stay under existing regulatory pathways (Circular 148/2026, 31 July 2026).
assertions.quote: 1.Low-risk peptides Products: These include products that have no systematic effect (e.g., topical cosmetic peptides) which will remain subject to existing regulatory pathways.
assertions.note: DoH Circular 148/2026 specifies that low-risk peptide products, such as topical cosmetic peptides with no systemic effect, remain subject to existing regulatory pathways.

assertions.text: In Abu Dhabi, the DoH subjects systemic, regenerative, or weakly evidenced peptides to enhanced regulatory controls (Circular 148/2026, 31 July 2026).
assertions.quote: 2.Moderate- and high-risk peptides: including products that have systemic effects (clinical), regenerative applications, or products supported only by emerging or insufficient clinical evidence, are subject to enhanced regulatory controls, strengthened quality assurance requirements, and stricter clinical governance, consistent with the above standard.
assertions.note: The circular classifies systemic, regenerative, and insufficiently evidenced peptides as moderate- and high-risk products subject to enhanced regulatory controls.

units.text: In the UAE, food supplements are medical products under Federal Decree-Law 38/2024, defined as oral products that support the diet and do not treat, diagnose or prevent disease.
units.note: no cited source has readable text — nothing can be verified

units.text: In the UAE, advertising or promoting any medical product by any means, including social media, requires EDE approval, and advertising controlled or semi-controlled products to the public is prohibited (Federal Decree-Law 38/2024, Art. 44).
units.note: no cited source has readable text — nothing can be verified

units.text: In the UAE, an EDE licence to advertise a medical product requires a valid EDE marketing authorisation for the product (only products exempted by the Cabinet under Art. 5(3) of Federal Decree-Law 38/2024 are excused), a licensed pharmaceutical or healthcare establishment as applicant, and truthful, evidence-based content matching the approved indications (EDE service page, read 25 Sep 2026).

assertions.text: An EDE licence to advertise a medical product requires a valid EDE marketing authorisation, with an exemption for products exempted by the Cabinet under Art. 5(3) of Federal Decree-Law 38/2024.
assertions.quote: 1. A valid Marketing Authorisation from EDE must exist for the medical product to be advertised. Products exempted from the Marketing Authorisation requirement under the provisions of Clause (3) of Article (5) of Federal Decree-Law No. (38) are excluded from this condition
assertions.note: The service page confirms the marketing authorisation condition and the Article 5(3) exemption, but does not mention that exemptions are issued by the Cabinet.

assertions.text: The applicant for an EDE medical product advertisement licence must be a licensed pharmaceutical or healthcare establishment.
assertions.quote: 2. The applicant must be a licensed pharmaceutical establishment or a licensed healthcare establishment
assertions.note: The service page explicitly requires the applicant to be a licensed pharmaceutical or healthcare establishment.

assertions.text: Medical product advertising content must be truthful, non-misleading, and supported by evidence reflecting the approved indications.
assertions.quote: 3. The advertising material must be truthful, non-misleading, and supported by evidence reflecting the approved information and approved indications of the medical product
assertions.note: The service page specifies that advertising material must be truthful, non-misleading, and supported by evidence reflecting approved indications.

units.text: In Dubai, the DHA bans misleading or unproven peptide claims, including anti-aging, cell regeneration, weight loss, muscle building and improved appearance, unless the use is within the product's approved status, and requires any promotion of unregistered materials, including through influencers or social media, to stop (29 July 2026).

assertions.text: In Dubai, the DHA bans misleading or unproven peptide claims, including anti-aging, cell regeneration, weight loss, muscle building, and improved appearance, unless the use is within the product's approved status.
assertions.quote: It is prohibited to make misleading or scientifically unproven claims, including claims related to anti -aging or cell regeneration, or improving immunity, energy, or focus, or weight loss, muscle building, improving athletic performance, treating hormonal or sexual disorders, or improving appearance or public health in a guaranteed or risk -free manner, or any other therapeutic or physiological use, unless such use is approved and permitted within the regulatory status of the product.
assertions.note: The DHA circular prohibits misleading or scientifically unproven peptide claims across these indications unless approved within the product's regulatory status.

assertions.text: The DHA requires any promotion of unregistered materials, including through influencers or social media, to stop.
assertions.quote: Any advertising, promotion, or direct or indirect marketing of unregistered or unlicensed materials must be stopped, whether through the health facility, doctors, websites, social media platforms, phone messages, promotional offers, influencers, or any other media outlet.
assertions.note: The circular instructs that all marketing and promotion of unregistered or unlicensed materials, including via social media and influencers, must cease.

units.text: In Abu Dhabi, healthcare providers may not promote peptide therapies with misleading or unsubstantiated claims, or advertise, market or publish media content about them without prior approval from the DoH and relevant authorities (Circular 148/2026, 31 July 2026).

assertions.text: In Abu Dhabi, healthcare providers may not promote peptide therapies with misleading or unsubstantiated claims (Circular 148/2026, 31 July 2026).
assertions.note: DoH Circular 148/2026 explicitly prohibits healthcare providers from promoting peptide therapies through misleading or unsubstantiated therapeutic claims.

assertions.text: In Abu Dhabi, healthcare providers and facilities may not advertise, market, or publish media content relating to peptide therapies without prior approval from the DoH and relevant authorities (Circular 148/2026, 31 July 2026).
assertions.note: The circular requires prior approval from DoH and relevant authorities before advertising, marketing, or publishing media content concerning peptide therapies.

units.text: In Abu Dhabi, emerging and non-monographed compounded substances such as peptides may not be advertised, promoted or marketed, directly or indirectly, to patients or healthcare professionals (DoH compounding standard, August 2026).

assertions.text: In Abu Dhabi, emerging and non-monographed compounded substances such as peptides may not be advertised, promoted, or marketed directly or indirectly to patients or healthcare professionals under the DoH compounding standard.
assertions.quote: 3.3.1 Emerging and non-monographed substances shall not be advertised, promoted, or marketed directly or indirectly to patients or healthcare professionals.
assertions.note: Section 3.3.1 explicitly prohibits advertising, promoting, or marketing emerging and non-monographed substances directly or indirectly to patients or healthcare professionals.

units.text: In Dubai, peptide products may be prescribed, dispensed or administered only by licensed, authorised professionals in a licensed facility, and injections or IV therapies for 'wellness', 'recovery', 'detoxification' or 'energy enhancement' are not permitted without a documented medical indication and treatment plan (DHA External Circular 0867, 29 July 2026).

assertions.text: In Dubai, peptide products may be prescribed, dispensed or administered only by licensed, authorised professionals in a licensed facility.
assertions.quote:
No peptide product (licensed and authorized) shall 
be prescribed, dispensed, or administered except 
by a health professional licensed and authorized  
to do so, working within the limits of their 
professional competence and in a licensed health 
facility, provided that the relevant competence 
and training are available.
assertions.note: The circular explicitly restricts prescribing, dispensing, or administering peptide products to licensed and authorized health professionals in a licensed facility.

assertions.text: Injections or IV therapies for 'wellness', 'recovery', 'detoxification' or 'energy enhancement' are not permitted without a documented medical indication and treatment plan.
assertions.quote:
In particular, it is not permitted to prescribe or 
administer intravenous fluids, injections, or 
intravenous therapies for the purposes of 
"wellness," "recovery," "detoxification," "energy 
enhancement," or other non-therapeutic purposes, 
except when there is a documented medical 
indication and a clear treatment plan based on the 
clinical assessment stipulated in the previous 
point.
assertions.note: The circular explicitly prohibits IV therapies and injections for wellness, recovery, detox, or energy enhancement without a documented medical indication and clear treatment plan.

units.text: In Abu Dhabi, physicians may prescribe peptide therapies only for clinical indications supported by available scientific evidence, after a documented eligibility assessment and with informed consent that covers benefits, uncertainties, risks, alternatives and the product's regulatory approval status (DoH Circular 148/2026, 31 July 2026).

assertions.text: In Abu Dhabi, physicians are required to prescribe peptide therapies only for clinical indications supported by available scientific evidence.
assertions.quote:
Accordingly, all physicians are required to prescribe 
peptide therapies only for the appropriate clinical 
indications supported by available scientific 
evidence, and shall adhere to the following:
assertions.note: DoH Circular 148/2026 explicitly requires physicians to prescribe peptide therapies only for indications supported by available scientific evidence.

assertions.text: Physicians must conduct and document an eligibility assessment and obtain informed consent covering expected benefits, uncertainties, risks, alternatives, and regulatory approval status before initiating peptide therapy.
assertions.quote:
1. Conduct and document patient eligibility 
assessment and clinical evaluation prior to 
initiation of therapy;
2. Obtain documented patient informed 
consent specific to peptide therapy, 
including expected benefits, uncertainties, 
potential risks, available alternatives, and the 
product’s regulatory approval status;
assertions.note: The circular mandates documented pre-treatment eligibility evaluation and informed consent detailing benefits, uncertainties, risks, alternatives, and approval status.

units.text: In the UAE, the EDE warned on 20 Jul 2026 (Circular 31/2026) that 1,659 packs of Mounjaro and Ozempic stolen from a German wholesaler are outside the legitimate supply chain, and told the public to buy these medicines only from licensed pharmacies.

assertions.text: In the UAE, the EDE warned on 20 Jul 2026 (Circular 31/2026) that 1,659 packs of Mounjaro and Ozempic stolen from a German wholesaler are outside the legitimate supply chain.
assertions.quote: A total of 1,659 packs of Mounjaro® (tirzepatide) and Ozempic® (semaglutide) were identified as missing from the warehouse and are considered to be outside the legitimate pharmaceutical supply chain.
assertions.note: EDE Circular 31/2026 confirms 1,659 packs of Mounjaro and Ozempic stolen from a German warehouse are outside the legitimate supply chain.

assertions.text: The EDE told the public to buy these medicines only from licensed pharmacies.
assertions.quote: To protect public health,  the Emirates Drug Establishment (EDE) warns the public not to purchase these products from unknown or unauthorized sellers and to obtain them only through licensed pharmacies and legitimate supply channels.
assertions.note: The circular directs the public to obtain these medicines only through licensed pharmacies and legitimate supply channels.

units.text: In Dubai, the DHA sent MOHAP Circular 06 of 2025 on the serious safety concerns of Melanotan II ('Barbie drug') to all private health facilities for adherence (25 Jun 2025).

assertions.text: On 25 June 2025, the Dubai Health Authority (DHA) issued MOHAP Circular 06 of 2025 regarding the serious safety concerns of Melanotan II ('Barbie drug') to private health facilities in Dubai for adherence.
assertions.quote: Referring to the above subject, DHA notifies all health facilities regarding the circulars issued by the MOHAP for perusal and adherence to what is stated.
assertions.note: The circular published on 25 June 2025 notifies private health facilities in Dubai of MOHAP Circular 06 of 2025 concerning Melanotan II for adherence.

units.text: In Brazil, Ozempic (semaglutide, Novo Nordisk) has been registered by ANVISA since 6 Aug 2018; its label (Sep 2026 check) indicates it only for adults with inadequately controlled type 2 diabetes, including kidney-outcome risk reduction in type 2 diabetes with chronic kidney disease.
units.note: no cited source has readable text — nothing can be verified

units.text: In Brazil, Wegovy (semaglutide, Novo Nordisk) has been registered by ANVISA since 2 Jan 2023 for chronic weight management in adults (BMI ≥30, or ≥27 with a weight-related comorbidity) and in adolescents aged 12 or over with obesity and body weight above 60 kg.
units.note: no cited source has readable text — nothing can be verified

units.text: In Brazil, the semaglutide patent expired on 20 Mar 2026 and ANVISA registered the first synthetic semaglutide pen (Ozivy, EMS) on 26 May 2026, followed by five more synthetic pens on 29 Jul 2026; these copies are indicated for type 2 diabetes, not weight management. ANVISA's register listed 15 active semaglutide products on 25 Sep 2026.

assertions.text: In Brazil, the semaglutide patent expired on 20 Mar 2026.
assertions.quote: O medicamento usa o mesmo princípio ativo do Ozempic, que teve sua patente expirada em 20 de março.
assertions.note: ANVISA's May 2026 announcement confirms the patent expired on March 20.

assertions.text: ANVISA registered the first synthetic semaglutide pen (Ozivy) on 26 May 2026.
assertions.quote: A Agência Nacional de Vigilância Sanitária (Anvisa) publicou nesta terça-feira (26/5) o registro do medicamento Ozivy. O produto é a primeira caneta de semaglutida sintética análoga ao produto biológico liberado para comercialização no Brasil.
assertions.note: The agency announced the approval of Ozivy as the first synthetic semaglutide pen on 26 May 2026.

assertions.text: The registration for Ozivy was requested by the EMS laboratory.
assertions.quote: O pedido de registro foi feito pelo laboratório EMS/SA e seguiu a ordem cronológica e de prioridade para medicamentos do tipo GLP-1, popularmente conhecidos como canetas emagrecedoras.
assertions.note: The source confirms that the registration request for Ozivy was submitted by EMS/SA.

assertions.text: ANVISA registered five additional synthetic semaglutide pens on 29 Jul 2026.
assertions.quote: Nesta quarta-feira (29/7), a Agência Nacional de Vigilância Sanitária (Anvisa) aprovou o registro de cinco novos medicamentos injetáveis agonistas do receptor de GLP-1.
assertions.note: On 29 July 2026, ANVISA registered five new synthetic GLP-1 pens containing semaglutide.

assertions.text: These synthetic copies are indicated for type 2 diabetes, not weight management.
assertions.quote: Os medicamentos aprovados foram registrados por comparação com o produto biológico Ozempic, sendo indicados para o tratamento de pacientes adultos com diabetes mellitus tipo 2 insuficientemente controlado.
assertions.note: The approvals specify that the synthetic semaglutide pens are indicated for insufficiently controlled type 2 diabetes mellitus.

assertions.text: ANVISA's register listed 15 active semaglutide products on 25 Sep 2026.
assertions.note: The search database source is unavailable and the figure is not mentioned in the other provided sources.

Any medicinal product which is prepared in a pharmacy in accordance with the prescriptions of a pharmacopoeia and is intended to be supplied directly to the patients served by the pharmacy in question (commonly known as the officinal formula).
assertions.note: Article 3(2) of Directive 2001/83/EC excludes officinal formula preparations from the Directive's scope.

units.text: EU law exempts pharmacists who prepare medicines solely for retail supply in dispensing pharmacies from the manufacturing authorisation that all other manufacture needs (Directive 2001/83/EC, Article 40(2)).

assertions.text: Under EU law, pharmacists who prepare medicines solely for retail supply in dispensing pharmacies are exempt from the manufacturing authorisation required for manufacture (Directive 2001/83/EC, Article 40(2)).
assertions.quote: However, such authorization shall not be required for preparation, dividing up, changes in packaging or presentation where these processes are carried out, solely for retail supply, by pharmacists in dispensing pharmacies or by persons legally authorized in the Member States to carry out such processes.
assertions.note: Directive 2001/83/EC explicitly exempts preparation solely for retail supply by pharmacists in dispensing pharmacies from the manufacturing authorisation requirement.

units.text: In the EU, no medicine may be placed on a member state's market without a national marketing authorisation or an EU-wide (central) authorisation (Directive 2001/83/EC, Article 6(1)).

assertions.text: In the EU, no medicinal product may be placed on a member state's market without a national marketing authorisation or an EU-wide authorisation under Regulation (EC) No 726/2004.
assertions.note: Directive 2001/83/EC Article 6(1) provides that no medicinal product may be placed on a member state's market without a national or centralized marketing authorisation.

units.text: EU law lets each member state, under its own legislation, allow an unauthorised medicine for an individual patient on a bona fide unsolicited order from an authorised health professional, under that professional's direct personal responsibility (Directive 2001/83/EC, Article 5(1)).

assertions.text: Under EU Directive 2001/83/EC, Article 5(1), a Member State may, under its legislation in force, exclude from the Directive's provisions (allow) medicinal products supplied in response to a bona fide unsolicited order from an authorised health professional for an individual patient under that professional's direct personal responsibility.
assertions.quote: A Member State may, in accordance with legislation in force and to fulfil special needs, exclude from the provisions of this Directive medicinal products supplied in response to a bona fide unsolicited order, formulated in accordance with the specifications of an authorised health-care professional and for use by an individual patient under his direct personal responsibility.
assertions.note: Directive 2001/83/EC Article 5(1) directly provides this exemption.

units.text: EMA and HMA's shortage steering group asked EU prescribers in June 2024 to prescribe GLP-1 receptor agonists only for their authorised uses and said these medicines are not approved for, and should not be used for, cosmetic weight loss.

assertions.text: In June 2024, EMA and HMA's shortage steering group recommended that healthcare professionals prescribe GLP-1 receptor agonists only in line with their authorised uses.
assertions.quote: The MSSG therefore recommends that healthcare professionals prescribe these medicines in line with their authorised use(s) only, taking into account guidance issued by national authorities or applicable national therapeutic guidelines.
assertions.note: The MSSG issued recommendations in June 2024 advising prescribers to use GLP-1 receptor agonists only for authorised indications.

assertions.text: The steering group stated that GLP-1 receptor agonists are not approved for, and should not be used for, cosmetic weight loss.
assertions.quote: GLP-1 receptor agonists are not approved for, and should not be used for, cosmetic weight loss, i.e. use for weight loss in people without obesity or people with overweight who do not have weight-related health problems.
assertions.note: The statement explicitly notes that GLP-1 receptor agonists are not approved and should not be used for cosmetic weight loss.

units.text: Under EU law a product is a medicine by presentation (presented as treating or preventing disease) or by function (restoring, correcting or modifying physiological functions by a pharmacological, immunological or metabolic action), and where a product could be both a medicine and another regulated product, medicines law applies (Directive 2001/83/EC, Articles 1(2) and 2(2)).

assertions.text: Under EU law, a product is a medicine by presentation (presented as treating or preventing disease) or by function (restoring, correcting or modifying physiological functions by a pharmacological, immunological or metabolic action) (Directive 2001/83/EC, Article 1(2)).
assertions.quote:
(a) 

Any substance or combination of substances presented as having properties for treating or preventing disease in human beings; or

(b) 

Any substance or combination of substances which may be used in or administered to human beings either with a view to restoring, correcting or modifying physiological functions by exerting a pharmacological, immunological or metabolic action, or to making a medical diagnosis.
assertions.note: Directive 2001/83/EC Article 1(2) defines a medicinal product by presentation or by physiological function.

assertions.text: Under EU law, where a product could be both a medicine and another regulated product, medicines law applies (Directive 2001/83/EC, Article 2(2)).
assertions.quote: In cases of doubt, where, taking into account all its characteristics, a product may fall within the definition of a ‘medicinal product’ and within the definition of a product covered by other Community legislation the provisions of this Directive shall apply.
assertions.note: Directive 2001/83/EC Article 2(2) specifies that where a product falls under both medicinal product and other Community legislation definitions, the Directive applies.

units.text: The research exclusion in Directive 2001/83/EC concerns medicinal products intended for research and development trials and is without prejudice to EU clinical-trials law (Article 3(3)).

assertions.text: The research exclusion in Directive 2001/83/EC concerns medicinal products intended for research and development trials and is without prejudice to EU clinical-trials law (Article 3(3)).
assertions.note: Article 3(3) excludes medicinal products intended for research and development trials from Directive 2001/83/EC without prejudice to Directive 2001/20/EC.

units.text: On 3 September 2025 EMA and HMA warned of a sharp rise in illegal medicines sold online and on social media as GLP-1 receptor agonists (semaglutide, liraglutide, tirzepatide); these products are unauthorised and may not contain the stated substance.

assertions.text: On 3 September 2025, EMA and HMA warned of a sharp rise in illegal medicines sold online and on social media as GLP-1 receptor agonists (semaglutide, liraglutide, tirzepatide).
assertions.quote: In recent months there has been a sharp rise in the number of illegal medicines marketed as GLP-1 receptor agonists such as semaglutide, liraglutide and tirzepatide for weight loss and diabetes. These products, often sold via fraudulent websites and promoted on social media, are not authorised and do not meet necessary standards of quality, safety and efficacy.
assertions.note: The EMA/HMA communication on 3 September 2025 warns of a sharp rise in illegal medicines marketed as semaglutide, liraglutide, and tirzepatide.

assertions.text: These illegal products are unauthorised and may not contain the stated substance.
assertions.quote: Such illegal products pose a serious risk to public health. They may not contain the claimed active substance at all and may contain harmful levels of other substances.
assertions.note: The warning confirms that these products are not authorised and may not contain the claimed active substance.

units.text: In the EU, anything intended to be ingested, inhaled, injected or implanted is not a cosmetic (Regulation (EC) No 1223/2009, Article 2(2)), so an injected peptide can never be a cosmetic.

assertions.text: Under EU Regulation (EC) No 1223/2009, Article 2(2), a substance or mixture intended to be ingested, inhaled, injected or implanted into the human body is not considered a cosmetic product.
assertions.quote: For the purposes of point (a) of paragraph 1, a substance or mixture intended to be ingested, inhaled, injected or implanted into the human body shall not be considered to be a cosmetic product.
assertions.note: Article 2(2) explicitly excludes substances or mixtures intended to be ingested, inhaled, injected, or implanted from the definition of cosmetic products.

assertions.text: In the EU, an injected peptide cannot be classified as a cosmetic product.
assertions.quote: For the purposes of point (a) of paragraph 1, a substance or mixture intended to be ingested, inhaled, injected or implanted into the human body shall not be considered to be a cosmetic product.
assertions.note: Because substances or mixtures intended for injection are excluded from being cosmetics under Article 2(2), an injected peptide cannot be a cosmetic.

units.text: The EU borderline manual (version 5.4, November 2024, retained in 5.5) says a product in a vial or ampoule for injection cannot be a cosmetic, and one sold as a cosmetic must be clearly for external use and not marketed with a device allowing injection or delivery below the epidermis.

assertions.text: The EU borderline manual (version 5.4, November 2024, retained in version 5.5) states that a product in a vial or ampoule for injection cannot be a cosmetic product.
assertions.quote: If a substance or mixture presented in a vial or ampoule is for use by injection, then the product cannot be considered to meet the definition of a cosmetic product by virtue of Article 2(2) of the Cosmetics Regulation which provides that “ a substance or a mixture intended to be (…) injected or implanted into the human body shall not be considered to be a cosmetic product”.
assertions.note: Section 3.3.34 of the manual confirms that products presented in a vial or ampoule for use by injection cannot meet the definition of a cosmetic product.

assertions.text: According to the EU borderline manual, a product in a vial or ampoule sold as a cosmetic must be clearly for external use and not marketed with a device allowing injection or delivery below the epidermis.
assertions.quote: Furthermore, the product should not be marketed with a device which could allow the injection of this product or its delivery below the epidermis (77).
assertions.note: The manual requires presentation/instructions to clearly indicate external use only and prohibits marketing with devices that allow injection or sub-epidermal delivery.

units.text: Whether an EU product is a cosmetic is decided case by case by national authorities; the borderline manual says an anti-wrinkle product that significantly restores, corrects or modifies physiological functions by a pharmacological, immunological or metabolic action does not qualify as a cosmetic (June 2025).

assertions.text: Whether an EU product is a cosmetic is decided case by case by national authorities.
assertions.quote: IT IS FOR THE NATIONAL COMPETENT AUTHORITIES AND NATIONAL COURTS TO ASSESS ON A CASE -BY-CASE BASIS , WHICH REGULATORY FRAMEWORK APPLIES.
assertions.note: The borderline manual states that national competent authorities and courts determine which regulatory framework applies on a case-by-case basis.

assertions.text: The borderline manual (June 2025) says an anti-wrinkle product that significantly restores, corrects or modifies physiological functions by a pharmacological, immunological or metabolic action does not qualify as a cosmetic.
assertions.quote: However, some products presented as anti -wrinkle may  significantly restore, correct or modify physiological functions by exerting a pharmacological, immunological or metabolic action. In that case, they would not qualify as cosmetics.
assertions.note: Section 3.3.21 of the June 2025 borderline manual confirms that anti-wrinkle products with such significant physiological actions do not qualify as cosmetics.

units.text: Before an EU cosmetic is placed on the market it needs a responsible person in the EU, a safety assessment with a cosmetic product safety report, and electronic notification to the Commission (Regulation (EC) No 1223/2009, Articles 4, 10 and 13).

assertions.text: Before an EU cosmetic product is placed on the market, a responsible person within the EU must be designated under Article 4 of Regulation (EC) No 1223/2009.
assertions.quote: Only cosmetic products for which a legal or natural person is designated within the Community as ‘responsible person’ shall be placed on the market.
assertions.note: Article 4(1) requires a designated responsible person within the Community before a cosmetic product is placed on the market.

assertions.text: Before placing a cosmetic product on the market, the responsible person must ensure it has undergone a safety assessment and that a cosmetic product safety report is set up under Article 10.
assertions.quote: In order to demonstrate that a cosmetic product complies with Article 3, the responsible person shall, prior to placing a cosmetic product on the market, ensure that the cosmetic product has undergone a safety assessment on the basis of the relevant information and that a cosmetic product safety report is set up in accordance with Annex I.
assertions.note: Article 10(1) mandates a safety assessment and cosmetic product safety report prior to placing the product on the market.

assertions.text: Before placing a cosmetic product on the market, electronic notification must be submitted to the Commission under Article 13.
assertions.quote: Prior to placing the cosmetic product on the market the responsible person shall submit, by electronic means, the following information to the Commission:
assertions.note: Article 13(1) requires information to be submitted electronically to the Commission prior to placing the product on the market.

units.text: EU cosmetic claims must be supported by adequate and verifiable evidence, and a claim that extrapolates an ingredient's properties (for example a peptide's) to the finished product needs evidence such as the ingredient's presence at an effective concentration (Regulation (EU) No 655/2013).

assertions.text: Under EU cosmetic regulations, claims must be supported by adequate and verifiable evidence.
assertions.quote: Claims for cosmetic products, whether explicit or implicit, shall be supported by adequate and verifiable evidence regardless of the types of evidential support used to substantiate them, including where appropriate expert assessments.
assertions.note: Regulation (EU) No 655/2013 specifies that cosmetic product claims must be supported by adequate and verifiable evidence.

assertions.text: Under Regulation (EU) No 655/2013, extrapolating an ingredient's properties to the finished product requires evidence such as demonstrating the ingredient's presence at an effective concentration.
assertions.quote: A claim extrapolating (explicitly or implicitly) ingredient properties to the finished product shall be supported by adequate and verifiable evidence, such as by demonstrating the presence of the ingredient at an effective concentration.
assertions.note: Regulation (EU) No 655/2013 explicitly requires adequate and verifiable evidence, such as presence at an effective concentration, when extrapolating ingredient properties to the finished product.

units.text: In the EU, food supplements are foods that supplement the normal diet, are concentrated sources of nutrients or other substances with a nutritional or physiological effect, and are sold in measured doses such as capsules, tablets or sachets (Directive 2002/46/EC, Article 2(a)).

assertions.text: Under EU Directive 2002/46/EC, Article 2(a), food supplements are defined as foodstuffs intended to supplement the normal diet, which are concentrated sources of nutrients or other substances with a nutritional or physiological effect, and are marketed in dose forms such as capsules, tablets, or sachets.
assertions.quote: ‘food supplements’ means foodstuffs the purpose of which is to supplement the normal diet and which are concentrated sources of nutrients or other substances with a nutritional or physiological effect, alone or in combination, marketed in dose form, namely forms such as capsules, pastilles, tablets, pills and other similar forms, sachets of powder
assertions.note: Directive 2002/46/EC, Article 2(a) explicitly defines food supplements using these terms and examples.

units.text: In the EU, a health claim on a food is prohibited unless it is authorised and included in the EU lists of authorised claims (Regulation (EC) No 1924/2006, Article 10(1)).

assertions.text: In the EU, a health claim on a food is prohibited unless it is authorised and included in the EU lists of authorised claims pursuant to Regulation (EC) No 1924/2006, Article 10(1).
assertions.quote: Health claims shall be prohibited unless they comply with the general requirements in Chapter II and the specific requirements in this Chapter and are authorised in accordance with this Regulation and included in the lists of authorised claims provided for in Articles 13 and 14.
assertions.note: Article 10(1) explicitly states that health claims are prohibited unless authorised under the regulation and included in the lists provided for in Articles 13 and 14.

units.text: In the EU, food information, including advertising, must not attribute to any food the property of preventing, treating or curing a human disease (Regulation (EU) No 1169/2011, Article 7(3) and (4)).

assertions.text: In the EU, food information, including advertising, must not attribute to any food the property of preventing, treating or curing a human disease under Regulation (EU) No 1169/2011.
assertions.quote: Subject to derogations provided for by Union law applicable to natural mineral waters and foods for particular nutritional uses, food information shall not attribute to any food the property of preventing, treating or curing a human disease, nor refer to such properties.
assertions.note: Regulation (EU) No 1169/2011 prohibits food information from attributing disease prevention, treatment, or cure to any food, extended to advertising by Article 7(4).

units.text: EU law requires member states to prohibit any advertising of a medicine that has no marketing authorisation, and advertising of authorised medicines must match the summary of product characteristics (Directive 2001/83/EC, Article 87).

assertions.text: EU law requires member states to prohibit any advertising of a medicine that has no marketing authorisation.
assertions.quote: Member States shall prohibit any advertising of a medicinal product in respect of which a marketing authorization has not been granted in accordance with Community law.
assertions.note: Directive 2001/83/EC requires Member States to prohibit advertising of medicinal products lacking a marketing authorization.

assertions.text: Advertising of authorised medicines must match the summary of product characteristics under EU law.
assertions.quote: All parts of the advertising of a medicinal product must comply with the particulars listed in the summary of product characteristics.
assertions.note: Directive 2001/83/EC requires all parts of advertising to comply with the summary of product characteristics.

units.text: EU law requires member states to prohibit advertising of prescription-only medicines to the general public (Directive 2001/83/EC, Article 88(1)(a)); 'advertising' includes any inducement designed to promote prescription, supply, sale or consumption (Article 86(1)).

assertions.text: EU law requires member states to prohibit advertising of prescription-only medicines to the general public (Directive 2001/83/EC, Article 88(1)(a)).
assertions.quote:
Member States shall prohibit the advertising to the general public of medicinal products which:

(a) 

are available on medical prescription only, in accordance with Title VI;

(b) 

contain substances defined as psychotropic or narcotic by international convention, such as the United Nations Conventions of 1961 and 1971.
assertions.note: Directive 2001/83/EC Article 88(1)(a) requires member states to prohibit advertising to the general public of medicinal products available on medical prescription only.

assertions.text: Under Directive 2001/83/EC, Article 86(1), 'advertising' includes any inducement designed to promote prescription, supply, sale or consumption.
assertions.quote: For the purposes of this Title, ‘advertising of medicinal products’ shall include any form of door-to-door information, canvassing activity or inducement designed to promote the prescription, supply, sale or consumption of medicinal products; it shall include in particular:
assertions.note: Directive 2001/83/EC Article 86(1) defines advertising to include any inducement designed to promote the prescription, supply, sale or consumption of medicinal products.

units.text: EU audiovisual law bans audiovisual commercial communications for prescription-only medicines and medical treatment, and video-sharing platforms must take measures to apply this to advertising on their services, including advertising they do not sell themselves (Directive 2010/13/EU, Articles 9(1)(f) and 28b(2)).

assertions.text: EU audiovisual law bans audiovisual commercial communications for prescription-only medicines and medical treatment.
assertions.quote: audiovisual commercial communications for medicinal products and medical treatment available only on prescription in the Member State within whose jurisdiction the media service provider falls shall be prohibited;
assertions.note: Directive 2010/13/EU explicitly prohibits audiovisual commercial communications for medicinal products and medical treatments available only on prescription.

recheck.note: Directive 2010/13/EU explicitly prohibits audiovisual commercial communications for medicinal products and medical treatments available only on prescription.

assertions.text: Video-sharing platform providers must take appropriate measures to comply with Article 9(1) requirements for audiovisual commercial communications on their services that are not marketed, sold, or arranged by them.
assertions.quote: Member States shall ensure that the video-sharing platform providers under their jurisdiction take appropriate measures to comply with the requirements set out in Article 9(1) with respect to audiovisual commercial communications that are not marketed, sold or arranged by those video-sharing platform providers, taking into account the limited control exercised by those video-sharing platforms over those audiovisual commercial communications.
assertions.note: Article 28b(2) requires Member States to ensure platforms take appropriate measures to comply with Article 9(1) for communications they do not market, sell, or arrange.
