Terapêutica hormonal de substituição (THS) para os sintomas de deficiência de estrogénios em 
mulheres pós-menopáusicas.
assertions.note: Section 4.1 of the SmPC covers only symptoms of oestrogen deficiency in postmenopausal women, with no indication for skin.

units.text: In Portugal, an oral collagen product sold as a food supplement must be notified to DGAV before it is placed on the market; notification involves no evaluation of the product or its label, so it is not an authorisation (DGAV, read 25 Sep 2026).

assertions.text: In Portugal, an oral food supplement must be notified to DGAV before it is placed on the market.
assertions.quote: Os Suplementos Alimentares têm de ser notificados à DGAV , antes de serem colocados no mercado nacional, mesmo os que já se encontram comercializados noutro Estado-Membro da UE, de acordo com o “ Procedimento de notificação de suplementos alimentares “.
assertions.note: DGAV states that food supplements must be notified prior to being placed on the national market.

assertions.text: Notification to DGAV involves no evaluation of the product or validation of its labeling.
assertions.quote: Não existe avaliação do produto ou validação da rotulagem, sendo que o controlo é feito posteriormente e por amostragem, podendo ser efetuado a qualquer momento.
assertions.note: The notification procedure explicitely notes that there is no evaluation of the product or validation of the labeling.

assertions.text: Notification to DGAV does not constitute an authorisation.
assertions.quote: A inexistência de resposta significa que a DGAV aceitou a submissão do processo, mas não significa que tenham sido verificados os requisitos legais, pelo que, em caso algum, o operador poderá concluir que o produto se encontra autorizado ou que se encontra conforme.
assertions.note: The guidelines state that acceptance of notification in no way allows the operator to conclude that the product is authorised.

units.text: In Portugal, a magistral formula is a medicine prepared in a community or hospital pharmacy on a medical prescription naming the patient, and every compounded medicine is prepared and dispensed under a pharmacist's responsibility (Decreto-Lei 95/2004, Art 1).

assertions.text: Under Portuguese law (Decreto-Lei 95/2004, Art 1), a magistral formula is defined as a medicine prepared in a community or hospital pharmacy according to a medical prescription specifying the patient.
assertions.quote: b) «Fórmula magistral» o medicamento preparado em farmácia de oficina ou nos serviços farmacêuticos hospitalares segundo receita médica que especifica o doente a quem o medicamento se destina;
assertions.note: Article 1(2)(b) defines a magistral formula as a medicine prepared in a community pharmacy or hospital pharmaceutical services according to a medical prescription specifying the patient.

assertions.text: Under Portuguese law (Decreto-Lei 95/2004, Art 1), compounded medicines are defined as any magistral formula or officinal preparation prepared and dispensed under a pharmacist's responsibility.
assertions.quote: a) «Medicamento manipulado» qualquer fórmula magistral ou preparado oficinal preparado e dispensado sob a responsabilidade de um farmacêutico;
assertions.note: Article 1(2)(a) explicitly defines compounded medicine as any magistral formula or officinal preparation prepared and dispensed under the responsibility of a pharmacist.

units.text: In Portugal, a physician who prescribes a magistral formula must satisfy themselves of its safety and efficacy, including possible interactions (Decreto-Lei 95/2004, Art 3(1)).

assertions.text: In Portugal, a physician who prescribes a magistral formula must satisfy themselves of its safety and efficacy, including possible interactions (Decreto-Lei 95/2004, Art 3(1)).
assertions.quote: Ao prescrever uma fórmula magistral, o médico deve certificar-se da sua segurança e eficácia, verificando, designadamente, a possibilidade de existência de interacções que coloquem em causa a acção do medicamento ou a segurança do doente.
assertions.note: Article 3(1) of Decreto-Lei 95/2004 establishes that a physician prescribing a magistral formula must ensure its safety and efficacy, particularly checking for possible interactions.

units.text: In Portugal, compounded medicines may only use raw materials listed in the Portuguese or European pharmacopoeia, another European pharmacopoeia or compendial scientific documentation, and a compounded medicine containing any other raw material may not be prescribed (Decreto-Lei 95/2004, Art 6).

assertions.text: In Portugal, compounded medicines may only use raw materials listed in the Portuguese or European pharmacopoeia, another European pharmacopoeia, or compendial scientific documentation.
assertions.quote:
1 - Só podem ser utilizadas na prep aração de um medicamento manipulado 
matérias-primas inscritas na Farmacopeia  Portuguesa, nas farmacopeias de outros 
Estados Partes na Convenção Relativa à El aboração de Uma Farmacopeia Europeia, na 
Farmacopeia Europeia ou na documentação científica compendial e desde que os 
medicamentos que as contenham não haja m sido objecto de qualquer decisão de 
suspensão ou revogação da respectiva auto rização, adoptada por uma autoridade 
competente para o efeito.
assertions.note: Decreto-Lei 95/2004, Art 6(1) restricts raw materials used in compounded medicines to those listed in specified pharmacopoeias or compendial scientific documentation.

assertions.text: In Portugal, a compounded medicine containing any other raw material may not be prescribed.
assertions.quote:
3 - Não podem ser prescritos medicamen tos manipulados que incluam matérias-
primas diferentes das referidas no n.º 1 ou qualquer das matérias-primas proibidas nos 
termos previstos no número anterior.
assertions.note: Decreto-Lei 95/2004, Art 6(3) prohibits prescribing compounded medicines containing raw materials other than those permitted in paragraph 1.

units.text: In Portugal, INFARMED may authorise exceptional use (AUE) of a medicine without a marketing authorisation, for example when it is clinically justified as indispensable and no authorised alternative exists (Estatuto do Medicamento, Art 92).

assertions.text: In Portugal, INFARMED may authorise exceptional use (AUE) of a medicine under Article 92 of the Estatuto do Medicamento (Decreto-Lei n.º 176/2006).
assertions.quote: A utilização excecional de medicamentos (AUE) reveste-se de carácter excecional e carece de autorização prévia a conceder pelo Infarmed, ao abrigo do disposto no artigo 92.º do Decreto-Lei n.º 176/2006, de 30 de agosto, na sua atual redação, observados os requisitos e condições definidas no regulamento aprovado pela Deliberação n.º 840/2023, de 31 de agosto..
assertions.note: INFARMED's page confirms that exceptional use authorisation (AUE) is granted by INFARMED under Article 92 of Decreto-Lei n.º 176/2006.

assertions.text: Exceptional use authorisation (AUE) may be granted when a medicine is clinically justified as indispensable and no authorised alternative exists.
assertions.note: The available text does not detail the criteria of clinical indispensability and lack of alternatives, and the statutory source text is unavailable.

units.text: In Portugal, a patient-specific AUE is granted to institutions authorised to buy medicines directly (e.g., hospitals) or used by community pharmacies under set conditions, and always requires an individual clinical justification that the medicine is indispensable (INFARMED Deliberação 840/2023, 31 Aug 2023).

assertions.text: In Portugal, a patient-specific AUE is granted to institutions authorised to directly purchase medicines (e.g., hospitals).
assertions.quote: 1 — A AUE destinada a doente específico pode ser concedida às entidades com autorização de aquisição direta de medicamentos, concedida ao abrigo do artigo 79.º do Estatuto, mediante apresentação de pedido e instrução do mesmo de acordo com o estabelecido no artigo 3.º do presente Regulamento.
assertions.note: Deliberação 840/2023 provides that patient-specific AUE can be granted to entities with direct acquisition authorisation upon submitting an application.

assertions.text: A patient-specific AUE can be used by community pharmacies under set conditions.
assertions.quote: 2 — A AUE destinada a doente específico pode também ser utilizada pela farmácia de oficina para adquirir medicamentos, que se consideram automaticamente abrangidos por autorização excecional, desde que observadas as condições previstas no artigo 4.º do presente Regulamento.
assertions.note: The regulation permits community pharmacies to use patient-specific AUE provided the regulatory conditions in Article 4 are fulfilled.

assertions.text: A patient-specific AUE always requires an individual clinical justification showing that the medicine is indispensable.
assertions.quote: 3 — As autorizações previstas no presente artigo carecem de comprovação da imprescindibilidade do medicamento face às alternativas terapêuticas, mediante justificação clínica individualizada.
assertions.note: Article 2(3) mandates proof of the medicine's indispensability compared to therapeutic alternatives via an individualized clinical justification.

units.text: In Portugal, INFARMED told prescribers in July 2024 that Ozempic, Trulicity and Victoza should not be prescribed to people without diabetes, because off-label use (notably for weight loss) threatens supply for diabetic patients (Circular 045/CD/100.20.200, 4 Jul 2024).

assertions.text: In July 2024, INFARMED advised prescribers that Ozempic, Trulicity, and Victoza should not be prescribed to individuals without diabetes.
assertions.quote: Os medicamentos Ozempic, Trulicity e Victoza não devem ser prescritos a doentes que não sejam diabéticos;
assertions.note: INFARMED expressly recommended that Ozempic, Trulicity, and Victoza must not be prescribed to non-diabetic patients.

assertions.text: INFARMED stated that off-label use (notably for weight loss) compromises the supply of these GLP-1 medications for diabetic patients.
assertions.quote: A utilização offlabel dos medicamentos Ozempic, Trulicity e Victoza coloca em risco a sua disponibilidade para o tratamento de doentes diabéticos para os quais foram aprovados e que deles mais beneficiam;
assertions.note: The circular explicitly notes that off-label use threatens availability for the diabetic patients for whom the drugs were approved.

units.text: In Portugal, a medicine is any substance presented as treating or preventing disease or used to restore, correct or modify physiological functions by pharmacological, immunological or metabolic action, so a 'research use only' label does not take such a product outside medicines law (Estatuto do Medicamento, Art 3).
units.note: no cited source has readable text — nothing can be verified

units.text: In Portugal, placing any medicine on the market requires authorisation by INFARMED's governing body, unless the law provides otherwise (e.g., EU central authorisation) (Estatuto do Medicamento, Art 14(1)).
units.note: no cited source has readable text — nothing can be verified

units.text: In Portugal, making, selling, supplying or administering medicines without the required authorisation, or falsified medicines, is an administrative offence fined from €2,000 up to 15% of turnover or €180,000, whichever is lower (Estatuto do Medicamento, Art 181(2)(a)).
units.note: no cited source has readable text — nothing can be verified

units.text: In Portugal, INFARMED does not authorise the import of medicines for personal use (Circular 148/CD, 29 Jul 2011).

assertions.text: In Portugal, INFARMED does not authorise the import of medicines for personal use.
assertions.quote: Assim, o Infarmed não autoriza a importação de medicamentos para uso pessoal.
assertions.note: INFARMED states explicitly that it does not authorise the import of medicines for personal use.

units.text: In Portugal, INFARMED is the national competent authority for cosmetic products under the EU Cosmetics Regulation (Decreto-Lei 23/2025 of 19 March 2025).

assertions.text: In Portugal, INFARMED is the national competent authority for cosmetic products under the EU Cosmetics Regulation (Decreto-Lei 23/2025 of 19 March 2025).
assertions.quote: O INFARMED — Autoridade Nacional do Medicamento e Produtos de Saúde, I. P. (INFARMED, I. P.), é a autoridade nacional competente para efeitos do n.º 1 do artigo 34.º do Regulamento (CE) n.º 1223/2009 e do presente decreto-lei.
assertions.note: Decreto-Lei 23/2025 designates INFARMED as the national competent authority under the EU Cosmetics Regulation.

units.text: In Portugal, INFARMED states that products administered by ingestion, inhalation, injection or implantation are not cosmetics, so an injected 'peptide' cannot be sold as a cosmetic (INFARMED cosmetics FAQ, read 25 Sep 2026).

assertions.text: In Portugal, INFARMED states that products administered by ingestion, inhalation, injection or implantation are not cosmetics, so an injected 'peptide' cannot be sold as a cosmetic.
assertions.quote: Não são considerados cosméticos produtos cuja administração se faça por ingestão, inalação, injeção ou implantação no corpo.
assertions.note: INFARMED states in its FAQ that products administered by injection, ingestion, inhalation, or implantation are not considered cosmetics.

units.text: In Portugal, borderline products (such as topical 'peptide' serums with medicinal-sounding claims) must be classified case by case by the Responsible Person, using the European Commission borderline manual; cosmetics need no prior authorisation but are subject to INFARMED market surveillance (INFARMED cosmetics FAQ).

assertions.text: In Portugal, borderline products must be evaluated case by case by the Responsible Person, considering all their characteristics.
assertions.quote: Os produtos fronteira devem ser avaliados caso a caso pela Pessoa Responsável, tendo em conta todas as suas características.
assertions.note: The INFARMED FAQ confirms that borderline products must be evaluated case by case by the Responsible Person.

assertions.text: The European Commission borderline manual can be consulted to clarify whether a product is classified as a cosmetic.
assertions.quote: Para esclarecimento sobre algumas questões relativas à classificação de um produto como cosmético, poderá consultar o Manual de Produtos Borderline e as normas orientadoras publicadas pela Comissão Europeia.
assertions.note: The INFARMED FAQ states that the European Commission Borderline Manual provides clarification on product classification.

assertions.text: Cosmetics do not require prior administrative authorization before being placed on the market.
assertions.quote: Os cosméticos não são objeto de uma autorização administrativa prévia à colocação no mercado, sendo que, para cada produto cosmético colocado no mercado, a pessoa responsável garante o cumprimento das obrigações previstas no Regulamento (CE) n.º 1223/2009.
assertions.note: The INFARMED FAQ confirms that cosmetics do not require prior administrative authorization before entering the market.

assertions.text: Cosmetics on the market are subject to market surveillance by INFARMED.
assertions.quote: Após o início da sua comercialização, e de modo a garantir que não representam risco para a saúde do consumidor, estes produtos são controlados pela autoridade nacional competente de fiscalização do mercado - INFARMED, I.P., sem prejuízo das atribuições e competências legalmente adstritas a outras entidades, designadamente, à Autoridade de Segurança Alimentar e Económica (ASAE).
assertions.note: The INFARMED FAQ states that after market entry, cosmetics are monitored by INFARMED as the competent market surveillance authority.

units.text: In Portugal, food supplements are intended to maintain the body's homeostasis, not to prevent, treat or cure disease (DGAV, read 25 Sep 2026).

assertions.text: In Portugal, according to DGAV, food supplements are intended to maintain the body's homeostasis, not to prevent, treat or cure disease.
assertions.quote: Os suplementos alimentares destinam-se a manter a homeostasia do organismo e não à prevenção, tratamento ou cura de doenças.
assertions.note: The DGAV page directly states that food supplements are intended to maintain homeostasis and not to prevent, treat, or cure disease.

units.text: In Portugal, every food supplement must be notified to DGAV before it is placed on the national market, even if already sold in another EU Member State (DGAV, read 25 Sep 2026).

assertions.text: In Portugal, every food supplement must be notified to DGAV before it is placed on the national market, even if already sold in another EU Member State.
assertions.quote: Os Suplementos Alimentares têm de ser notificados à DGAV , antes de serem colocados no mercado nacional, mesmo os que já se encontram comercializados noutro Estado-Membro da UE, de acordo com o “ Procedimento de notificação de suplementos alimentares “.
assertions.note: The DGAV guidelines explicitly state that food supplements must be notified before entering the national market, including those already marketed in another EU Member State.

units.text: In Portugal, DGAV warns that notifying a supplement does not mean it is authorised or compliant; there is no pre-market evaluation and control is by later sampling (DGAV, read 25 Sep 2026).

assertions.text: DGAV warns that notifying a supplement does not mean it is authorised or compliant.
assertions.quote: A inexistência de resposta significa que a DGAV aceitou a submissão do processo, mas não significa que tenham sido verificados os requisitos legais, pelo que, em caso algum, o operador poderá concluir que o produto se encontra autorizado ou que se encontra conforme.
assertions.note: DGAV explicitly states that submitting a notification does not imply legal requirements were verified, nor that the product is authorized or compliant.

assertions.text: There is no pre-market evaluation for dietary supplements in Portugal, and control is carried out later by sampling.
assertions.quote: Não existe avaliação do produto ou validação da rotulagem, sendo que o controlo é feito posteriormente e por amostragem, podendo ser efetuado a qualquer momento.
assertions.note: DGAV explains that there is no prior evaluation of the product or label, and control is carried out later through sampling.

units.text: In Portugal, advertising any medicine that lacks a valid authorisation for the national market, or that is used only under an exceptional-use authorisation (Arts 92-93), is prohibited (Estatuto do Medicamento, Art 152(1)).
units.note: no cited source has readable text — nothing can be verified

units.text: In Portugal, advertising prescription-only medicines to the general public is prohibited; they may be advertised only in technical publications or media intended for and accessible only to health professionals (Estatuto do Medicamento, Arts 152(2) and 154(1)).
units.note: no cited source has readable text — nothing can be verified

units.text: In Portugal, the advertiser, the advertising agency, anyone disseminating the advertising and the owner of the advertising medium are all liable for breaches of the medicine-advertising rules, which can also bring publication of the sanction and a suspension of the medicine's advertising for up to two years (Estatuto do Medicamento, Art 182).
units.note: no cited source has readable text — nothing can be verified

units.text: In Portugal, advertising of health services by any provider, public or private (including clinics offering aesthetic treatments), is regulated by Decreto-Lei 238/2015, which bans false claims of guaranteed cure or results or of absence of side effects.
units.note: no cited source has readable text — nothing can be verified

units.text: In Portugal, the health regulator ERS (Entidade Reguladora da Saúde) enforces the health-advertising rules, with fines of €250–€3,740.98 for individuals and €1,000–€44,891.81 for companies, plus possible bans of up to two years (Decreto-Lei 238/2015, Art 8).
units.note: no cited source has readable text — nothing can be verified

units.text: In Portugal, every medicine intended for parenteral administration (injection) is prescription-only by law (Estatuto do Medicamento, Art 114(1)(d)).
units.note: no cited source has readable text — nothing can be verified

units.text: In Portugal, 'restricted prescription' medicines (MSRM restrita) are reserved to specialised settings: alínea a) means exclusive hospital use (e.g., Olumiant, Scenesse) and alínea b) means conditions diagnosed only in hospital or specialised settings (e.g., somatropin) (Estatuto do Medicamento, Art 118).
units.note: no cited source has readable text — nothing can be verified

units.text: In Portugal, growth hormone is distributed free of charge through hospitals with endocrinology or paediatric services, and a national commission (CNNHC) sets the conditions for its administration (INFARMED, read 25 Sep 2026).

assertions.text: In Portugal, growth hormone is distributed free of charge through hospital institutions with endocrinology or paediatric services.
assertions.quote: À Comissão Nacional para a Normalização da Hormona do Crescimento compete a definição das condições de administração da hormona de crescimento, que é distribuída gratuitamente nas instituições hospitalares com serviços de endocrinologia e/ou serviços de pediatria, bem como propor a individualização das situações suscetíveis de comparticipação por parte do Estado.
assertions.note: INFARMED states that growth hormone is distributed free of charge in hospital institutions with endocrinology and/or paediatric services.

assertions.text: A national commission (CNNHC) sets the conditions for the administration of growth hormone.
assertions.quote: À Comissão Nacional para a Normalização da Hormona do Crescimento compete a definição das condições de administração da hormona de crescimento, que é distribuída gratuitamente nas instituições hospitalares com serviços de endocrinologia e/ou serviços de pediatria, bem como propor a individualização das situações suscetíveis de comparticipação por parte do Estado.
assertions.note: The INFARMED page confirms that the CNNHC is responsible for defining the conditions for administering growth hormone.

units.text: In Portugal, INFARMED relayed on 5 Sep 2025 the EMA/HMA warning of a sharp rise in illegal online sales of products presented as GLP-1 agonists (semaglutide, liraglutide, tirzepatide), promoted on social media and not authorised.

assertions.text: INFARMED relayed an EMA/HMA warning on 5 September 2025 regarding a sharp rise in illegal sales of products presented as GLP-1 agonists (semaglutide, liraglutide, tirzepatide).
assertions.quote: Nos últimos meses, verificou-se um aumento acentuado na comercialização ilegal de medicamentos apresentados como agonistas do recetor GLP-1 – como o semaglutido, o liraglutido e a tirzepatida – destinados à perda de peso e ao tratamento da diabetes.
assertions.note: INFARMED published the alert on 5 September 2025 citing an EMA and HMA warning about a sharp increase in illegal marketing of GLP-1 agonists.

assertions.text: These products are promoted on social media and are not authorised.
assertions.quote: Estes produtos, vendidos através de sites fraudulentos e promovidos nas redes sociais, não estão autorizados nem cumprem os padrões exigidos de qualidade, segurança e eficácia, representando um risco significativo para a saúde.
assertions.note: The release confirms these products are promoted on social media and are unauthorised.

units.text: In Portugal, INFARMED stated in Sep 2025 that medicines can be bought online only on the websites of pharmacies and licensed non-prescription outlets, and that GLP-1 agonists are prescription-only medicines sold only in pharmacies.

assertions.text: In Portugal, INFARMED stated in September 2025 that medicines can be bought online only on the websites of pharmacies and licensed non-prescription outlets.
assertions.quote: Em Portugal, a aquisição de medicamentos na internet só é possível nos sites das farmácias e LVMNSRM.
assertions.note: INFARMED explicitly stated that online medicine purchases in Portugal are only possible via authorized pharmacy and LVMNSRM websites.

assertions.text: INFARMED stated that GLP-1 agonists are prescription-only medicines sold only in pharmacies.
assertions.quote: Os medicamentos apresentados como agonistas do recetor GLP-1 – como o semaglutido, o liraglutido e a tirzepatida – são medicamentos sujeitos a receita médica e só podem ser vendidos em farmácia;
assertions.note: The release notes that GLP-1 receptor agonists are prescription-only medicines that may only be sold in pharmacies.

units.text: The skin works as a peripheral neuro-immuno-endocrine organ: reviews describe four immuno-endocrine units (epidermal, dermal, hypodermal, adnexal) whose cells make and respond to hormones and signal to neighbouring cells, through sensory nerves, and through the circulation. This is a mechanistic framework drawn from cell, tissue and animal work.

assertions.text: Reviews describe the skin as a peripheral neuro-immuno-endocrine organ composed of four immuno-endocrine units: epidermal, dermal, hypodermal, and adnexal.
assertions.quote: The skin neuro–immuno–endocrine system is composed of epidermal, dermal, hypodermal and adnexal immune–endocrine units, the activities of which are coordinated by sensory nerves.
assertions.note: Slominski et al. explicitly describe the cutaneous neuro-immuno-endocrine system as organized into epidermal, dermal, hypodermal, and adnexal units.

assertions.text: Resident cells within these cutaneous units produce and respond to hormones.
assertions.quote: Each contains resident cells with both hormone-making and immune capacity (keratinocytes, melanocytes, fibroblasts, sebocytes, adipocytes, mast cells, dendritic and Langerhans cells), wired together by sensory nerves that penetrate to the stratum corneum.
assertions.note: The guide notes that resident cells across these units possess hormone-making capacity and express relevant receptors.

assertions.text: These units communicate with neighbouring cells, through sensory nerves, and through the systemic circulation.
assertions.quote: Communication runs three ways: soluble factors between neighboring cells, rapid neural transmission, and release into the circulation that can reach distant organs.
assertions.note: The guide confirms the three pathways of signaling: soluble factors locally, rapid neural transmission, and systemic circulation.

assertions.text: This neuro-immuno-endocrine model represents a mechanistic framework established through experimental work across cell types, tissues, and species.
assertions.quote: This is not a fringe idea — the hypothesis that the skin is a self-contained neuroendocrine organ, articulated decades ago, has since been validated experimentally across cell types and species.[3] What follows is the mechanistic foundation, framed deliberately as biology rather than a menu of interventions.
assertions.note: The guide affirms that this mechanistic concept has been validated experimentally across cell types and species.

units.text: Skin cells carry the enzymes to make steroids from cholesterol (CYP11A1) and to activate circulating precursors (11β-HSD1, 5α-reductase, aromatase), producing cortisol, DHT and estradiol locally; this rests mainly on cell, tissue and biochemical studies.

assertions.text: Skin cells carry the enzymes to synthesize steroids from cholesterol (such as CYP11A1) and to activate circulating precursors (such as 11β-HSD1, 5α-reductase, and aromatase).
assertions.quote: Most recently it has been established that skin cells contain the entire biochemical apparatus necessary for production of glucocorticoids, androgens and estrogens either from precursors of systemic origin or, alternatively, through the conversion of cholesterol to pregnenolone and its subsequent transformation to biologically active steroids.
assertions.note: Slominski et al. describe the complete cutaneous enzymatic apparatus for steroid synthesis de novo from cholesterol and from systemic precursors.

assertions.text: Skin cells produce cortisol, DHT, and estradiol locally.
assertions.quote: Examples of these products are corticosterone, cortisol, testosterone, dihydrotesterone and estradiol.
assertions.note: The review identifies cortisol, dihydrotestosterone, and estradiol among the active steroids produced in the skin.

assertions.text: The evidence for local skin steroidogenesis rests primarily on cell, tissue, and mechanistic studies.
assertions.quote: much of the local-steroidogenesis literature is mechanistic (cell and ex-vivo); it explains biology, but is not a dosing rationale.
assertions.note: The guide notes that local cutaneous steroidogenesis evidence is predominantly mechanistic (cell and ex-vivo studies).

units.text: Human scalp hair follicles kept in organ culture respond to CRH by making POMC products, secrete cortisol, and switch off their own CRH in response to glucocorticoid — an HPA-like loop running without systemic connections (human tissue, ex vivo).

assertions.text: Human scalp hair follicles kept in organ culture respond to CRH by producing POMC products and secreting cortisol.
assertions.quote: We show that microdissected, organ-cultured human scalp hair follicles respond to CRH stimulation by up-regulating proopiomelanocortin (POMC) transcription and immunoreactivity (IR) for ACTH and alpha-MSH, which must have been processed from POMC.
assertions.note: The abstract reports that organ-cultured human scalp hair follicles up-regulate POMC transcription and ACTH/alpha-MSH immunoreactivity in response to CRH, and secrete cortisol.

assertions.text: Human hair follicles down-regulate their own CRH in response to glucocorticoids, establishing an HPA-like loop running in the absence of systemic connections.
assertions.quote: Thus, even in the absence of endocrine, neural, or vascular systemic connections, normal human scalp hair follicles directly respond to CRH stimulation in a strikingly similar manner to what is seen in the classical HPA axis, including synthesis and secretion of cortisol and activation of prototypic neuroendocrine feedback loops.
assertions.note: The abstract confirms that hydrocortisone down-regulates follicular CRH expression, demonstrating an HPA-like feedback loop operating without endocrine, neural, or vascular systemic connections.

units.text: In mice, deleting glucocorticoid synthesis in keratinocytes causes spontaneous skin inflammation and worse experimental dermatitis: keratinocyte-made glucocorticoids set local immune tone (animal evidence, with a human association with inflammatory skin disease).

assertions.text: In mice, deleting glucocorticoid synthesis in keratinocytes causes spontaneous skin inflammation.
assertions.quote: In line with 11β-hydroxylase deficiency in human inflammatory skin disorders, genetic in vivo Cyp11b1 ablation and long-term GC deficiency in keratinocytes primed the murine skin immune system resulting in spontaneous skin inflammation.
assertions.note: Ablation of Cyp11b1 in keratinocytes in mice led to spontaneous skin inflammation.

assertions.text: In mice, deleting glucocorticoid synthesis in keratinocytes exacerbates experimental dermatitis and skin inflammation.
assertions.quote: Deficient skin GC in experimental models for inflammatory skin disorders led to exacerbated contact hypersensitivity and psoriasiform skin inflammation accompanied by decreased regulatory T cells and the involvement of unconventional T cells.
assertions.note: Skin GC deficiency exacerbated experimental contact hypersensitivity and psoriasiform dermatitis.

assertions.text: Deficient glucocorticoid synthesis in skin is associated with human inflammatory skin disease.
assertions.quote: These results confirm previous studies indicating that epidermal steroidogenesis is dysregulated in prevalent inflammatory skin disorders, such as AD and psoriasis.
assertions.note: Key steroidogenic enzymes like CYP11B1 are downregulated in patients with inflammatory skin disorders such as psoriasis and atopic dermatitis.

units.text: The skin also runs shortened thyroid-like (TRH, TSH, deiodinase-generated T3) and somatotropic (GH/IGF-1) loops; the thyroid-like evidence comes mainly from mouse models and the follicle GH/IGF-1 loop from human follicles ex vivo.

assertions.text: The skin runs shortened thyroid-like (TRH, TSH, deiodinase-generated T3) and somatotropic (GH/IGF-1) loops.
assertions.quote: A cutaneous hypothalamic–pituitary–thyroid loop (local TRH and TSH, with deiodinases generating T3) modulates keratinocyte proliferation, the hair cycle, and mitochondrial function,[7] and a local somatotropic loop (growth hormone and dermally produced IGF-1) influences dermal thickness, wound healing, and the hair follicle.[8]
assertions.note: The guide confirms that the skin operates truncated equivalents of the central thyroid and somatotropic axes.

assertions.text: Evidence for the cutaneous thyroid-like loop comes mainly from mouse models.
assertions.quote: The role of the deiodinases in the regulation of skin homeostasis and pathophysiology has mainly been investigated using conditional, epidermal-specific mice models of D2 and D3 expression ( 38 , 62 – 64 ).
assertions.note: Mancino et al. state that the role of deiodinases in cutaneous homeostasis has been investigated mainly using mouse models.

assertions.text: The hair follicle somatotropic (GH/IGF-1) loop operates in human follicles ex vivo.
assertions.quote: The human hair follicle runs functional peripheral equivalents of the central axes: it synthesizes cortisol and operates a local HPA-like loop,[11] and ex vivo it sustains a hypothalamic–pituitary–somatotropic equivalent (GHRH, GH, IGF-1) that paces its own growth.[12]
assertions.note: The guide notes that human hair follicles ex vivo sustain a peripheral equivalent of the somatotropic axis.

units.text: The skin supplies a whole-body hormone system: UVB converts 7-dehydrocholesterol to previtamin D3 in human skin, and vitamin D3 is carried into the circulation to be hydroxylated to 25(OH)D and then calcitriol (skin-to-body signalling).

assertions.text: UVB converts 7-dehydrocholesterol to previtamin D3 in human skin.
assertions.quote: D3 (cholecalciferol) is produced from 7-dehydrocholesterol (7-DHC) through a two-step process in which the B ring is broken by UV light (spectrum 280–320 UVB) radiation from the sun, forming pre-D3 that isomerizes to D3 in a thermo-sensitive but noncatalytic process.
assertions.note: Bikle confirms that UVB radiation converts 7-dehydrocholesterol into previtamin D3 in the skin.

assertions.text: Vitamin D3 is translocated from the skin into the systemic circulation.
assertions.quote: The vitamin D-binding protein preferentially translocates the thermal product, vitamin D3, into the circulation.
assertions.note: Holick confirms that vitamin D-binding protein translocates vitamin D3 from skin into the circulation.

assertions.text: Vitamin D is hydroxylated to 25(OH)D and subsequently to calcitriol, serving as a hormonal signaling system.
assertions.quote: Vitamin D is metabolized first to 25 hydroxyvitamin D (25OHD), then to the hormonal form 1,25-dihydroxyvitamin D (1,25(OH)2D).
assertions.note: Bikle states that vitamin D is metabolized to 25(OH)D and then to its hormonal form 1,25(OH)2D.

units.text: Reviews describe a skin contribution to circulating androgens and estrogens, especially in older people — a second skin-to-body route, supported mainly by biochemical data.

assertions.text: Reviews describe a skin contribution to circulating androgens and estrogens, especially in older people.
assertions.quote: Human skin produces, activates or inactivates metabolically numerous hormones which are probably important for skin functions but also for functions of the entire human organism, such as sex hormones, especially in aged individuals, insulin-like growth factor and -binding proteins, neuropeptides, prolactin, catecholamines, retinoids, steroids, vitamin D and eicosanoids.
assertions.note: The review explicitly notes that skin produces and metabolizes sex hormones for systemic function, especially in aged individuals.

assertions.text: The skin contribution of androgens and estrogens to the circulation is supported mainly by biochemical data.
assertions.note: Neither cited review states that the skin contribution to circulating sex steroids is supported primarily or mainly by biochemical data.

recheck.note: Neither cited source mentions that the contribution of skin androgens and estrogens to the circulation is supported mainly by biochemical data.

units.text: Systemic hormones act on skin (body-to-skin): cortisol excess thins the dermis and causes striae and bruising; hypothyroidism gives dry, coarse skin and myxoedema. The Aesthetic & Regenerative Endocrinology guide treats the aesthetic exam as a systemic screen and lists suspected Cushing syndrome (violaceous striae, central obesity, proximal weakness, new hypertension or diabetes) and rapidly progressive virilisation among reasons to refer promptly to endocrinology.

assertions.text: Cortisol excess thins the dermis and causes striae and bruising.
assertions.quote: Sustained glucocorticoid excess is visibly catabolic: it suppresses fibroblast collagen synthesis, thins the dermis and epidermis, delays barrier and wound repair, and produces the easy bruising, striae, and atrophy familiar from topical-steroid overuse.[3]
assertions.note: The guide confirms that glucocorticoid excess thins the dermis and produces easy bruising and striae.

assertions.text: Hypothyroidism gives dry, coarse skin and myxoedema.
assertions.quote: Hypothyroidism gives dry, coarse, cool skin and myxedema; hyperthyroidism gives warm, moist skin and, in Graves' disease, pretibial myxedema.[8]
assertions.note: The guide states that hypothyroidism causes dry, coarse, cool skin and myxedema.

assertions.text: The Aesthetic & Regenerative Endocrinology guide treats the aesthetic exam as a systemic screen.
assertions.quote: CLINICAL PEARL — THE AESTHETIC EXAM IS A SYSTEMIC SCREEN — Sudden skin thinning and easy bruising suggest cortisol excess; coarse, dry, cool skin suggests hypothyroidism; new acanthosis nigricans flags insulin resistance; rapid photoaging tracks UV, glycation, and smoking.
assertions.note: The guide explicitly highlights that the aesthetic exam functions as a systemic screen for endocrine issues.

assertions.text: The Aesthetic & Regenerative Endocrinology guide lists suspected Cushing syndrome (violaceous striae, central obesity, proximal weakness, new hypertension or diabetes) and rapidly progressive virilisation among reasons to refer promptly to endocrinology.
assertions.quote: R E F E R T O E N D O C R I N O L O G Y P R O M P T L Y I F — Suspected Cushing syndrome (violaceous striae, central obesity, proximal weakness, new hypertension or diabetes). — Rapidly progressive virilization (deepening voice, clitoromegaly, rapid hirsutism) — possible androgen-secreting tumor.
assertions.note: The guide lists suspected Cushing syndrome and rapidly progressive virilization as prompt referral criteria.

units.text: The Hormone Cell Atlas (Science 2026) analysed RNA for 379 hormone and receptor genes in about 14 million single cells and nuclei from 47 human tissues, skin among them, and mapped putative hormone-producing and hormone-receiving cell types.

assertions.text: The Hormone Cell Atlas (Science 2026) analysed RNA for 379 hormone and receptor genes in about 14 million single cells and nuclei from 47 human tissues, mapping putative hormone-producing and hormone-receiving cell types.
assertions.quote: Drawing inspiration from the Human Cell Atlas, we analyzed the expression of 379 hormone and receptor genes in a transcriptomic dataset comprising 14 million single cells and nuclei across 47 human tissues. Using hormone2cell, we mapped putative hormone-producing and hormone-receiving cell types, defining tissue-specific and cross-tissue endocrine signatures.
assertions.note: The abstract confirms analyzing 379 hormone and receptor genes across 14 million cells and nuclei from 47 human tissues to map putative hormone-producing and hormone-receiving cell types.

assertions.text: The 47 human tissues analysed in the Hormone Cell Atlas included skin.
assertions.note: The provided source texts do not mention skin among the 47 tissues analysed.

units.text: The atlas's authors describe its scores as putative and hypothesis-generating, not functional hormones and receptors, and leave validation to in vitro and in vivo work; more generally, transcript levels alone often fail to predict protein levels. A transcriptomic map therefore shows capacity, not secretion or effect.

assertions.text: The Hormone Cell Atlas's authors describe its scores as putative and hypothesis-generating rather than functional hormones and receptors, and leave validation to in vitro and in vivo work.
assertions.quote: Important: these predictions are based on transcriptomic data and should be considered as putative and hypothesis-generating, rather than as functional hormones and receptors. The user takes responsibility for validation using appropriate methods (e.g. in vitro, in vivo) and for describing appropriately their use of transcriptome-based scores and predictions.
assertions.note: The Hormone Cell Atlas portal explicitly notes that its predictions are putative and hypothesis-generating rather than functional hormones and receptors, placing responsibility for in vitro or in vivo validation on users.

assertions.text: More generally, transcript levels alone often fail to predict protein levels.
assertions.quote: We conclude that transcript levels by themselves are not sufficient to predict protein levels in many scenarios and to thus explain genotype-phenotype relationships and that high-quality data quantifying different levels of gene expression are indispensable for the complete understanding of biological processes.
assertions.note: Liu et al. conclude that transcript levels by themselves are insufficient to predict protein levels in many scenarios.

assertions.text: A transcriptomic map therefore shows capacity rather than secretion or effect.
assertions.quote: A cellular-resolution map now lets us infer that activity cell by cell — as transcriptomic predictions (which cells express the machinery to make or sense a hormone), not direct measurements of secretion or function.
assertions.note: The pocket guide notes that single-cell transcriptomic maps infer the cellular machinery to produce or sense hormones rather than directly measuring secretion or function.

units.text: The guide infers from the atlas that the skin, built from every major cell lineage, is plausibly one of the body's largest distributed endocrine signalling networks — an inference from transcriptomic prediction, not a measurement.

assertions.text: The guide infers from the atlas that the skin, built from every major cell lineage, is plausibly one of the body's largest distributed endocrine signalling networks, as an inference from transcriptomic prediction rather than a direct measurement.
assertions.quote: Second, it follows that the skin — the body's largest organ, built from every major lineage (epithelial, mesenchymal, endothelial, adipocyte, immune, neural) in vast quantity — is plausibly one of the body's largest distributed endocrine signaling networks — an inference from transcriptomic prediction rather than direct measurement of secretion.[2]
assertions.note: The guide states that the skin is plausibly one of the body's largest distributed endocrine signaling networks as an inference from transcriptomic prediction rather than direct measurement.

units.text: Topical and transdermal treatments act through receptors the skin already carries, and local steroid-metabolising enzymes modify potency, so the cutaneous response need not mirror the dose; receptor presence is a hypothesis-generating starting point that needs validation, and says nothing yet about efficacy in people.

assertions.text: Topical and transdermal treatments act through receptors the skin already carries, and local steroid-metabolising enzymes modify potency, so the cutaneous response need not mirror the dose.
assertions.quote: Therapy: topical and transdermal routes exploit the skin's native receptors — retinoids (RAR), vitamin D analogs (VDR), estrogens (ER), glucocorticoids (GR) — but local steroid-metabolizing enzymes modify potency, so the cutaneous response need not mirror the systemic dose.
assertions.note: Supported by the clinician's guide discussing topical and transdermal therapies and cutaneous steroid-metabolizing enzymes.

assertions.text: Receptor presence is a hypothesis-generating starting point that needs validation, and says nothing yet about efficacy in people.
assertions.quote: Important: these predictions are based on transcriptomic data and should be considered as putative and hypothesis-generating, rather than as functional hormones and receptors. The user takes responsibility for validation using appropriate methods (e.g. in vitro, in vivo) and for describing appropriately their use of transcriptome-based scores and predictions.
assertions.note: Supported by the portal documentation stating that predictions are putative, hypothesis-generating, and require in vitro/in vivo validation rather than indicating functional activity.

units.text: The guide's testing pearl says serum 25-hydroxyvitamin D falls with sunscreen use; an independent systematic review found that sunscreen blocks vitamin D synthesis under artificial UV, but randomized field trials of daily moderate-SPF sunscreen did not lower 25(OH)D, and high-SPF products have not been trialled.

assertions.text: The guide's testing pearl states that serum 25-hydroxyvitamin D falls with sunscreen use.
assertions.quote: CLINICAL PEARLS — TESTING & THERAPY — Testing: serum 25-OH vitamin D partly reflects cutaneous synthesis, so it falls with low UVB exposure and sunscreen use regardless of oral intake.
assertions.note: The pocket guide's testing pearl explicitly states that serum 25-OH vitamin D falls with sunscreen use.

assertions.text: A systematic review found that sunscreen abrogates vitamin D synthesis under artificially generated UV radiation.
assertions.quote: In the experimental studies sunscreen use considerably abrogated the vitamin D 3 or 25(OH)D production induced by exposure to artificially generated UVR.
assertions.note: The review reported that experimental studies using artificial UVR found sunscreen considerably abrogated vitamin D production.

assertions.text: Randomized controlled field trials of daily moderate-SPF sunscreen did not lower 25(OH)D levels.
assertions.quote: The randomized controlled field trials found no effect of daily sunscreen application, but the sunscreens used had moderate protection [sun protection factor SPF) ~16].
assertions.note: The review found that randomized field trials using moderate-protection sunscreen found no effect on 25(OH)D levels.

assertions.text: High-SPF sunscreen products have not been evaluated in trials.
assertions.quote: However, there have been no trials of the high-SPF sunscreens that are now widely recommended.
assertions.note: The review concludes that there have been no trials testing high-SPF sunscreens.

units.text: Senescent cells are permanently growth-arrested yet still secreting; the senescence-associated secretory phenotype (IL-6, IL-8, matrix metalloproteinases, growth factors) was characterised in cultured human cells after DNA damage.

assertions.text: Senescent cells are permanently growth-arrested yet still secreting.
assertions.quote: Senescent cells are characterized by their inability to proliferate, resistance to apoptosis, and secretion of factors that promote inflammation and tissue deterioration ( Campisi and d’Adda di Fagagna, 2007 ; Kuilman et al., 2010 ; He and Sharpless, 2017 ).
assertions.note: Wang and Dreesen (2018) describe senescent cells as unable to proliferate yet actively secreting factors.

assertions.text: The senescence-associated secretory phenotype comprises IL-6, IL-8, matrix metalloproteinases, and growth factors.
assertions.quote: For instance, senescent cells modulate their environment by secreting inflammatory cytokines, chemokines, matrix metalloproteinases (MMPs) and growth factors, collectively known as the senescence-associated secretory phenotype (SASP) ( Acosta et al., 2008 ; Coppé et al., 2008b ; Kuilman et al., 2008 ; Rodier et al., 2009 ) or senescence-messaging secretome (SMS) ( Kuilman and Peeper, 2009 ).
assertions.note: Wang and Dreesen (2018) state that the senescence-associated secretory phenotype includes cytokines such as IL-6 and IL-8, chemokines, matrix metalloproteinases, and growth factors.

assertions.text: The senescence-associated secretory phenotype was characterised in cultured human cells after DNA damage.
assertions.quote: We show that human cells induced to senesce by genotoxic stress secrete myriad factors associated with inflammation and malignancy. This senescence-associated secretory phenotype (SASP) developed slowly over several days and only after DNA damage of sufficient magnitude to induce senescence.
assertions.note: Coppé et al. (2008) show that human cells induced to senesce in culture by DNA damage secrete the SASP.

units.text: In human skin, cells carrying the senescence marker p16INK4a are more numerous with age in both epidermis and dermis; no single universal marker identifies senescent cells, so counts depend on the marker used.

assertions.text: In human skin, cells carrying the senescence marker p16INK4a are more numerous with age in both epidermis and dermis.
assertions.quote: The number of p16INK4A positive cells was found to be increased in both epidermis and dermis, compartments with strictly different proliferative activities.
assertions.note: Ressler et al. confirmed that p16INK4a-positive cells increase with age in both epidermal and dermal compartments.

assertions.text: No single universal marker identifies senescent cells, so counts depend on the marker used.
assertions.quote: However, a significant hurdle in the aging field has been the identification of a universal biomarker that facilitates the unequivocal detection and quantification of senescent cell types in vitro and in vivo .
assertions.note: Wang and Dreesen note that identifying a universal biomarker that unequivocally detects and quantifies senescent cell types remains a major hurdle.

units.text: In 178 adults of the Leiden Longevity Study, more p16-positive cells in sun-protected arm skin were associated with ageing-type elastic fibres, more facial wrinkles and higher perceived age independent of chronological age; people in the lowest tertile of epidermal p16 counts looked about 3 years younger than those in the highest. This is an association, not evidence of cause.

assertions.text: In 178 adults of the Leiden Longevity Study, more p16-positive cells in sun-protected arm skin were associated with ageing-type elastic fibres, more facial wrinkles, and higher perceived age independent of chronological age.
assertions.quote: The numbers of epidermal and dermal p16INK4a positive cells were significantly associated with age-associated elastic fiber morphologic characteristics, such as longer and a greater number of elastic fibers. The p16INK4a positive epidermal cells (identified as primarily melanocytes) were also significantly associated with more facial wrinkles and a higher perceived age.
assertions.note: The abstract confirms that in 178 participants of the Leiden Longevity Study, p16-positive cells in sun-protected arm biopsies were associated with age-associated elastic fibre characteristics, facial wrinkles, and perceived facial age, adjusted for chronological age.

assertions.text: People in the lowest tertile of epidermal p16 counts looked about 3 years younger than those in the highest tertile.
assertions.quote: Participants in the lowest tertile of epidermal p16INK4a counts looked 3 years younger than those in the highest tertile, independently of chronological age and elastic fiber morphology.
assertions.note: The abstract reports that participants in the lowest tertile of epidermal p16 counts looked 3 years younger than those in the highest tertile.

units.text: Skin collagen falls with age; aged human dermis shows more fibroblast MMP-1, fragmented collagen and fibroblasts under less mechanical tension that make less procollagen, and culture work shows fragmentation feeds back to raise MMP-1. That senescent cells drive this in living skin is plausible but not shown.

assertions.text: Skin collagen decreases with age.
assertions.quote: Skin collagen decreased with age and was less in the females at all ages.
assertions.note: Shuster et al. found that skin collagen decreased with age.

assertions.text: Aged human dermis shows increased fibroblast MMP-1 expression.
assertions.quote: We report here that dermal fibroblasts express increased levels of collagen-degrading matrix metalloproteinases-1 (MMP-1) in aged (>80 years old) compared with young (21 to 30 years old) human skin in vivo.
assertions.note: Fisher et al. reported elevated MMP-1 expression in fibroblasts from aged versus young human skin.

assertions.text: Aged human skin is characterized by fragmented collagen.
assertions.quote: Aged human skin is fragile because of fragmentation and loss of type I collagen fibrils, which confer strength and resiliency.
assertions.note: Fisher et al. state that aged skin experiences fragmentation and loss of type I collagen fibrils.

assertions.text: Fibroblasts in aged skin experience less mechanical tension and produce less procollagen.
assertions.quote: The reduction in collagen synthesis due to fibroblast aging was demonstrated by a lower in vitro production of type I procollagen by dermal fibroblasts isolated from skin of young (18 to 29 years) versus old (80+ years) individuals (82 +/- 16 versus 56 +/- 8 ng/ml; P < 0.05).
assertions.note: Varani et al. demonstrated decreased procollagen synthesis and morphological features consistent with reduced mechanical stimulation in aged fibroblasts.

assertions.text: In vitro work shows that collagen fragmentation feeds back to increase MMP-1 levels.
assertions.quote: Furthermore, fibroblasts cultured in fragmented collagen lattices express elevated levels of MMP-1, AP-1, and alpha2beta1 integrin.
assertions.note: Fisher et al. demonstrated that culturing fibroblasts in fragmented collagen lattices elevates MMP-1 expression.

assertions.text: That senescent cells drive this in living skin is plausible but not shown.
assertions.note: The provided source texts do not mention senescent cells or whether they drive this process in living skin.

units.text: Causal evidence that senescent cells drive ageing comes from mice: clearing p16-positive cells extended healthy lifespan and senolytics improved function and survival in old mice; skin was checked only for safety (thickness, fibrosis, wound closure), and clearing p16-positive cells during healing slowed wound closure.

assertions.text: In mice, clearing p16-positive cells extended healthy lifespan.
assertions.quote: Clearance of p16 Ink4a -positive cells delayed tumorigenesis and attenuated age-related deterioration of several organs without apparent side effects, including kidney, heart and fat, where clearance preserved the functionality of glomeruli, cardio-protective K ATP channels, and adipocytes, respectively.
assertions.note: Baker et al. showed that clearance of p16-positive cells extended median lifespan and delayed age-related organ deterioration.

assertions.text: Senolytics improved function and survival in old mice.
assertions.quote: Moreover, intermittent oral administration of senolytics to both senescent cell-transplanted younger and naturally-aged mice alleviated physical dysfunction and increased post-treatment survival by 36% while reducing mortality hazard to 65%.
assertions.note: Xu et al. demonstrated that intermittent senolytics alleviated physical dysfunction and increased survival in naturally aged mice.

assertions.text: Skin was checked only for safety (thickness, fibrosis, wound closure).
assertions.quote: Furthermore, 18-month-old AP-treated mice showed no evidence of increased fibrosis in skin and other tissues, despite a role for senescent cells in limiting fibrosis during tissue repair ( Extended Data Fig. 10d ).
assertions.note: Wound closure and skin fibrosis were evaluated as safety and off-target checks, but skin thickness was listed under age-related phenotypes and the paper does not state skin was checked only for safety.

assertions.text: Clearing p16-positive cells during healing slowed wound closure.
assertions.quote: When AP was administered during wound closure, healing was delayed with similar kinetics as 4- or 18-month-old ATTAC mice without prior AP treatment, indicating that acute senescence mechanisms are preserved with aging and not influenced by constitutive clearance of senescent cells 3 .
assertions.note: Administering the clearing dimerizer AP during healing delayed cutaneous wound closure.

units.text: Human senotherapy data are small pilots with tissue-marker endpoints — an open-label senolytic pilot in 9 patients reduced epidermal p16/p21-positive cells; an exploratory topical rapamycin RCT (36 enrolled, 19 lost) reduced skin p16 — clinical improvement in that trial was described only in 'multiple participants', and no adequately sized trial with clinical skin-ageing outcomes was found on PubMed or ClinicalTrials.gov (checked 24 September 2026). The guide advises that senolytics generally be confined to clinical trials.

assertions.text: An open-label senolytic pilot study in 9 patients reduced epidermal p16- and p21-positive cells.
assertions.quote: Skin epidermal p16 INK4A+ and p21 CIP1+ cells were reduced, as were circulating SASP factors, including IL-1α, IL-6, and MMPs-9 and −12.
assertions.note: The pilot trial of dasatinib plus quercetin in 9 patients with diabetic kidney disease confirmed reductions in epidermal p16 and p21 positive cells.

assertions.text: An exploratory topical rapamycin RCT enrolled 36 participants, had 19 lost to follow-up or discontinued, and showed reduced skin p16 expression.
assertions.quote: Thirty-six participants were enrolled in the study, and nineteen discontinued or were lost to follow-up. A significant (P = 0.008) reduction in p16INK4A protein levels and an increase in collagen VII protein levels (P = 0.0077) were observed among participants at the end of the study.
assertions.note: The trial enrolled 36 participants, recorded 19 discontinuations or losses to follow-up, and showed a significant reduction in p16 protein.

assertions.text: Clinical improvement in the topical rapamycin trial was described only in 'multiple participants'.
assertions.quote: Clinical assessment of the 13 subjects completing the study is presented in Table 2. Of the 13 subjects, all except 2 showed improvement in clinical signs of cutaneous aging.
assertions.note: The trial reported detailed clinical ratings across three validated scales in Table 2 and explicitly stated that 11 of 13 evaluated subjects improved.

assertions.text: No adequately sized trial with clinical skin-ageing outcomes was found on PubMed or ClinicalTrials.gov as of 24 September 2026.
assertions.note: None of the provided sources document a literature or registry search performed on 24 September 2026.

recheck.note: The provided texts do not mention any search on PubMed or ClinicalTrials.gov as of 24 September 2026.

assertions.text: The clinician's guide advises that senolytics generally be confined to clinical trials.
assertions.quote: Senolytics in particular should generally be confined to clinical trials.
assertions.note: The pocket guide explicitly counsels that senolytics should generally be confined to clinical trials.

units.text: Interventions on the ageing matrix with human trials: daily sunscreen slowed photoageing in a 903-person community RCT (B); topical tretinoin improves photoageing consistently across randomized trials and the guide rates topical retinoids first-line GRADE A; topical retinol improved fine wrinkles in very old skin in a small RCT (C), and within a week lowered MMPs and raised collagen synthesis in aged human skin.

assertions.text: Daily sunscreen slowed photoageing in a 903-person community RCT.
assertions.quote: Skin aging from baseline to the end of the trial was 24% less in the daily sunscreen group than in the discretionary sunscreen group (relative odds, 0.76 [95% CI, 0.59 to 0.98]).
assertions.note: A community-based RCT in 903 adults showed 24% less skin aging over 4.5 years with daily sunscreen versus discretionary use.

assertions.text: Topical tretinoin improves photoageing consistently across randomized trials.
assertions.quote: With regard to efficacy, all studies consistently reported that topical tretinoin was efficacious in improving clinical appearance of photoaging in terms of wrinkling, mottled hyperpigmentation, sallowness, and lentigines as early as 1 month and lasted after 24 months.
assertions.note: The systematic review found consistent improvement across all 7 included RCTs.

assertions.text: The guide rates topical retinoids first-line GRADE A for photoaging.
assertions.quote: Among topical agents, retinoids have the strongest dermatologic evidence for reversing measurable signs of photoaging and remain first-line GRADE A.
assertions.note: The guide explicitly assigns topical retinoids first-line GRADE A status.

assertions.text: Topical retinol improved fine wrinkles in very old skin in a small RCT.
assertions.quote: After 24 weeks, an intent-to-treat analysis using the last-observation-carried-forward method revealed that there were significant differences between retinol-treated and vehicle-treated skin for changes in fine wrinkling scores (-1.64 [95% CI, -2.06 to -1.22] vs -0.08 [95% CI, -0.17 to 0.01]; P<.001).
assertions.note: A double-blind vehicle-controlled trial in 36 elderly participants (mean age 87) found significant improvement in fine wrinkling scores.

assertions.text: Topical retinol (vitamin A) lowered MMPs and raised collagen synthesis within a week in aged human skin.
assertions.quote: In a separate group of 53 individuals (80+ y of age), topical application of 1% vitamin A for 7 d increased fibroblast growth and collagen synthesis, and concomitantly reduced the levels of matrix-degrading matrix metalloproteinases.
assertions.note: Application of 1% vitamin A for 7 days increased collagen synthesis and reduced matrix metalloproteinases in individuals aged 80+.

units.text: The skin expresses the elements of a local HPA-like axis (CRH, POMC, ACTH) and regenerates active cortisol from cortisone through 11β-HSD1 in keratinocytes and dermal fibroblasts; 11β-HSD1 activity is higher in aged and photo-exposed human skin, local glucocorticoid availability is regulated independently of circulating levels, and 11β-HSD1 knockout mice are protected from age-induced dermal atrophy.

assertions.text: The skin expresses elements of a local HPA-like axis, including CRH, POMC, and ACTH.
assertions.quote: In fact, all of the elements controlling the activity of the hypothalamus-pituitary-adrenal axis are expressed in the skin including CRH, urocortin, and POMC, with its products ACTH, alpha-MSH, and beta-endorphin.
assertions.note: Slominski and Wortsman confirm cutaneous expression of CRH, POMC, and ACTH within a local HPA axis.

assertions.text: 11β-HSD1 is expressed in keratinocytes and dermal fibroblasts, where it activates cortisol from cortisone.
assertions.quote: 11β-HSD1 (which activates cortisol), but not 11β-HSD2 (which inactivates cortisol), was expressed in epidermal keratinocytes and dermal fibroblasts in human skin and also in outer hair follicle root sheath cells in murine skin.
assertions.note: Tiganescu et al. (2011) demonstrate that 11β-HSD1 activates cortisol and is expressed in epidermal keratinocytes and dermal fibroblasts.

assertions.text: 11β-HSD1 activity is elevated in aged and photo-exposed human skin.
assertions.quote: 11β-HSD1 activity was elevated in aged human and mouse skin and in PE compared with donor-matched photo-protected human biopsies.
assertions.note: Tiganescu et al. (2013) show higher 11β-HSD1 activity in aged and photo-exposed skin compared to photo-protected skin.

assertions.text: Local tissue glucocorticoid availability is regulated independently of systemic circulating levels.
assertions.quote: Within target tissues, GC availability is regulated at a prereceptor level, independently of systemic levels, by isozymes of 11β-hydroxysteroid dehydrogenase (11β-HSD) that interconvert active cortisol and inactive cortisone.
assertions.note: Tiganescu et al. (2011) confirm prereceptor regulation of GC availability occurs independently of systemic levels.

assertions.text: 11β-HSD1 knockout mice are protected against age-induced dermal atrophy.
assertions.quote: Age-induced dermal atrophy with deranged collagen structural organization was prevented in 11β-HSD1 KO mice, which also exhibited increased collagen density.
assertions.note: Tiganescu et al. (2013) confirm age-induced dermal atrophy is prevented in 11β-HSD1 KO mice.

units.text: The only human RCT of 11β-HSD1 inhibition with skin outcomes is a 28-person pilot in type 2 diabetes: it missed its primary outcome (skin 11β-HSD1 activity), showed an exploratory reduction in wound size, and modestly impaired barrier function. No registered trial tests an 11β-HSD1 inhibitor for skin ageing, and the compound tested has no FDA approval (ClinicalTrials.gov and Drugs@FDA checked 24 Sep 2026).

assertions.text: The only human RCT of 11β-HSD1 inhibition with skin outcomes is a 28-person pilot in type 2 diabetes.
assertions.quote: This first-in-human randomized, controlled, clinical trial found novel evidence that 11β-HSD type 1 regulates skin function in humans, including improved wound healing, epidermal integrity, and increased water loss.
assertions.note: The study confirms it was a 28-person pilot RCT and the first in humans, but does not establish that no other human trials have been conducted since.

assertions.text: The pilot RCT missed its primary outcome of skin 11β-HSD1 activity.
assertions.quote: In this pilot study, data on our primary outcome measure failed to show 11β-HSD1 inhibition in the skin.
assertions.note: The trial authors report that the treatment failed to show 11β-HSD1 inhibition in skin on the primary outcome.

assertions.text: The trial showed an exploratory reduction in wound size.
assertions.quote: Wound diameter was 34% (7–63%) smaller with AZD4017 at day 2, and 48% (12–85%) smaller after repeat wounding at day 30.
assertions.note: Wound diameter was smaller by 34% at day 2 and by 48% at day 30 with AZD4017.

assertions.text: The trial showed that 11β-HSD1 inhibition modestly impaired barrier function.
assertions.quote: AZD4017 improved epidermal integrity but modestly impaired barrier function.
assertions.note: The authors state that AZD4017 modestly impaired barrier function.

assertions.text: No registered trial tests an 11β-HSD1 inhibitor for skin ageing.
assertions.note: The provided sources do not include a comprehensive database search confirming that no registered trials test this indication.

assertions.text: The compound tested (AZD4017) has no FDA approval.
assertions.note: The provided texts do not mention the FDA regulatory approval status of AZD4017.

units.text: Per the Endocrine Society diagnostic guideline, the features that best discriminate Cushing's syndrome are easy bruising, facial plethora, proximal myopathy and striae that are reddish-purple and wider than 1 cm; facial fullness, dorsocervical fat pad, weight gain, acne, hirsutism, thin skin and fatigue are common in the general population and less discriminatory.

assertions.text: Per the Endocrine Society diagnostic guideline, the features that best discriminate Cushing's syndrome are easy bruising, facial plethora, proximal myopathy, and striae that are reddish-purple and wider than 1 cm.

units.text: Endogenous Cushing's syndrome is uncommon (2–3 new cases per million per year in European population studies); the commonest cause of Cushing's syndrome is iatrogenic, and the guideline recommends a drug history (oral, inhaled, topical, injected — including skin-bleaching creams, herbal tonics and joint or nerve injections) before any biochemical testing.

assertions.quote: After excluding exogenous glucocorticoid use, we recommend testing for Cushing's syndrome in patients with multiple and progressive features compatible with the syndrome, particularly those with a high discriminatory value, and patients with adrenal incidentaloma.

units.text: The guideline recommends testing patients with multiple and progressive features (particularly the discriminating ones) or features unusual for age, recommends against widespread testing and against random serum cortisol, and sends abnormal results to an endocrinologist. The Aesthetic & Regenerative Endocrinology guide adds that consumer cortisol panels are poorly validated and reads most popular 'cortisol face' as a lifestyle-and-fluid picture.

assertions.note: The abstract supports testing patients with multiple and progressive features compatible with the syndrome, particularly those with high discriminatory value, but does not mention features unusual for age.

assertions.note: The provided abstract does not mention recommendations against widespread testing or against random serum cortisol.

assertions.note: The guide notes that consumer cortisol panels are poorly validated for the worried-well.
