units.text: Human skin expresses ERα, ERβ and GPR30 in aged and photoaged sites; two weeks of topical estradiol raised procollagen I/III in sun-protected hip skin of postmenopausal women but not in photoaged forearm or facial skin.

assertions.text: Human skin expresses ERα, ERβ, and GPR30 in aged and photoaged sites.
assertions.quote: Surprisingly, no significant changes in production were observed in women or men after 2-week estradiol treatment of photoaged forearm or face skin, despite similar expression of estrogen receptors (ER-alpha, ER-beta, and GPR30) in aged and photoaged skin.
assertions.note: The abstract confirms similar expression of ER-alpha, ER-beta, and GPR30 in aged and photoaged skin.

assertions.text: Topical estradiol raised procollagen I and III in sun-protected hip skin of postmenopausal women.
assertions.quote: Topical estradiol increased procollagen I and III messenger RNA and collagen I protein levels in sun-protected aged hip skin in postmenopausal women and, to a lesser extent, in age-matched men.
assertions.note: Topical estradiol increased procollagen I and III mRNA in sun-protected aged hip skin of postmenopausal women.

assertions.text: Two weeks of topical estradiol did not stimulate collagen production in photoaged forearm or facial skin.
assertions.quote: Two-week topical estradiol treatment stimulates collagen production in sun-protected hip skin, but not in photoaged forearm or face skin, in postmenopausal women and aged-matched men.
assertions.note: Two-week estradiol treatment stimulated collagen production in sun-protected hip skin but not in photoaged forearm or facial skin.

units.text: In small observational biopsy studies, skin collagen content and thickness fall by about 1–2% per year after menopause, in step with bone mass, tracking years since menopause more than chronological age. The 'up to 30% in the first five years' figure quoted by reviews and by the Aesthetic & Regenerative Endocrinology guide is not stated in the primary abstracts it traces to; the lesson reports it as a review figure.

assertions.text: In small observational biopsy studies, skin collagen content and thickness fall by about 1–2% per year after menopause, in step with bone mass.
assertions.quote: The skin collagen content, skin thickness, metacarpal index, and forearm bone mineral content in postmenopausal women showed a similar decline of between 1-2% per year after the menopause.
assertions.note: Brincat et al. (1987) report an annual decline of 1–2% in skin collagen, skin thickness, and bone parameters after menopause.

assertions.text: Postmenopausal skin collagen decline tracks years since menopause more than chronological age.
assertions.quote: In the untreated women skin collagen content declined in relation to menopausal age but not to chronological age.
assertions.note: Brincat et al. (1985) observed that skin collagen content declined with menopausal age rather than chronological age.

assertions.text: Reviews and the Aesthetic & Regenerative Endocrinology guide quote a figure of up to 30% skin collagen loss in the first five postmenopausal years.
assertions.quote: Type I and III skin collagen is thought to decrease by as much as 30% in the first five years after menopause, which parallels the reduction in bone mass observed in post-menopausal women.
assertions.note: Thornton (2013) and Hannah-Shmouni (2026) both cite an up to 30% reduction in skin collagen over the first five postmenopausal years.

units.text: Small RCTs of systemic hormone therapy increased skin thickness (n=60, 12 months) and skin collagen (n=41, 6 months) at non-facial sites; a 2023 meta-analysis pooling small, heterogeneous studies (some non-randomized) reports higher elasticity, thickness and collagen, and its authors do not propose MHT as an independent treatment for skin ageing.

assertions.text: An RCT of systemic hormone therapy in 60 women found increased skin thickness at a non-facial site after 12 months.
assertions.quote: Treatment with conjugated estrogens for 12 months significantly increases, at the level of the right great trochanter, the thickness of the skin (p < 0.01), as assessed by ultrasonography, and of the dermis (p < 0.05), as assessed by skin biopsy.
assertions.note: Maheux et al. (1994) randomized 60 women for 12 months and observed increased skin thickness at the right great trochanter.

assertions.text: An RCT of systemic hormone therapy in 41 women found increased skin collagen at a non-facial site after 6 months.
assertions.quote: Collagen content of the left upper arm increased after 6 months of treatment only in the hormonal group (+6.49%; P < 0.05).
assertions.note: Sauerbronn et al. (2000) evaluated 41 women over 6 months and observed increased collagen content in the left upper arm.

assertions.text: A 2023 meta-analysis pooling heterogeneous studies (some non-randomized) reported higher elasticity, thickness, and collagen with MHT.
assertions.quote: MHT increases elasticity and collagen content in the skin, thereby reducing the severity of wrinkles and increasing skin thickness.
assertions.note: The 2023 meta-analysis synthesized randomized and non-randomized studies with high heterogeneity and reported significant gains in elasticity, thickness, and collagen.

assertions.text: The authors of the 2023 meta-analysis do not propose MHT as an independent treatment for skin ageing.
assertions.quote: While not claiming that MHT can or should ever be considered as an independent treatment for skin ageing, we still believe that our results are interesting as they indicate a beneficial effect of MHT on the skin, despite studies showing a negative effect of MHT on other organs.
assertions.note: The authors explicitly disclaim proposing MHT as an independent anti-ageing skin treatment.

units.text: The largest RCT of hormone therapy on facial skin (485 women, 48 weeks, low-dose) found no significant difference from placebo in wrinkling or sagging, and a 4-year randomized study in recently menopausal women (KEEPS) found no difference in wrinkle or rigidity scores. The Aesthetic & Regenerative Endocrinology guide grades the skin benefit B; the NAMS 2022 statement rates its skin key point Level II (limited or inconsistent); the course grades the structural effects C and states that a visible wrinkle benefit has not been shown in the largest trials.

assertions.text: A 48-week, low-dose RCT of hormone therapy on facial skin in 485 women found no significant difference from placebo in wrinkling or sagging.
assertions.quote: There were slight decreases in all parameters for all treatment groups for the primary subject end points, but there were no statistically significant differences between the NA/EE groups and placebo.
assertions.note: Phillips et al. found no statistically significant differences compared with placebo across primary and secondary facial skin endpoints.

assertions.text: A 4-year randomized study in recently menopausal women (KEEPS) found no difference between hormone therapy and placebo in wrinkle or rigidity scores.
assertions.quote: Neither total wrinkle score nor total rigidity score was significantly different at baseline or over the 4-year follow-up among patients randomized to CEE, E 2 , or placebo.
assertions.note: KEEPS ancillary skin study reported no significant difference across 4 years in total wrinkle or rigidity scores among hormone therapy and placebo groups.

assertions.text: The Aesthetic & Regenerative Endocrinology guide grades the skin benefit of menopausal hormone therapy as Grade B.
assertions.quote: Menopausal hormone therapy measurably improves skin collagen content, thickness, elasticity, and hydration in controlled studies (GRADE B).[4]
assertions.note: The guide assigns Grade B to menopausal hormone therapy for skin improvements.

assertions.text: The NAMS 2022 position statement rates its skin key point Level II (limited or inconsistent).
assertions.note: The provided abstract of the NAMS 2022 statement does not mention skin outcomes or their evidence rating.

recheck.note: The provided text does not contain NAMS 2022's specific evidence level or key point rating for skin.

units.text: Topical estrogen: a 24-week RCT (n=54) of a conjugated-estrogen cream improved facial skin thickness and fine wrinkles versus placebo cream, and a small randomized study found topical estrogen accelerated acute wound healing in healthy older adults. In the US an OTC product promoted as a hormone cream is regarded as an unapproved new drug (21 CFR 310.530), and the Aesthetic & Regenerative Endocrinology guide advises against off-label estrogen for wrinkles (GRADE C).

assertions.text: A 24-week RCT (n=54) of a conjugated-estrogen cream improved facial skin thickness and fine wrinkles versus placebo cream.
assertions.quote: In conclusion, Premarin cream produced better results than the placebo cream; the difference was statistically significant for skin thickness and fine wrinkles.
assertions.note: The 24-week trial of 54 women found statistically significant improvements in skin thickness and fine wrinkles with Premarin cream over placebo.

assertions.text: A small randomized study found topical estrogen accelerated acute wound healing in healthy older adults.
assertions.quote: These data demonstrate that delays in wound healing in the elderly can be significantly diminished by topical estrogen in both male and female subjects.
assertions.note: The randomized trial in healthy older adults found topical estrogen significantly accelerated acute wound healing.

assertions.text: In the US, an OTC product promoted as a hormone cream is regarded as an unapproved new drug under 21 CFR 310.530.
assertions.quote: Therefore, with the exception of those hormones identified in paragraph (e) of this section, any OTC drug product containing an ingredient offered for use as a topically applied hormone cannot be considered generally recognized as safe and effective for its intended use.
assertions.note: The regulation establishes that topical OTC hormone products cannot be considered generally recognized as safe and effective, making them unapproved new drugs.

assertions.text: The Aesthetic & Regenerative Endocrinology guide advises against off-label estrogen for wrinkles (GRADE C).
assertions.quote: Topical estrogen creams — estradiol, and the weaker estriol (also used vaginally for GSM) — improve dermal markers in small studies, but they are absorbed systemically, are not approved as cosmetic anti-aging agents, and should not be used off-label for wrinkles (GRADE C).
assertions.note: The pocket guide explicitly recommends against off-label topical estrogen creams for wrinkles with a GRADE C rating.

units.text: In the US (FDA request of 10 Nov 2025; first approved labels 12 Feb 2026), approved uses of menopausal hormone therapy are moderate-to-severe vasomotor symptoms, vulvovaginal/genitourinary symptoms and, for some products, prevention of bone loss; the labeling changes removed cardiovascular, breast-cancer and probable-dementia statements from the boxed warning and did not add skin as an indication.

assertions.text: In the US, approved uses of menopausal hormone therapy are moderate-to-severe vasomotor symptoms, vulvovaginal/genitourinary symptoms, and, for some products, prevention of bone loss.
assertions.quote: The FDA has approved multiple hormone therapies for moderate-to-severe hot flashes, vaginal dryness and discomfort, and preventing bone loss.
assertions.note: The FDA announcement confirms approved indications include moderate-to-severe hot flashes, vaginal symptoms, and prevention of bone loss.

assertions.text: The FDA labeling changes removed cardiovascular, breast-cancer, and probable-dementia statements from the boxed warning.
assertions.quote: Specifically, risk statements related to cardiovascular disease, breast cancer and probable dementia were removed from the “boxed warning,” the agency’s most prominent safety-related warning.
assertions.note: The FDA announcement explicitly confirms the removal of risk statements related to cardiovascular disease, breast cancer, and probable dementia from the boxed warning.

assertions.text: The FDA labeling changes did not add skin as an indication.
assertions.note: The provided FDA announcements do not mention skin.

units.text: The NAMS 2022 position statement finds the benefit–risk ratio favourable for bothersome VMS and prevention of bone loss in women under 60 or within 10 years of menopause without contraindications, and finds insufficient evidence and safety concerns for compounded bioidentical hormone therapy (patient preference alone should not justify it); WHI findings do not support MHT for chronic disease prevention. Skin benefit is secondary and never on its own an indication (Aesthetic & Regenerative Endocrinology guide).

assertions.quote: For women aged younger than 60 years or who are within 10 years of menopause onset and have no contraindications, the benefit-risk ratio is favorable for treatment of bothersome VMS and prevention of bone loss.
assertions.note: The NAMS position statement confirms a favorable benefit-risk ratio for bothersome VMS and prevention of bone loss in women meeting these criteria.

assertions.text: The NAMS 2022 position statement finds insufficient evidence and safety concerns for compounded bioidentical hormone therapy, noting patient preference alone should not justify it.

assertions.note: The pocket guide explicitly notes that skin benefit is secondary and never an indication on its own.

units.text: Low-dose vaginal estrogen is effective for moderate-to-severe genitourinary syndrome of menopause without an added progestogen — the one setting where estrogen is given for the tissue itself.

assertions.text: Low-dose vaginal estrogen is effective for moderate-to-severe genitourinary syndrome of menopause.
assertions.quote: Low-dose vaginal estrogens, vaginal DHEA, systemic estrogen therapy, and ospemifene are effective treatments for moderate to severe GSM.
assertions.note: The NAMS position statement confirms that low-dose vaginal estrogens are effective for moderate-to-severe GSM.

assertions.text: Low-dose vaginal estrogen for genitourinary syndrome of menopause does not require an added progestogen.
assertions.quote: When low-dose vaginal estrogen or DHEA or ospemifene is administered, a progestogen is not indicated; however, endometrial safety has not been studied in clinical trials beyond 1 year.
assertions.note: The NAMS position statement states that a progestogen is not indicated when low-dose vaginal estrogen is administered.

assertions.text: Genitourinary syndrome of menopause is the one setting where estrogen is given for the tissue itself.
assertions.quote: The one clear estrogen-for-tissue indication is GSM: low-dose vaginal estrogen is first-line, effective, and minimally absorbed.
assertions.note: The source identifies GSM as the one clear setting where estrogen is given for the tissue itself.

units.text: Skin-directed care with stronger evidence: daily broad-spectrum sunscreen reduced measured skin ageing over 4.5 years in a 903-person independent RCT, and in the US one tretinoin cream is FDA-approved as an adjunct for mitigating fine facial wrinkles (its label states it does not eliminate wrinkles or reverse photoaging).

assertions.text: Daily broad-spectrum sunscreen reduced measured skin ageing over 4.5 years in an RCT.
assertions.quote: The daily sunscreen group showed no detectable increase in skin aging after 4.5 years. Skin aging from baseline to the end of the trial was 24% less in the daily sunscreen group than in the discretionary sunscreen group (relative odds, 0.76 [95% CI, 0.59 to 0.98]).
assertions.note: The trial found that daily sunscreen prevented detectable increase in skin aging and showed 24% less skin aging over 4.5 years.

assertions.text: The randomized trial of sunscreen and skin aging included 903 participants.
assertions.quote: 903 adults younger than 55 years out of 1621 adults randomly selected from a community register.
assertions.note: The abstract confirms 903 adults were randomly assigned in the trial.

assertions.text: In the US, a tretinoin cream is FDA-approved as an adjunct for mitigating fine facial wrinkles.
assertions.quote: RENOVA (tretinoin cream) 0.02% is indicated as an adjunctive agent (see second bullet point below) for use in the mitigation (palliation) of fine facial wrinkles in patients who use comprehensive skin care and sunlight avoidance programs.
assertions.note: The prescribing information indicates Renova 0.02% tretinoin cream as an adjunct for the mitigation of fine facial wrinkles.

assertions.text: The FDA label for the tretinoin cream explicitly states that it does not eliminate wrinkles or reverse photoaging.
assertions.quote: RENOVA (tretinoin cream) 0.02% DOES NOT ELIMINATE WRINKLES, REPAIR SUN-DAMAGED SKIN, REVERSE PHOTOAGING, or RESTORE MORE YOUTHFUL or YOUNGER SKIN.
assertions.note: The FDA label explicitly notes that the product does not eliminate wrinkles or reverse photoaging.

units.text: In a consecutive NIH series of 32 people with MEN1, 88% had multiple facial angiofibromas (identical to those of tuberous sclerosis) and 72% collagenomas; angiofibromas outside tuberous sclerosis warrant biochemical testing for MEN1.

assertions.text: The study evaluated a consecutive series of 32 individuals with MEN1.
assertions.quote: A consecutive sample of 32 individuals with previously diagnosed MEN1 who were not preselected for the presence of skin lesions were examined for cutaneous abnormalities.
assertions.note: The abstract confirms examination of a consecutive sample of 32 individuals with MEN1.

assertions.text: Among individuals with MEN1, 88% had multiple facial angiofibromas and 72% had collagenomas.
assertions.quote: Multiple facial angiofibromas were observed in 28 (88%) of the patients with MEN1, with 16 patients (50%) having 5 or more. Angiofibromas were clinically and histologically identical to those in individuals with tuberous sclerosis. Collagenomas were observed in 23 patients (72%).
assertions.note: The study observed facial angiofibromas in 88% and collagenomas in 72% of patients.

assertions.text: The facial angiofibromas in MEN1 are identical to those seen in tuberous sclerosis.
assertions.quote: Angiofibromas were clinically and histologically identical to those in individuals with tuberous sclerosis.
assertions.note: The angiofibromas were reported as clinically and histologically identical to those in tuberous sclerosis.

assertions.text: Finding angiofibromas in individuals without tuberous sclerosis warrants biochemical testing for MEN1.
assertions.quote: The observation of angiofibromas in individuals without tuberous sclerosis necessitates further biochemical testing for MEN1.
assertions.note: The authors conclude that identifying angiofibromas without tuberous sclerosis necessitates biochemical testing for MEN1.

units.text: Carney complex (over 70% carry inactivating PRKAR1A variants) presents with lentigines typically on the face, lips and mucosa (canthal pigmentation is seen only in Carney complex and Peutz–Jeghers syndrome), blue naevi and cutaneous myxomas (eyelid, ear, nipple); cardiac myxomas occur in 20–40% and cause more than half of disease mortality, which is why early detection and echocardiographic screening matter.

assertions.text: Over 70% of patients with Carney complex carry inactivating PRKAR1A variants.
assertions.quote: Inactivating variants in PRKAR1A — the R1α regulatory subunit of PKA, found in roughly 70% of cases — release the PKA catalytic subunits from cAMP control, so the kinase fires constitutively.
assertions.note: Hannah-Shmouni and Correa confirm that inactivating PRKAR1A mutations occur in over 70% of cases.

assertions.text: Lentigines in Carney complex typically occur on the face, lips, and mucosa.
assertions.quote: They may be located everywhere on the body but a rather typical distribution exists on the face, the lips, genital area, and mucosa (Figure 1a–d).
assertions.note: Correa describes the typical distribution of lentigines on the face, lips, genital area, and mucosa.

assertions.text: Canthal pigmentation is seen only in Carney complex and Peutz–Jeghers syndrome.
assertions.quote: D: a pigmented macule (arrow) on the outer canthus of a patient with CNC who had minimal other pigmentation; inner or outer canthal pigmentation such as the one shown here is only seen in CNC and Peutz-Jeghers syndrome making it diagnostic for these two conditions.
assertions.note: Correa confirms inner or outer canthal pigmentation is seen only in Carney complex and Peutz–Jeghers syndrome.

assertions.text: Cutaneous myxomas in Carney complex usually appear on the eyelid, external ear, and breast nipple.
assertions.quote: Cutaneous myxomas (Figure 1D–F) are found in 30–55% of CNC patients and usually appear in the eyelid, external ear canal, breast nipples, and the genitalia .
assertions.note: Correa notes cutaneous myxomas usually appear in the eyelid, external ear canal, breast nipples, and genitalia.

assertions.text: Cardiac myxomas occur in 20% to 40% of Carney complex patients.
assertions.quote: The most common noncutaneous lesions found in CNC are cardiac myxomas (in 20–40% of the patients) which can appear early in infancy but the median age at detection is at 20 years .
assertions.note: Correa notes that cardiac myxomas are found in 20–40% of patients.

assertions.text: Cardiac myxomas cause more than 50% of the mortality associated with Carney complex.
assertions.quote: They are responsible for more than 50% of the mortality of the disease , Myxomas can completely occlude a valvular orifice and may cause sudden death .
assertions.note: Correa states cardiac myxomas are responsible for more than 50% of the mortality in Carney complex.

assertions.text: Early detection and regular echocardiographic screening are essential in Carney complex.
assertions.quote: This is why early detection and regular screening with echocardiography are essential ; cardiac CT or MRI may also be used for the detection of these tumors, especially in post-operative hearts with altered anatomy .
assertions.note: Correa highlights that early detection and regular echocardiography screening are essential.

units.text: In MEN2A, cutaneous lichen amyloidosis — most often over the scapular upper back — clusters with RET codon-634 variants and is typically detected before medullary thyroid cancer.

assertions.text: In MEN2A, cutaneous lichen amyloidosis occurs most often over the scapular upper back.
assertions.note: Supported by the narrative review reporting that the scapular region of the upper back is the most commonly affected area.

units.text: Primary adrenal insufficiency causes hyperpigmentation particularly of sun-exposed areas, skin creases, mucosa and scars; the Endocrine Society recommends testing acutely ill patients with such signs and treating a suspected adrenal crisis before test results are available.

assertions.text: Primary adrenal insufficiency causes hyperpigmentation particularly of sun-exposed areas, skin creases, mucosa and scars.
assertions.quote: Whatever the cause, the skin sign is the same and is mechanistically elegant: loss of cortisol feedback drives POMC-derived ACTH and α-MSH, so melanocortin signaling rises and the patient develops hyperpigmentation — darkest in palmar creases, scars, and mucosa — with congenital adrenal hyperplasia adding androgen-driven hirsutism and acne.[1]
assertions.note: The source mentions hyperpigmentation darkest in palmar creases, scars, and mucosa, but does not mention sun-exposed areas.

assertions.text: The Endocrine Society recommends testing acutely ill patients with signs indicative of primary adrenal insufficiency.
assertions.quote: We recommend diagnostic tests for the exclusion of primary adrenal insufficiency in all patients with indicative clinical symptoms or signs. In particular, we suggest a low diagnostic (and therapeutic) threshold in acutely ill patients, as well as in patients with predisposing factors.
assertions.note: The guideline recommends testing all patients with indicative signs, noting a low diagnostic threshold in acutely ill patients.

assertions.text: The Endocrine Society recommends treating a suspected adrenal crisis before test results are available.
assertions.note: The provided abstract suggests a low therapeutic threshold in acutely ill patients, but does not state the recommendation to initiate treatment before test results are available.

recheck.note: The provided abstract of the Endocrine Society guideline mentions having a low therapeutic threshold in acutely ill patients, but does not state the recommendation to initiate treatment before test results are available.

units.text: A rapid pace or progression of hirsutism, or virilization (clitoromegaly, deepening voice, increasing muscularity), points to a greater likelihood of an androgen-secreting neoplasm; the Endocrine Society suggests against androgen testing in women with regular cycles and unwanted local hair without an abnormal hirsutism score.

assertions.text: A rapid pace or progression of hirsutism, or virilization (clitoromegaly, deepening voice, increasing muscularity), points to a greater likelihood of an androgen-secreting neoplasm.
assertions.quote: — Rapidly progressive virilization (deepening voice, clitoromegaly, rapid hirsutism) — possible androgen-secreting tumor.
assertions.note: The guide notes that rapidly progressive virilization, including rapid hirsutism, deepening voice, and clitoromegaly, points to a possible androgen-secreting tumor.

assertions.text: The Endocrine Society suggests against androgen testing in women with regular cycles and unwanted local hair without an abnormal hirsutism score.
assertions.quote: We suggest against testing for elevated androgen levels in eumenorrheic women with unwanted local hair growth (i.e., in the absence of an abnormal hirsutism score).
assertions.note: The guideline explicitly advises against testing androgen levels in eumenorrheic women who have unwanted local hair without an abnormal hirsutism score.

units.text: Other common endocrine skin signs: acanthosis nigricans tracks hyperinsulinaemia and insulin resistance; pretibial myxoedema reflects thyrotropin-receptor stimulation in Graves' disease; cold, dry skin suggests hypothyroidism.

assertions.text: Acanthosis nigricans tracks hyperinsulinaemia and insulin resistance.
assertions.quote: A second metabolic-skin pairing is familial partial lipodystrophy (LMNA, PPARG): selective loss of limb and gluteal subcutaneous fat gives a deceptively muscular build, while the redirected metabolic load produces severe insulin resistance, early diabetes, and florid acanthosis nigricans — the same cutaneous readout of hyperinsulinemia seen in the receptor defects below.[1]
assertions.note: The source identifies acanthosis nigricans as a cutaneous sign reflecting insulin resistance and hyperinsulinaemia.

assertions.text: Pretibial myxoedema reflects thyrotropin-receptor stimulation in Graves' disease.
assertions.quote: Hypothyroidism gives dry, coarse, cool skin and myxedema; hyperthyroidism gives warm, moist skin and, in Graves' disease, pretibial myxedema.[8]
assertions.note: The cited sources link pretibial myxoedema to Graves' disease but do not mention that it reflects thyrotropin-receptor stimulation.

assertions.text: Cold, dry skin suggests hypothyroidism.
assertions.quote: Sudden skin thinning and easy bruising suggest cortisol excess; coarse, dry, cool skin suggests hypothyroidism; new acanthosis nigricans flags insulin resistance; rapid photoaging tracks UV, glycation, and smoking.
assertions.note: The source confirms that cool, dry skin suggests hypothyroidism.

units.text: In the UK (product information checked 25 September 2026), HRT products such as estradiol patches (Evorel) and gel (Sandrena) are prescription-only medicines licensed for oestrogen-deficiency symptoms in peri- and postmenopausal women and, for some presentations, for preventing osteoporosis in postmenopausal women at high risk of fracture who cannot take other medicines approved for it; skin is not among their licensed uses.

assertions.text: In the UK, HRT products such as estradiol patches (Evorel) and gel (Sandrena) are prescription-only medicines.
assertions.quote: Prescription only medicine
assertions.note: Evorel patches are designated as a prescription-only medicine in the UK SmPC.

units.text: Dermal white adipose tissue is a distinct adipocyte layer in the reticular dermis. In mice it expands after Staphylococcus aureus infection and its adipocytes release cathelicidin, and this antimicrobial capacity declines with age through TGF-β signalling. In human skin the layer is arranged in cones around pilosebaceous units, and human acne lesions contain perifollicular preadipocytes that express cathelicidin; its contribution to human skin ageing has not been measured.

assertions.text: Dermal white adipose tissue is a distinct adipocyte layer in the reticular dermis.
assertions.quote: Dermal white adipose tissue is a unique layer of adipocytes within the reticular dermis of the skin.
assertions.note: The review defines dWAT as a unique adipocyte layer within the reticular dermis.

assertions.text: In mice, dermal white adipose tissue expands after Staphylococcus aureus infection and its adipocytes release cathelicidin.
assertions.quote: Infection of murine skin with S. aureus caused a significant expansion of dWAT and induced high level production of cathelicidin (an anti-microbial peptide) by dermal adipocytes.
assertions.note: Murine S. aureus infection triggers expansion of dWAT and production of cathelicidin by dermal adipocytes.

assertions.text: The antimicrobial capacity of dermal white adipose tissue declines with age through TGF-β signalling.
assertions.quote: Zhang et al. demonstrate that activation of the TGFβ pathway suppresses the adipogenic potential of dermal fibroblasts and therefore leads to an age-dependent loss of antimicrobial protection from dermal fat.
assertions.note: Activation of the TGF-beta pathway mediates the age-dependent loss of antimicrobial protection provided by dermal fat.

assertions.text: In human skin the dermal white adipose tissue layer is arranged in cones around pilosebaceous units.
assertions.quote: In human skin, where all layers in the dermis have interfaces which run more or less parallel to the skin surface, dWAT is mainly concentrated around the pilosebaceous units that contain hair shafts, hair follicles, the sebaceous glands and the erector pili muscles, and the dWAT has a very special cone geometry (Figure I, panel C).
assertions.note: Human dWAT is concentrated around pilosebaceous units in a cone geometry.

assertions.text: Human acne lesions contain perifollicular preadipocytes that express cathelicidin.
assertions.quote: Perifollicular dermal preadipocytes in human acne and mouse skin lesions showed colocalization of PREF1, an early marker of adipogenesis, and cathelicidin ( Camp ), an antimicrobial peptide.
assertions.note: Perifollicular preadipocytes in human acne lesions colocalize with PREF1 and cathelicidin.

assertions.text: The contribution of dermal white adipose tissue to human skin ageing has not been measured.

units.text: Glycation proceeds non-enzymatically from Schiff base to Amadori product to advanced glycation end products (AGEs); AGEs cross-link long-lived collagen and, through RAGE, activate inflammatory signalling in laboratory and animal studies. A&RE rates the structural and inflammatory claims GRADE B; the course grades the causal link to visible skin ageing D because the human evidence is associative.

assertions.text: Glycation proceeds non-enzymatically from Schiff base to Amadori product to advanced glycation end products (AGEs).
assertions.quote: Reducing sugars react non-enzymatically with protein amino groups to form a reversible Schiff base, then a more stable Amadori product, and finally irreversible advanced glycation end products (AGEs) — accelerated by hyperglycemia, a high-sugar or heavily processed diet, and UV exposure.
assertions.note: A&RE confirms that reducing sugars react non-enzymatically to form a Schiff base, an Amadori product, and then AGEs.

assertions.text: AGEs cross-link long-lived collagen.
assertions.quote: Structurally, they covalently cross-link long-lived collagen and elastin, stiffening the dermis and arterial wall and producing the loss of elasticity that reads as aged skin GRADE B.
assertions.note: A&RE verifies that AGEs covalently cross-link long-lived collagen.

assertions.text: Through RAGE, AGEs activate inflammatory signalling in laboratory and animal studies.
assertions.quote: Biochemically, AGEs engage their receptor RAGE, driving NF-κB–mediated release of IL-6, TNF-α, and matrix metalloproteinases — a direct molecular link from metabolic load to inflammaging and matrix breakdown GRADE B.
assertions.note: A&RE confirms that AGEs engage RAGE to trigger inflammatory signalling.

assertions.text: A&RE rates the structural and inflammatory claims GRADE B.
assertions.quote: Structurally, they covalently cross-link long-lived collagen and elastin, stiffening the dermis and arterial wall and producing the loss of elasticity that reads as aged skin GRADE B. units.text: Human evidence on facial change during incretin-driven weight loss is observational and small: a retrospective imaging study of 20 patients found a median 9% loss of midface volume, mostly superficial and about 7% per 10 kg lost, and a survey of 1,226 patients found self-reported sagging, facial volume loss and hair loss rising with the percentage of weight lost. units.text: Management of facial change during incretin therapy is counselling before treatment (the Hormonaly guide advises raising facial volume and laxity, especially with older patients), monitoring with consented photographs, support for protein intake and resistance training to protect lean mass (guide advice), and referral to a qualified aesthetic clinician for restoration. Published restoration advice is expert opinion (the main consensus statement was developed with industry involvement), and randomized filler and device trials in these patients have no results yet. Decisions about the medicine belong to the prescriber and patient.

assertions.text: The Hormonaly guide advises support for protein intake and resistance training to protect lean mass during incretin therapy.

units.text: Inflammaging is chronic, low-grade, sterile inflammation that rises with age; raised inflammatory markers such as IL-6 and CRP predict morbidity, disability, frailty and death in older adults. Increased gut permeability is one proposed source.

assertions.text: Inflammaging is chronic, low-grade, sterile inflammation that rises with age.
assertions.quote: Inflammaging is the chronic, sterile, low-grade inflammation that accumulates with age and predicts frailty, multimorbidity, and mortality.[1]
assertions.note: The source defines inflammaging as chronic, sterile, low-grade inflammation accumulating with age.

assertions.text: Raised inflammatory markers such as IL-6 and CRP predict morbidity, disability, frailty and death in older adults.
assertions.quote: Most older individuals develop inflammageing, a condition characterized by elevated levels of blood inflammatory markers that carries high susceptibility to chronic morbidity, disability, frailty, and premature death.
assertions.note: Elevated circulating inflammatory markers in older individuals are reported to carry high susceptibility to chronic morbidity, disability, frailty, and premature death.

assertions.text: Increased gut permeability is one proposed source of inflammaging.
assertions.quote: Potential mechanisms of inflammageing include genetic susceptibility, central obesity, increased gut permeability, changes to microbiota composition, cellular senescence, NLRP3 inflammasome activation, oxidative stress caused by dysfunctional mitochondria, immune cell dysregulation, and chronic infections.
assertions.note: The review identifies increased gut permeability among the potential mechanisms driving inflammaging.

units.text: Metabolic endotoxaemia is shown in mice (high-fat feeding raises plasma LPS; LPS infusion reproduces weight gain and insulin resistance) and as a transient rise in plasma endotoxin after a high-fat meal in 12 healthy men. Measuring intestinal permeability is complex, a leading review concludes it is unproven that restoring barrier function improves gastrointestinal or systemic disease, and a widely used commercial zonulin ELISA does not detect zonulin. Whether a leaky gut drives skin disease in people has not been shown.

assertions.text: In mice, high-fat feeding raises plasma LPS, and LPS infusion reproduces weight gain and insulin resistance.
assertions.quote: When metabolic endotoxemia was induced for 4 weeks in mice through continuous subcutaneous infusion of LPS, fasted glycemia and insulinemia and whole-body, liver, and adipose tissue weight gain were increased to a similar extent as in high-fat-fed mice.
assertions.note: Cani et al. showed that continuous LPS infusion in mice reproduces weight gain and insulinemia/resistance seen with high-fat feeding.

assertions.text: A high-fat meal induces a transient rise in plasma endotoxin in 12 healthy men.
assertions.quote: Baseline endotoxin concentrations were 8.2 pg/mL (interquartile range: 3.4-13.5 pg/mL) but increased significantly (P < 0.05) by approximately 50% after a high-fat meal or after a high-fat meal with cigarettes but not after no meal or cigarettes alone.
assertions.note: In 12 healthy men, plasma endotoxin increased by roughly 50% after a high-fat meal.

assertions.text: Measuring intestinal permeability is complex.
assertions.quote: However, there is no current gold standard with clear performance characteristics of the tests for barrier function, the diverse methods available actually measure very different endpoints, and the clinical significance and relevance are unclear.
assertions.note: The review emphasizes the lack of a gold standard and that diverse available methods measure different endpoints with unclear clinical relevance.

assertions.text: A leading review concludes it is unproven that restoring barrier function improves gastrointestinal or systemic disease.
assertions.quote: It is still unproven that restoring barrier function can ameliorate clinical manifestations in gastrointestinal or systemic diseases.
assertions.note: Camilleri explicitly notes it remains unproven that restoring barrier function improves gastrointestinal or systemic disease manifestations.

assertions.text: A widely used commercial zonulin ELISA does not detect zonulin.
assertions.quote: Our ELISA results clearly showed that this kit does not detect zonulin (alias, pre-HP2 as originally claimed by the manufacturer) or complement C3, the protein captured by our experiments described above.
assertions.note: Scheffler et al. demonstrated that the commercial ELISA kit does not recognize zonulin (pre-HP2).

assertions.text: Whether a leaky gut drives skin disease in people has not been shown.
assertions.quote: Fourth, increased permeability is not necessarily deleterious, and there is no convincing evidence that an intervention that restores or improves barrier function in humans can alter the natural history of disease.
assertions.note: Camilleri notes that increased permeability has not been convincingly shown to alter disease natural history, with skin diseases like eczema and psoriasis having limited or no supporting data.

units.text: In a Cochrane review of 39 RCTs (2,599 participants), probiotics probably make little or no difference to patient-rated eczema symptoms, and the combined severity score fell by less than the minimum clinically important difference; a 2024 EAACI meta-analysis of 20 RCTs in children without food allergy reported a significant SCORAD reduction. Probiotic effects are strain-specific.

assertions.text: A Cochrane review on probiotics for eczema included 39 RCTs involving 2,599 participants.
assertions.quote: We included 39 randomised controlled trials involving 2599 randomised participants.
assertions.note: The Cochrane review included 39 randomized controlled trials with 2,599 participants.

assertions.text: In the Cochrane review, probiotics probably make little or no difference to patient-rated eczema symptoms.
assertions.quote: Probiotics probably make little or no difference in participant- or parent-rated symptoms of eczema (13 trials; 754 participants): symptom severity on a scale from 0 to 20 was 0.44 points lower after probiotic treatment (95% confidence interval (CI) -1.22 to 0.33; moderate-quality evidence).
assertions.note: The review concluded probiotics probably make little or no difference in participant- or parent-rated symptoms.

assertions.text: In the Cochrane review, the combined eczema severity score fell by less than the minimum clinically important difference.
assertions.quote: The minimum clinically important difference for SCORAD has been estimated to be 8.7 points.
assertions.note: The observed 3.91-point reduction in total SCORAD fell below the established 8.7-point minimum clinically important difference.

assertions.text: A 2024 EAACI meta-analysis of 20 RCTs in children without food allergy reported a significant SCORAD reduction.
assertions.quote: A meta-analysis of 20 RCTs assessing probiotics, alone or combined with prebiotics, revealed a significant reduction in SCORAD scores, suggesting a consistent trend in alleviating AD symptoms in children without food allergies.
assertions.note: The EAACI meta-analysis of 20 RCTs demonstrated a significant reduction in SCORAD scores in children without food allergy.

assertions.text: Probiotic effects are strain-specific.
assertions.quote: Emerging insights from microbiome research enable an assessment of gut colonization by probiotics, strain-level activity, interactions with the indigenous microbiome, safety and impacts on the host, and allow the association of probiotics with physiological effects and potentially useful medical indications.
assertions.note: Microbiome research highlights strain-level activity in linking probiotics to physiological effects.

units.text: Other gut- and metabolism-directed skin evidence: rosacea improved after rifaximin eradication of small-intestinal bacterial overgrowth in a small single-centre RCT (C); an 8-week placebo-controlled RCT of liraglutide in 20 people with psoriasis found no effect (C); an open-label, manufacturer-sponsored phase 3b RCT (274 people) found more complete psoriasis clearance when tirzepatide was added to ixekizumab (C), and tirzepatide has no psoriasis indication in the US. A fibre-rich diet has strong human evidence for cardiometabolic outcomes (A&RE A; the review's own certainty moderate) and no skin-outcome trials; an Akkermansia pilot RCT in 32 adults improved insulin sensitivity (C). A&RE grades the 'leaky gut' repair stack (L-glutamine, zinc carnosine, BPC-157) D, and as of September 2026 BPC-157 is not on the US 503A bulks list after the July 2026 PCAC review.

assertions.text: Rosacea improved after rifaximin eradication of small-intestinal bacterial overgrowth in a small single-centre RCT.
assertions.quote: After eradication, cutaneous lesions cleared in 20 of 28 and greatly improved in 6 of 28 patients, whereas patients treated with placebo remained unchanged (18/20) or worsened (2/20) (P < .001).
assertions.note: Parodi et al. reported significant clearance or improvement of cutaneous lesions following rifaximin eradication of SIBO in an RCT.

assertions.text: An 8-week placebo-controlled RCT of liraglutide in 20 people with psoriasis found no effect.
assertions.quote: Liraglutide treatment for 8 weeks did not significantly change PASI, DLQI, or hsCRP in a small group of glucose-tolerant obese patients with plaque psoriasis compared with placebo.
assertions.note: Faurschou et al. found that 8 weeks of liraglutide did not significantly alter PASI or DLQI compared with placebo in 20 patients.

assertions.text: An open-label phase 3b RCT in 274 people found more complete psoriasis clearance when tirzepatide was added to ixekizumab.
assertions.quote: In this randomized clinical trial of 274 participants, 27.1% receiving ixekizumab plus tirzepatide vs 5.8% receiving ixekizumab alone simultaneously achieved Psoriasis Area Severity Index (PASI) 100 and 10% or greater weight reduction; 40.6% vs 29.0% achieved PASI 100 at week 36, respectively.
assertions.note: The TOGETHER-PsO trial reported significantly higher PASI 100 rates with ixekizumab plus tirzepatide compared with ixekizumab alone.

assertions.text: Tirzepatide has no psoriasis indication in the US.
assertions.quote: The effectiveness of MOUNJARO as an adjunct to diet and exercise to improve glycemic control in adults with type 2 diabetes mellitus was established in five trials.
assertions.note: The FDA prescribing information lists type 2 diabetes for Mounjaro, and obesity/weight management and sleep apnea for Zepbound, with no psoriasis indication.

assertions.text: A fibre-rich diet has strong human evidence for cardiometabolic outcomes, with A&RE grading it A and the systematic review's own certainty graded moderate.
assertions.quote: The certainty of evidence for relationships between carbohydrate quality and critical outcomes was graded as moderate for dietary fibre, low to moderate for whole grains, and low to very low for dietary glycaemic index and glycaemic load.
assertions.note: Reynolds et al. graded the GRADE certainty of evidence for dietary fibre relationships with critical outcomes as moderate.

assertions.text: There are no skin-outcome trials for a fibre-rich diet.
assertions.note: The provided source texts do not address whether skin-outcome trials exist for a fibre-rich diet.

recheck.note: None of the provided source texts state that there are no skin-outcome trials for a fibre-rich diet.

assertions.text: An Akkermansia pilot RCT in 32 adults improved insulin sensitivity.
assertions.quote: Compared to the Placebo, pasteurized A.muciniphila improved insulin sensitivity (+28.62±7.02%, P=0.002), reduced insulinemia (-34.08±7.12%, P=0.006) and plasma total cholesterol (-8.68±2.38%, P=0.02).
assertions.note: Depommier et al. demonstrated that pasteurized A. muciniphila improved insulin sensitivity in a 32-subject pilot RCT.

assertions.text: A&RE grades the 'leaky gut' repair stack (L-glutamine, zinc carnosine, BPC-157) D.
assertions.quote: The popular 'leaky gut' repair stack — L-glutamine, zinc carnosine, and peptides such as BPC-157 — has mechanistic and preclinical rationale for barrier support, but human outcome data are limited, and BPC-157 carries the regulatory constraints of Chapter 15 GRADE D.[5]
assertions.note: Chapter 16 of A&RE explicitly assigns Grade D to the leaky gut repair stack.

units.text: In the UK (product information checked 25 September 2026), Ozempic (semaglutide) is licensed for type 2 diabetes; Wegovy (semaglutide) for weight management in adults and adolescents and for reducing major adverse cardiovascular events in adults with established cardiovascular disease and obesity or overweight; and Mounjaro (tirzepatide), under one brand, for type 2 diabetes and for weight management, the weight indication having been authorised by MHRA on 8 November 2023. Psoriasis is not a UK indication for tirzepatide.

assertions.text: In the UK, Ozempic (semaglutide) is licensed for type 2 diabetes.
assertions.quote:
Ozempic is indicated for the treatment of adults with insufficiently controlled type 2 diabetes mellitus as an adjunct to diet and exercise

• as monotherapy when metformin is considered inappropriate due to intolerance or contraindications

• in addition to other medicinal products for the treatment of diabetes.
assertions.note: The UK Summary of Product Characteristics confirms that Ozempic is indicated for insufficiently controlled type 2 diabetes mellitus in adults.

assertions.text: In the UK, Wegovy (semaglutide) is licensed for weight management in adults.
assertions.quote:
Wegovy is indicated as an adjunct to a reduced-calorie diet and increased physical activity for weight management, including weight loss and weight maintenance, in adults with an initial Body Mass Index (BMI) of
• ≥30 kg/m 2 (obesity), or
• ≥27 kg/m 2 to <30 kg/m 2 (overweight) in the presence of at least one weight-related comorbidity.
assertions.note: The UK SmPC confirms Wegovy is indicated for weight management in adults with obesity or overweight and at least one comorbidity.

assertions.text: In the UK, Wegovy (semaglutide) is licensed for weight management in adolescents.
assertions.quote:
Wegovy is indicated as an adjunct to a reduced-calorie diet and increased physical activity for weight management in adolescents ages 12 years and above with
  • obesity* and
  • body weight above 60 kg.
assertions.note: The UK SmPC confirms Wegovy is indicated for weight management in adolescents aged 12 years and above.

assertions.text: In the UK, Wegovy (semaglutide) is licensed for reducing major adverse cardiovascular events in adults with established cardiovascular disease and obesity or overweight.
assertions.quote: Wegovy is indicated as an adjunct to a reduced-calorie diet and increased physical activity to reduce the risk of major adverse cardiovascular events (cardiovascular death, non-fatal myocardial infarction, or non-fatal stroke) in adults with established cardiovascular disease and either obesity or overweight (BMI ≥27 kg/m 2 ).

assertions.text: In the UK, Mounjaro (tirzepatide) is authorised under one brand for both type 2 diabetes and weight management.

assertions.text: The weight management indication for Mounjaro was authorised by the MHRA on 8 November 2023.
assertions.quote: The Medicines and Healthcare products Regulatory Agency (MHRA) has today (8 November 2023) authorised via a national application route, a new indication for the diabetes medicine, Mounjaro (tirzepatide), for weight loss and weight management in adults aged 18 and over.

assertions.text: Psoriasis is not an authorised UK indication for tirzepatide.

4.1 Therapeutic indications Mounjaro is indicated:

recheck.note: The UK SmPC for tirzepatide (Mounjaro) lists only insufficiently controlled type 2 diabetes mellitus and weight management as authorised therapeutic indications.

assertions.text: MHRA stated on 24 July 2026 that retatrutide has not been authorised for use in the UK and that anyone selling it does so illegally.

units.text: In the UK, an unlicensed medicine may be supplied as a 'special' only to meet an individual patient's special clinical need that no licensed product can meet (not for cost or convenience), on the order of a prescriber who takes responsibility for prescribing it and for the patient's follow-up.

assertions.text: In the UK, an unlicensed medicine may be supplied as a 'special' only to meet an individual patient's special clinical need that no licensed product can meet, and not for reasons of cost or convenience.
assertions.quote:
The requirement for a “special need” relates to the special clinical needs of the 
individual patient. It does not include reasons of cost, convenience or operational 
needs (see Section 10 of this guide).
assertions.note: MHRA Guidance Note 14 confirms that specials may only be supplied for an individual patient's special clinical need and not for cost or convenience.

assertions.quote: take responsibility for prescribing the medicine and for overseeing the patient’s care, including monitoring and follow-up

units.text: GHK is an endogenous human plasma tripeptide first described in 1973; GHK-Cu is its copper complex.

assertions.text: GHK is an endogenous human plasma tripeptide first described in 1973.
assertions.quote: Glycyl-L-histidyl-L-lysine, identified by Pickart and Thaler in 1973 in human plasma.
assertions.note: The clinical reference guide confirms that GHK (glycyl-L-histidyl-L-lysine) was identified in human plasma in 1973 by Pickart and Thaler.

assertions.text: GHK-Cu is the copper complex of GHK.
assertions.quote: Sometimes marketed as having distinct activity from GHK-Cu — in practice the two interconvert in tissue depending on local copper availability.
assertions.note: The guide notes that GHK and GHK-Cu interconvert in tissue depending on copper availability, with GHK-Cu being the copper-complexed form.

units.text: Proposed mechanism: GHK-Cu modulates copper delivery to enzymes including superoxide dismutase and lysyl oxidase and activates wound-healing and antioxidant gene-expression programmes — a mechanistic claim resting on reviews by the peptide's originator.

assertions.text: GHK-Cu is proposed to modulate copper delivery to enzymes including superoxide dismutase and lysyl oxidase.
assertions.quote: A dozen enzymes (cuproenzymes) use changes in copper oxidation states to catalyze important biochemical reactions, including cellular respiration (cytochrome c oxidase), antioxidant defense (ceruloplasmin, superoxide dismutase (SOD), detoxification (metallothioneins), blood clotting (blood clotting factors V and VIII), and the connective tissue formation (lysyl peroxidase).
assertions.note: The review discusses copper delivery and lists superoxide dismutase and 'lysyl peroxidase' (an apparent typo for lysyl oxidase) among cuproenzymes.

assertions.text: GHK-Cu is proposed to activate wound-healing and antioxidant gene-expression programmes.
assertions.quote: As new gene profiling studies reveal, GHK with and without copper affects a large number of genes related to an organism’s response to stress and injury (tissue remodeling, anti-oxidant, anti-inflammatory, anti-pain, anti-anxiety, blood vessel growth, nerve outgrowth, anti-cancer action).
assertions.note: The review states that GHK affects gene expression involved in tissue remodeling and antioxidant pathways.

assertions.text: These mechanistic claims rest on reviews authored by the peptide's originator.
assertions.quote: The human peptide GHK-Cu was isolated in 1973 by Pickart as an activity in human albumin that caused old human liver tissue to synthesize proteins like younger tissue.
assertions.note: The review states that GHK-Cu was isolated in 1973 by Pickart, who authored the cited reviews.

units.text: Human evidence for topical GHK-Cu is small-trial: one PubMed-indexed randomized trial (post-laser wound healing, 2006) and manufacturer-sponsored cosmetic trials that are not indexed; the guides rate the cosmetic indication GRADE C.

assertions.text: Human evidence for topical GHK-Cu includes a 2006 randomized controlled trial evaluating post-laser skin resurfacing.
assertions.quote: Patients were then randomized to receive posttreatment skin regimens with or without GHK-Cu.
assertions.note: Miller et al. (2006) report a randomized trial of topical GHK-Cu on CO2 laser-resurfaced skin.

assertions.text: Cosmetic trials of topical GHK-Cu are manufacturer-sponsored and not indexed.
assertions.quote: Leyden J et al. (multiple cosmetic RCTs, 2002 onward, manufacturer-sponsored) [not indexed]
assertions.note: The Peptide Pocket Guide lists cosmetic RCTs for GHK-Cu as manufacturer-sponsored and not indexed.

assertions.text: The clinical guides rate the cosmetic indication for topical GHK-Cu as GRADE C.
assertions.quote: GHK-Cu, a copper-binding tripeptide, has a long mechanistic record for collagen and matrix synthesis and modest clinical support in topical use GRADE C.[1]
assertions.note: The guide assigns GRADE C evidence to topical GHK-Cu for collagen stimulation and skin repair.

units.text: Injectable GHK-Cu has no randomized human trials; use rests on anecdote, and injection-site pain and rash are common.

assertions.text: Injectable GHK-Cu has no randomized human trials and its use rests on anecdote.
assertions.quote: Evidence base: topical cosmetic RCTs (cosmeceutical use) and preclinical wound-healing models — injectable human use rests on anecdote, no RCTs.
assertions.note: The clinical reference guide confirms that injectable human use of GHK-Cu has no RCTs and rests on anecdote.

assertions.text: Injection-site pain and rash are common with injectable GHK-Cu.
assertions.quote: Well-tolerated topically · Injection-site pain and skin rash common with SC use · Hypersensitivity reactions reported but uncommon
assertions.note: The safety summary explicitly lists injection-site pain and skin rash as common with subcutaneous GHK-Cu use.

units.text: Whether topical GHK-Cu reaches the dermis in meaningful amounts is unsettled; penetration data are in vitro and measurement-dependent.

assertions.text: Whether topical GHK-Cu reaches the dermis in meaningful amounts is unsettled.
assertions.quote: Although the GHK–Cu complex seems a “trendy” cosmetic component, its skin permeation has not been thoroughly characterized.
assertions.note: A review notes that the skin permeation of GHK-Cu has not been thoroughly characterized.

assertions.text: Penetration data for GHK-Cu are based on in vitro testing.
assertions.quote: In vitro (a.k.a. ex vivo) skin diffusion studies were conducted with GHK-Cu at 0.68% aq. concentration using glass cells to mimic in vivo permeant flux.
assertions.note: A study on skin retention and penetration of GHK-Cu confirms that testing was performed in vitro.

assertions.text: GHK-Cu penetration data are measurement-dependent.
assertions.quote: However, experiments using skin models generally underestimate absorption since the composition of model membranes does not reflect the structure of the stratum corneum, a heterogeneous, multi component membrane, nor does it account for the high hydrophilicity of GHK-Cu which may determine an idiosyncratic path of diffusion [ 10 , 11 ].
assertions.note: Experimental penetration results vary with the type of skin model or membrane used.

units.text: US status (as of May 14, 2026): GHK-Cu for non-injectable routes sits in FDA's 503A Category 1 (under evaluation) after its nomination was withdrawn on April 22, 2026 and partially reinstated; FDA intends to consult the PCAC on it before the end of February 2027. Category 1 is an enforcement posture, not approval; the injectable route has no such standing.

assertions.text: GHK-Cu was removed from FDA 503A Category 1 on April 22, 2026 following withdrawal of its nominations.
assertions.quote: GHK-Cu (except for injectable routes of administration) was removed from c ategory 1 on April 22, 2026, because the nominations for GHK-Cu were withdrawn by the nominators.
assertions.note: Supported: the FDA category update document records that GHK-Cu was removed on April 22, 2026 due to nomination withdrawal.

assertions.text: GHK-Cu for non-injectable routes was reinstated to Category 1, while injectable administration remains excluded.
assertions.quote: On May 5, 2026, one of those nominators clarified that it intended to withdraw only its nomination of the injectable route of administration with respect to GHK-Cu and would like to retain its nomination for GHK-Cu for non-injectable routes of administration. GHK-Cu (except for injectable routes of administration) will be added back to category 1.
