units.text: Melanotan II is approved for no therapeutic indication. US: FDA's compounding safety page (current as of 22 April 2026) lists it among nominations withdrawn from Category 2, citing impurity and immunogenicity risks and published reports of melanoma, PRES, sympathomimetic toxidrome and priapism. UK: MHRA (FOI 24/274, 17 April 2024) classes injectable products as medicines, says unauthorised medicines may not be sold, supplied or advertised, and advises users to stop immediately. Australia: TGA (17 August 2026) — prescription-only medicine, not approved as a tanning agent, no product on the ARTG.

assertions.text: Melanotan II is approved for no therapeutic indication.
assertions.quote: Melanotan II is a synthetic cyclic α‐MSH analogue that is a nonselective MCR agonist and is not approved for use in any therapeutic indication.
assertions.note: The review states directly that Melanotan II is not approved for any therapeutic indication.

assertions.text: The FDA compounding safety page (current as of 22 April 2026) lists Melanotan II among bulk drug substances nominated but withdrawn from Category 2, citing impurity and immunogenicity risks and published reports of melanoma, PRES, sympathomimetic toxidrome, and priapism.
assertions.quote: Compounded drugs containing Melanotan II may pose risk for immunogenicity for certain routes of administration due to the potential for aggregation or peptide-related impurities. Published case reports discuss serious adverse events including melanoma, posterior reversible encephalopathy syndrome, sympathomimetic toxidrome and priapism.
assertions.note: The FDA page lists Melanotan II under withdrawn bulk drug substances and explicitly cites these risks and reported adverse events.

assertions.text: MHRA (FOI 24/274) classes injectable Melanotan II products as medicines.
assertions.quote: Products containing Melanotan II are classified as medicines if they are injectable or pens.
assertions.note: The MHRA response confirms that Melanotan II products are classified as medicines if injectable or pens.

assertions.text: MHRA states that unauthorised medicines may not be sold, supplied, or advertised.
assertions.quote: It is important to note that the sale, supply and advertising of unauthorised medicines is not permitted under the Human Medicines Regulations.
assertions.note: The MHRA response notes that sale, supply, and advertising of unauthorised medicines is prohibited.

assertions.text: MHRA advises users of Melanotan II products to stop using them immediately.
assertions.quote: These products may cause serious side effects, so our advice to those who have used Melanotan II injections or nasal sprays is to stop using them immediately and if you have suffered side effects, speak to your doctor and report them to the MHRA through our Yellow Card Scheme.
assertions.note: The MHRA letter advises users of injections or nasal sprays to stop immediately.

assertions.text: Australia's TGA states that Melanotan II is a prescription-only medicine, not approved as a tanning agent, and has no product listed on the ARTG.
assertions.note: The cited TGA advisory is unavailable and the provided texts do not contain Australian regulatory classification details.

recheck.note: The provided source texts do not contain statements from Australia's TGA regarding Melanotan II's prescription-only status or absence from the ARTG (the cited TGA advisory text was not provided).

units.text: The Aesthetic & Regenerative Endocrinology guide treats a personal or family history of melanoma as an absolute contraindication to Melanotan II. A case report describes crops of new atypical naevi and growth of existing naevi in a man with prior melanoma who self-injected an α-MSH analogue, with lightening after he stopped; MC1R activation does not prevent melanoma, and regular skin examination remains critical in high-risk people.

assertions.text: The Aesthetic & Regenerative Endocrinology guide treats a personal or family history of melanoma as an absolute contraindication to Melanotan II.
assertions.note: The guide notes that a personal or family history of melanoma is an absolute contraindication to Melanotan II.

units.text: Skin monitoring matters with melanocortin agonists: during Melanotan II use, sequential videodermoscopy documented naevus changes that made naevus and melanoma hard to tell apart, and even the approved MC1R agonist's US label recommends a full-body skin examination twice yearly.

assertions.text: During Melanotan II use, sequential videodermoscopy documented naevus changes that made a naevus and melanoma difficult to differentiate.
assertions.quote: The changes of patient's nevi were documented by sequential videodermoscopy before and during treatment. The observed dermoscopic changes made it difficult to differentiate a nevus from a melanoma.
assertions.note: Supported by the case report abstract describing sequential videodermoscopy during Melanotan II autoinjections.

assertions.text: The approved MC1R agonist's US prescribing information recommends a full-body skin examination twice yearly.
assertions.quote: A full body skin examination (twice yearly) is recommended to monitor pre-existing nevi and new skin pigmentary lesions.
assertions.note: Supported by the Scenesse (afamelanotide) US label under Warnings and Precautions.

units.text: PTD-DBM is a cell-penetrating peptide that competes CXXC5 off Dishevelled, activating Wnt/β-catenin; in mice it accelerated hair regrowth and wound-induced follicle neogenesis, and CXXC5 is raised in human balding scalp. This single 2017 study from the developer's group is its whole evidence: no human trial is published (PubMed) or registered (ClinicalTrials.gov) as of 24 September 2026. The Peptide Pocket Guide grades it D.

assertions.text: PTD-DBM is a cell-penetrating peptide that competes CXXC5 off Dishevelled, activating Wnt/β-catenin and accelerating hair regrowth and wound-induced follicle neogenesis.
assertions.quote: Disrupting the CXXC5-Dishevelled interaction with a competitor peptide activated the Wnt/β-catenin pathway and accelerated hair regrowth and wound-induced hair follicle neogenesis.
assertions.note: Lee et al. confirm that disrupting the CXXC5-Dishevelled interaction with a competitor peptide activates Wnt/β-catenin and accelerates hair regrowth and wound-induced neogenesis.

assertions.text: CXXC5 is raised in human balding scalp.
assertions.quote: CXXC5 was upregulated in miniaturized hair follicles and arrector pili muscles in human balding scalps.
assertions.note: Lee et al. report that CXXC5 is upregulated in hair follicles and arrector pili muscles of human balding scalps.

assertions.text: The 2017 study from the developer's group is PTD-DBM's sole evidence base, with no human trial published on PubMed or registered on ClinicalTrials.gov as of 24 September 2026.
assertions.note: The provided text does not verify ClinicalTrials.gov registration status as of 24 September 2026.

recheck.note: The sources do not state that no human trials are published on PubMed or registered on ClinicalTrials.gov as of 24 September 2026.

assertions.text: The Peptide Pocket Guide grades PTD-DBM as D.
assertions.note: The provided excerpt of The Peptide Pocket Guide omits the header line containing the GRADE rating for PTD-DBM.

recheck.note: The Peptide Pocket Guide assigns PTD-DBM a GRADE D evidence rating.

units.text: A 2025 review's abstract speaks of 'clinical efficacy' for peptides such as PTD-DBM, but its own table describes PTD-DBM as unapproved and shown in mouse models, and flags an untested theoretical risk: off-target Wnt activation is associated with colorectal and hepatocellular carcinomas.

assertions.text: A 2025 review's abstract speaks of 'clinical efficacy' for peptides such as PTD-DBM.
assertions.quote: Investigations demonstrate clinical efficacy of small molecule inhibitors and peptides, such as PTD-DBM, which activates the Wnt/β-catenin pathway by interfering with CXXC5, a negative regulator that inhibits pathway activation.
assertions.note: The review's abstract explicitly cites clinical efficacy for peptides such as PTD-DBM.

assertions.text: The review's summary table describes PTD-DBM as having no official approval and demonstrated in mouse models.
assertions.quote: No official approvalSeen in mouse models to enhance hair growth in AGA through topical application
assertions.note: The review's summary table notes no official approval and that efficacy was seen in mouse models.

assertions.text: Off-target activation of the Wnt pathway is associated with colorectal and hepatocellular carcinomas.
assertions.quote: Due to the nature of this pathway to promote growth, one of the most prominent and noticeable concerns of this approach is that of off-target effects, as atypical and unnecessary activation of this pathway has been correlated with various cancers such as colorectal and hepatocellular carcinomas.
assertions.note: The review states that atypical activation of the pathway has been correlated with colorectal and hepatocellular carcinomas.

units.text: Thymulin is a thymic peptide that is biologically active only when zinc-bound. No indexed human study of zinc thymulin for hair was found (the Peptide Pocket Guide's cited case series could not be located); its proposed hair mechanism is undefined, and whether any effect comes from the peptide or the zinc is unresolved. The Peptide Pocket Guide grades it D.

assertions.text: Thymulin is a thymic peptide that is biologically active only when zinc-bound.
assertions.quote: These data indicate the existence of two forms of FTS. The first one lacks Zn and is biologically inactive; the second one contains Zn and is biologically active, for which we propose the name of "thymulin" (FTS-Zn).
assertions.note: Dardenne et al. confirm that thymulin is biologically active only when bound to zinc.

assertions.text: No indexed human study of zinc thymulin for hair was found, and the Peptide Pocket Guide's cited case series could not be located in PubMed.
assertions.quote: A reference marked [not indexed] returned no PubMed record when checked; it is printed as the source gave it so a reader can pursue it, not as a verified locator.
assertions.note: The guide notes that sources flagged as not indexed returned no PubMed record, including the cited hair-loss case series.

assertions.text: The proposed hair mechanism of zinc thymulin is undefined or less defined, and whether any effect comes from the peptide or the zinc is unresolved.
assertions.quote: The role of the zinc cofactor itself complicates the question of whether 'zinc thymulin' acts as a peptide or as a vehicle for topical zinc.
assertions.note: The guide states that the hair mechanism is less defined and whether it acts as a peptide or a zinc vehicle remains unresolved.

assertions.text: The Peptide Pocket Guide grades zinc thymulin D.
assertions.quote: Zinc Thymulin                                             GRADE D   59
assertions.note: The guide lists zinc thymulin with a GRADE D rating.

units.text: In the US, on FDA's 503A category lists of 14 May 2026, thymulin acetate sits in Category 3 (nominated without adequate support, not eligible for the Category 1 policy) and PTD-DBM appears in no category; neither is on the 503A bulks list (21 CFR 216.23).

assertions.text: On FDA's 503A category lists of 14 May 2026, thymulin acetate is placed in Category 3.
assertions.note: Thymulin acetate is listed under Category 3 in FDA's 503A category list updated May 14, 2026.

assertions.text: Substances in FDA's 503A Category 3 were nominated without adequate support and are not eligible for the Category 1 interim policy.
assertions.sourceId:
fda-503a-bulks-page",
      "quote": "These substances are not eligible for the policy that applies to substances in category 1."
assertions.note: FDA guidance specifies that Category 3 substances were nominated with insufficient supporting information and are ineligible for the Category 1 policy.

assertions.text: PTD-DBM does not appear in any category on FDA's 503A category lists of 14 May 2026.
assertions.sourceId:
fda-503a-categories-2026-05-14",
      "quote": "Includes three categories of bulk drug substances:  
 
• Category 1: Bulk Drug Substances Under Evaluation 
• Category 2: Bulk Drug Substances that Raise Significant Safety Concerns 
• Category 3: Bulk Drug Substances Nominated Without Adequate Support"
assertions.note: The full May 14, 2026 document enumerates Categories 1, 2, and 3, and PTD-DBM is absent across all categories.

assertions.text: Neither thymulin acetate nor PTD-DBM is on the 503A bulks list under 21 CFR 216.23.
assertions.sourceId:
ecfr-21-cfr-216-23-bulks-list",
      "quote": "( a ) The following bulk drug substances can be used in compounding under section 503A(b)(1)(A)(i)(III) of the Federal Food, Drug, and Cosmetic Act."
assertions.note: 21 CFR 216.23(a) provides the complete list of authorized bulk drug substances under Section 503A, and neither substance is listed.

units.text: In the UK, baricitinib (Olumiant) is a prescription-only medicine licensed for severe alopecia areata in adults; NICE (TA926, 25 October 2023) did not recommend it for NHS use because the cost-effectiveness estimates were uncertain and higher than NICE normally accepts.

assertions.text: In the UK, baricitinib (Olumiant) is licensed for the treatment of severe alopecia areata in adult patients.
assertions.quote: Baricitinib is indicated for the treatment of severe alopecia areata in adult patients (see section 5.1).
assertions.note: The UK Summary of Product Characteristics confirms baricitinib is indicated for severe alopecia areata in adults.

assertions.text: Baricitinib is classified as a prescription-only medicine in the UK.
assertions.quote: Prescription only medicine
assertions.note: The SmPC lists the legal category of baricitinib as a prescription-only medicine.

assertions.text: NICE technology appraisal guidance TA926 did not recommend baricitinib for NHS use because its cost-effectiveness estimates were uncertain and higher than NICE normally considers acceptable.
assertions.quote:
The cost-effectiveness estimates for baricitinib are uncertain and are higher than what 
NICE normally considers an acceptable use of NHS resources. So, baricitinib is not 
recommended.
assertions.note: NICE TA926 states baricitinib was not recommended because cost-effectiveness estimates were uncertain and exceeded normally acceptable thresholds.

units.text: In the UK, topical minoxidil is licensed for androgenetic alopecia and Regaine for Men Extra Strength Scalp Foam 5% is on the General Sales List; finasteride for hair loss (Propecia) is a prescription-only medicine licensed for male pattern hair loss in men, is not prescribed on the NHS and is available only by private prescription.

assertions.text: In the UK, topical minoxidil is licensed for androgenetic alopecia.
assertions.quote: Regaine for Men Extra Strength Scalp Foam 5% w/w Cutaneous Foam is indicated for the treatment of alopecia androgenetica in men.
assertions.note: The SmPC confirms that topical minoxidil is indicated for androgenetic alopecia in men.

assertions.text: Regaine for Men Extra Strength Scalp Foam 5% is on the General Sales List in the UK.
assertions.quote: Regaine for Men Extra Strength Scalp Foam 5% w/w Cutaneous Foam (GSL) - Summary of Product Characteristics (SmPC) - (emc) | 5781
assertions.note: The SmPC designates the product with GSL (General Sales List) status.

assertions.text: Finasteride for hair loss (Propecia) is a prescription-only medicine licensed for male pattern hair loss in men.
assertions.quote: 'Propecia' is indicated for the treatment of men with male pattern hair loss (androgenetic alopecia) to increase hair growth and prevent further hair loss.
assertions.note: The SmPC confirms Propecia is indicated for male pattern hair loss in men.

assertions.text: Finasteride for hair loss is not prescribed on the NHS and is available only by private prescription in the UK.
assertions.quote: As finasteride 1mg is not prescribed on the NHS and is only available by private prescription, accurate prescription numbers are not available.
assertions.note: The MHRA Drug Safety Update states that finasteride 1 mg is not prescribed on the NHS and is only available by private prescription.

units.text: On 11 May 2026 MHRA strengthened its warnings that finasteride is associated with depression, suicidal ideation and sexual dysfunction that may persist after treatment stops; it advises prescribers to inform patients when prescribing, point them to the patient card, ask about a history of depression or suicidal ideation, and review them regularly for psychiatric and sexual side effects.

assertions.text: On 11 May 2026 MHRA strengthened its warnings that finasteride is associated with depression, suicidal ideation and sexual dysfunction that may persist after treatment stops.
assertions.quote: finasteride is associated  with depression, suicidal ideation and sexual dysfunction which may persist after treatment is stopped
assertions.note: The MHRA Drug Safety Update published on 11 May 2026 explicitly states this association and persistence.

assertions.text: MHRA advises prescribers to inform patients when prescribing and point them to the patient card.
assertions.quote: inform patients of the risks at point of prescribing and advise patients to read the Finasteride patient cards  and the patient leaflet for finasteride which are both supplied in the 1 mg and 5 mg packs
assertions.note: The update advises healthcare professionals to inform patients of risks at prescribing and direct them to the patient card.

assertions.text: MHRA advises prescribers to ask about a history of depression or suicidal ideation and review patients regularly for psychiatric and sexual side effects.
assertions.quote: when prescribing finasteride, review their medical record, ask patients if they have a history of depression or suicidal ideation and review patients regularly for psychiatric and/or sexual side effects
assertions.note: The update instructs prescribers to check history of depression or suicidal ideation and regularly review psychiatric and sexual side effects.

units.text: In the UK, afamelanotide has a marketing authorisation under exceptional circumstances for preventing phototoxicity in adults with erythropoietic protoporphyria, to be prescribed only by specialist clinicians in recognised porphyria centres; NICE (HST27, 26 July 2023) did not recommend it for NHS use.

assertions.text: In the UK, afamelanotide has a marketing authorisation under exceptional circumstances for preventing phototoxicity in adults with erythropoietic protoporphyria.
assertions.quote: Afamelanotide has a marketing authorisation in the UK under 'exceptional circumstances' for the 'prevention of phototoxicity in adult patients with erythropoietic protoporphyria (EPP)'.
assertions.note: The NICE guidance confirms that afamelanotide holds a UK marketing authorisation under exceptional circumstances for this indication.

assertions.text: Afamelanotide is to be prescribed only by specialist clinicians in recognised porphyria centres.
assertions.quote: The marketing authorisation stipulates that afamelanotide should only be prescribed by specialist clinicians in recognised porphyria centres, and that it should only be given by a clinician trained and accredited by the marketing authorisation holder to insert the implants.
assertions.note: The marketing authorisation conditions explicitly stipulate that afamelanotide should only be prescribed by specialist clinicians in recognised porphyria centres.

assertions.text: NICE (HST27, published 26 July 2023) did not recommend afamelanotide for NHS use.
assertions.quote: Taking into account all of the evidence and factors affecting the decision, afamelanotide is not recommended for use in the NHS.
assertions.note: NICE HST27 concludes that afamelanotide is not recommended for use in the NHS.

units.text: In the UK, a medicine made up for one patient without a marketing authorisation is an unlicensed 'special'; MHRA guidance says an unlicensed product should not be used where a UK-licensed product could meet the patient's need, and special need excludes cost, convenience and operational reasons.

assertions.text: In the UK, an unlicensed medicine manufactured or imported for the treatment of an individual patient without a marketing authorisation is commonly referred to as a 'special'.
assertions.quote: This Guidance Note provides advice on the manufacture, importation, distribution and supply of unlicensed medicinal products for human use (commonly described as “specials”) which have been specially manufactured or imported to the order of a doctor, dentist, nurse independent prescriber, pharmacist independent prescriber or supplementary prescriber for the treatment of individual patients.
assertions.note: MHRA guidance confirms unlicensed products manufactured or imported for individual patients are commonly described as specials.

assertions.text: MHRA guidance states that an unlicensed product should not be used where a UK-licensed product could meet the patient's need.
assertions.quote: An unlicensed product should not be used where a product available and licensed within the UK could be used to meet the patient's special need.
assertions.note: The guidance hierarchy clearly states an unlicensed product should not be used if an available UK-licensed product meets the need.

assertions.text: Under MHRA guidance, 'special need' excludes reasons of cost, convenience, and operational needs.
assertions.quote: The requirement for a “special need” relates to the special clinical needs of the individual patient. It does not include reasons of cost, convenience or operational needs (see Section 10 of this guide).
assertions.note: The guidance explicitly notes that special clinical need does not include cost, convenience, or operational reasons.

units.text: Growth hormone acts mainly in the dermis: its receptor is expressed more by dermal fibroblasts than keratinocytes, and GH increases fibroblast numbers and supports collagen synthesis. IGF-1, made locally by fibroblasts and melanocytes, acts on keratinocytes through the IGF-1 receptor; in culture IGF-1, not GH, drives keratinocyte proliferation.

assertions.text: Growth hormone activity in the skin is primarily evident in the dermis, where it supports collagen synthesis.
assertions.quote: GH activity, sometimes mediated via IGF-I, is primarily evident in the dermis, particularly affecting collagen synthesis.
assertions.note: Edmondson et al. report that GH activity is primarily evident in the dermis and affects collagen synthesis.

assertions.text: The growth hormone receptor is expressed at higher levels in dermal fibroblasts than in keratinocytes.
assertions.quote: Northern analysis, using the cloned GH-R as probe, revealed relatively higher levels of GH-R transcripts in cultured human dermal fibroblasts compared to cultured keratinocytes or keratome biopsies.
assertions.note: Tavakkol et al. showed relatively higher levels of GH-R transcripts in cultured fibroblasts compared to keratinocytes.

assertions.text: Growth hormone increases fibroblast numbers.
assertions.quote: In contrast, GH (10 ng/ml) after 5 d markedly increased fibroblast cell numbers (70%, p less than 0.009) over 0.2% serum control.
assertions.note: Tavakkol et al. observed a marked increase in fibroblast cell numbers following GH treatment.

assertions.text: IGF-1 is produced locally by fibroblasts and melanocytes, but not by keratinocytes.
assertions.quote: mRNA transcripts for the major mediator of GH actions, insulin-like growth factor 1 (IGF-1), were detected by PCR in fibroblasts, melanocytes, and keratome biopsies, but not in keratinocytes.
assertions.note: Tavakkol et al. detected IGF-1 mRNA transcripts in fibroblasts and melanocytes, but not in keratinocytes.

assertions.text: In culture, IGF-1, rather than growth hormone, promotes keratinocyte proliferation.
assertions.quote: IGF-1 but not GH (5-50 ng/ml) promoted clonal proliferation of cultured keratinocytes.
assertions.note: Tavakkol et al. found that IGF-1 but not GH promoted clonal proliferation of cultured keratinocytes.

units.text: Human hair follicles operate a functional peripheral equivalent of the somatotropic (GHRH–GH–IGF-1) axis ex vivo.

assertions.text: Human hair follicles operate a functional peripheral equivalent of the somatotropic (GHRH–GH–IGF-1) axis ex vivo.
assertions.quote: The human hair follicle runs functional peripheral equivalents of the central axes: it synthesizes cortisol and operates a local HPA-like loop,[11] and ex vivo it sustains a hypothalamic–pituitary–somatotropic equivalent (GHRH, GH, IGF-1) that paces its own growth.[12]
assertions.note: The cited text confirms that human hair follicles sustain a functional hypothalamic-pituitary-somatotropic equivalent (GHRH, GH, IGF-1) ex vivo.

units.text: GH secretion and IGF-1 decline progressively with age (the somatopause); IGF-1 must be read against age- and sex-adjusted ranges, so a value low for a young adult is often normal for age.

assertions.text: GH secretion and IGF-1 decline progressively with age (a process termed the somatopause).
assertions.quote: The somatopause is the progressive fall in growth-hormone pulse amplitude and IGF-1, beginning in the third decade and among the steepest of all.[2]
assertions.note: The guide explicitly defines somatopause as the progressive fall in growth hormone pulse amplitude and IGF-1 with age.

assertions.text: IGF-1 must be evaluated against age- and sex-adjusted reference ranges, meaning a level low for a young adult is often normal for age.
assertions.quote: — Reference by age and sex: IGF-1 and DHEA-S decline normally with age — "low-for-young" is often normal-for-age.
assertions.note: The clinical reference checklist specifies referencing IGF-1 by age and sex because low-for-young is often normal-for-age.

units.text: Human skin reflects the axis at its extremes: adults with GH deficiency have a thinner epidermis and reduced sweating on biopsy, not fully reversed by treatment of childhood-onset deficiency; in acromegaly, dermal glycosaminoglycan deposition and oedema thicken and puff the skin of the face, hands and feet.

assertions.text: Adults with GH deficiency have a thinner epidermis on skin biopsy.
assertions.quote: Epidermal thickness was significantly decreased in both untreated (median 39 microm, range 28-55 microm) and GH-treated patients with GHD (median 53 microm, range 37-100 microm), compared with that in controls (median 66 microm, range 40-111 microm; P<0.02).
assertions.note: Biopsy demonstrated significantly reduced epidermal thickness in patients with GHD compared with controls.

assertions.text: Adults with GH deficiency have reduced sweating.
assertions.quote: The sweat secretion rate (SSR) was significantly decreased in both the untreated (median 41 mg/30 min, range 9-79 mg/30 min) and the GH-treated (median 98 mg/30 min, range 28-147 mg/30 min) patients with GHD compared with that in controls (median 119 mg/30 min, range 90-189 mg/30 min; P=0.001 and 0.01 respectively).
assertions.note: Sweat secretion rate was significantly lower in both untreated and treated GHD patients than in controls.

assertions.text: The skin changes of childhood-onset GH deficiency are not fully reversed by GH replacement therapy.
assertions.quote: Importantly, these changes are not fully reversed despite long-term and adequate GH treatment in patients with childhood onset GHD.
assertions.note: The source explicitly concludes that skin changes are not fully reversed by long-term GH treatment in childhood-onset GHD.

assertions.text: In acromegaly, dermal glycosaminoglycan deposition and oedema thicken and puff the skin of the face, hands and feet.
assertions.quote: Skin puffiness due to dermal glycosaminoglycan accumulation and edema are most prominent in the face, hands and feet.
assertions.note: Glycosaminoglycan accumulation and oedema cause skin puffiness prominently affecting the face, hands, and feet in acromegaly.

units.text: In people with burns over 40% of body surface, recombinant GH shortened burn-wound and donor-site healing in pooled small randomized trials (13 RCTs, 701 people), with more hyperglycaemia; the evidence carries risk of bias.

assertions.text: In people with burns over 40% of body surface, recombinant GH shortened burn-wound and donor-site healing in pooled randomized trials.
assertions.quote: There is some evidence that using rhGH in people with large burns (more than 40% of the total body surface area) could result in more rapid healing of the burn wound and donor sites in adults and children, and in reduced length of hospital stay, without increased mortality or scarring, but with an increased risk of hyperglycaemia.
assertions.note: Supported by the Cochrane review authors' conclusions.

assertions.text: The Cochrane review included 13 RCTs involving 701 people.
assertions.quote: We included 13 RCTs (701 people).
assertions.note: Supported by the review's main results.

assertions.text: Recombinant GH treatment was associated with an increased incidence of hyperglycaemia.
assertions.quote: Pooling the studies of adults and children yielded a significantly higher incidence of hyperglycaemia in the rhGH‐treated participants (RR 2.65; 95% CI 1.68 to 4.16).
assertions.note: Supported by pooled analyses of adults and children.

assertions.text: The evidence carries a risk of bias.
assertions.quote: This evidence is based on studies with small sample sizes and risk of bias and requires confirmation in higher quality, adequately powered trials.
assertions.note: Supported by the review's assessment of the trials.

units.text: A much-cited 1990 NEJM study gave GH to 12 healthy men over 60 with nine untreated men as comparison and no placebo; skin thickness rose 7.1% (P = 0.07, not significant). A 1996 RCT in 28 older men found 15% more collagen deposited in implanted wound tubes on GH — a laboratory surrogate.

assertions.text: A 1990 NEJM study gave growth hormone to 12 healthy men over 60 with nine untreated men as a comparison and no placebo.
assertions.quote: During the treatment period, 12 men (group 1) received approximately 0.03 mg of biosynthetic human growth hormone per kilogram of body weight subcutaneously three times a week, and 9 men (group 2) received no treatment.
assertions.note: The abstract reports 12 men receiving human growth hormone and 9 receiving no treatment.

assertions.text: In the 1990 study, skin thickness increased by 7.1% (P = 0.07, not statistically significant).
assertions.quote: Skin thickness increased 7.1 percent (P = 0.07).
assertions.note: The study reports a 7.1 percent increase in skin thickness with P = 0.07.

assertions.text: A 1996 RCT in 28 older men found 15% more collagen deposited in implanted wound tubes in those receiving growth hormone.
assertions.quote: Hydroxyproline content was 15% greater in the wounds of the growth hormone group (n = 13) compared with the placebo group (n = 15), (4.52 +/- 0.94 versus 3.92 +/- 0.78 microg/cm; p = 0.04).
assertions.note: The trial measured collagen content in implanted tubes and found a 15% increase in the growth hormone group compared with placebo.

units.text: In healthy older adults, randomized trials of GH show small body-composition changes (about 2 kg less fat, 2 kg more lean mass) with more oedema, arthralgia, carpal tunnel syndrome and gynaecomastia and a trend to diabetes, while strength and endurance change little; GH is not recommended as anti-ageing therapy. A&RE grades this advice A; on the course rule the trials give B, with the same conclusion.

assertions.text: In healthy older adults, randomized trials of GH show small body-composition changes of about 2 kg less fat and 2 kg more lean mass.
assertions.quote: In participants treated with GH compared with those not treated with GH, overall fat mass decreased (change in fat mass, -2.1 kg [95% CI, -2.8 to -1.35] and overall lean body mass increased (change in lean body mass, 2.1 kg [CI, 1.3 to 2.9]) (P < 0.001), and their weight did not change significantly (change in weight, 0.1 kg [CI, -0.7 to 0.8]; P = 0.87).
assertions.note: A systematic review found fat mass decreased by 2.1 kg and lean body mass increased by 2.1 kg with GH treatment.

assertions.text: In healthy older adults, trials of GH show increased rates of oedema, arthralgia, carpal tunnel syndrome, gynaecomastia, and a trend toward diabetes.
assertions.quote: Persons treated with GH were significantly more likely to experience soft tissue edema, arthralgias, carpal tunnel syndrome, and gynecomastia and were somewhat more likely to experience the onset of diabetes mellitus and impaired fasting glucose.
assertions.note: The systematic review confirmed significantly higher rates of these adverse events and increased likelihood of diabetes onset or impaired fasting glucose.

assertions.text: Strength and endurance change little with GH treatment in healthy older adults.
assertions.quote: Sex steroid + GH increased muscle strength marginally and VO( 2)max in men, but women had no significant change in strength or cardiovascular endurance.
assertions.note: An RCT found women had no significant change in strength or endurance, and men had only marginal changes.

assertions.text: GH is not recommended as an anti-aging therapy.
assertions.quote: On the basis of this evidence, GH cannot be recommended as an antiaging therapy.
assertions.note: The systematic review concluded that GH cannot be recommended as an antiaging therapy.

assertions.text: Aesthetic & Regenerative Endocrinology grades the recommendation against growth hormone for healthy aging as Grade A.
assertions.quote: Growth hormone in healthy older adults is not recommended — modest body-composition changes are outweighed by edema, arthralgia, insulin resistance, and carpal tunnel, and it is illegal to prescribe for anti-aging in the US GRADE A.[6]
assertions.note: The text states that GH in healthy older adults is not recommended and assigns this GRADE A.

units.text: In the US (21 U.S.C. 333(e), current text read September 2026), knowingly distributing human growth hormone for any use other than treating a disease or recognized condition authorised by FDA, on a physician's order, is a federal offence.

assertions.text: In the US under 21 U.S.C. 333(e), knowingly distributing human growth hormone for any use other than treating an FDA-authorized disease or recognized condition on a physician's order is a federal offense.
assertions.quote: Human growth hormone (GH) is widely used as an antiaging therapy, although its use for this purpose has not been approved by the U.S. Food and Drug Administration and its distribution as an antiaging agent is illegal in the United States.
assertions.note: The cited review confirms that distributing HGH as an antiaging agent is illegal in the US, but the provided texts do not contain the specific statutory language or citation of 21 U.S.C. 333(e).

units.text: Tesamorelin, a GHRH analogue, reduced visceral fat by about 15% versus placebo at 26 weeks in two developer-run phase 3 RCTs (806 patients pooled), with subcutaneous fat unchanged; in the US it has been FDA-approved since 2010 for reduction of excess abdominal fat in HIV-infected adults with lipodystrophy, and its label excludes weight loss. Both guides grade it A — for that indication only.

assertions.text: Tesamorelin reduced visceral fat by about 15% versus placebo at 26 weeks across two phase 3 RCTs pooling 806 patients.
assertions.quote: At wk 26, VAT decreased significantly in tesamorelin-treated patients (-24 +/- 41 vs. 2 +/- 35 cm(2), tesamorelin vs. placebo, P < 0.001; treatment effect, -15.4%).
assertions.note: A pooled analysis of two phase 3 RCTs in 806 patients demonstrated a 15.4% treatment effect reduction in visceral adipose tissue at 26 weeks.

assertions.text: In the pooled phase 3 trials of tesamorelin, subcutaneous adipose tissue remained unchanged.
assertions.quote: No significant changes were observed in abdominal sc adipose tissue (-2 +/- 32 vs. 2 +/- 29 cm(2), P = 0.08; treatment effect, -0.6%).
assertions.note: The pooled phase 3 analysis showed no significant change in abdominal subcutaneous adipose tissue.

assertions.text: In the US, tesamorelin has been FDA-approved since 2010 for the reduction of excess abdominal fat in HIV-infected adults with lipodystrophy.
assertions.quote: A GHRH(1-44) analogue, FDA-approved 2010 as Egrifta for HIV-associated lipodystrophy — the only approved GHRH analogue for a body-composition indication.
assertions.note: Tesamorelin was FDA-approved in 2010 specifically for HIV-associated lipodystrophy to reduce abdominal fat.

assertions.text: The FDA prescribing information for tesamorelin explicitly excludes weight loss management.
assertions.quote: EGRIFTA WR is not indicated for weight loss management as it has a weight neutral effect.
assertions.note: The limitations of use in the prescribing information state the drug is not indicated for weight loss management.

assertions.text: Both clinical guides grade tesamorelin Grade A for the HIV-associated lipodystrophy indication only.
assertions.quote: Tesamorelin is the instructive exception — a GHRH analog that completed the regulatory path for a defined indication (HIV-associated visceral adiposity) GRADE A, showing what real peptide evidence looks like.
assertions.note: Both guides assign Grade A evidence specifically to tesamorelin's approved indication for HIV-associated lipodystrophy/visceral adiposity.

units.text: Tesamorelin's label reports IGF-1 above +2 SDS in 47% (above +3 SDS in 36%) of treated patients at 26 weeks, states that the effects of prolonged IGF-1 elevation are unknown, reports diabetes-range HbA1c in 5% vs 1% on placebo, lists fluid retention, and contraindicates use in active malignancy.

assertions.text: Tesamorelin's label reports IGF-1 above +2 SDS in 47% and above +3 SDS in 36% of treated patients at 26 weeks.
assertions.quote: Among patients who received EGRIFTA for 26 weeks, 47% had IGF-1 levels greater than 2 standard deviation scores (SDS), and 36% had SDS >3, with this effect seen as early as 13 weeks of treatment.
assertions.note: The label reports these exact percentages at 26 weeks in Section 5.2.

assertions.text: Tesamorelin's label states that the effects of prolonged IGF-1 elevation are unknown.
assertions.quote: The effects of prolonged elevations in IGF-1 levels are unknown.
assertions.note: The label explicitly states that prolonged IGF-1 elevation effects are unknown.

assertions.text: Tesamorelin's label reports diabetes-range HbA1c in 5% of treated patients vs 1% on placebo.
assertions.quote: Patients receiving EGRIFTA had an increased risk of developing diabetes (HbA1c level ≥ 6.5%) compared with placebo (5% vs. 1%), with a hazard ratio of 3.3 (CI 1.4, 9.6).
assertions.note: The label notes an increased risk of diabetes with HbA1c >= 6.5% in 5% of EGRIFTA patients compared to 1% on placebo.

assertions.text: Tesamorelin's label lists fluid retention as a warning or adverse effect.
assertions.quote: Fluid retention may occur during EGRIFTA WR therapy and is thought to be related to the induction of GH secretion.
assertions.note: Fluid retention is listed under Warnings and Precautions.

assertions.text: Tesamorelin's label contraindicates use in active malignancy.
assertions.quote: Do not treat patients with active malignancy with EGRIFTA WR  [see Contraindications ( 4 )] .
assertions.note: Active malignancy is explicitly contraindicated.

units.text: A PubMed search in September 2026 found no randomized trial with a skin outcome for tesamorelin, CJC-1295, ipamorelin or IGF-1 LR3; the closest human skin data for a GHRH analogue are a 1997 single-blind study of [Nle27]GHRH(1-29) in 19 older adults, with caliper skin thickness rising after a placebo lead-in and no parallel control.

assertions.text: A PubMed search in September 2026 found no randomized trial with a skin outcome for tesamorelin, CJC-1295, ipamorelin or IGF-1 LR3.
assertions.note: The provided sources do not report a September 2026 PubMed search or its specific findings regarding skin outcomes for these peptides.

recheck.note: None of the provided sources mention a PubMed search conducted in September 2026 regarding skin outcomes for these compounds.

assertions.text: The closest human skin data for a GHRH analogue are from a 1997 single-blind study of [Nle27]GHRH(1-29).
assertions.quote: Body composition was determined by dual energy x-ray absorptiometry scan, and skin thickness was measured at four sites, including the right and left hand and volar forearm, by Harpenden skin calipers.
assertions.note: The cited study reports skin thickness measurements from a single-blind trial of [Nle27]GHRH(1-29), but the provided sources do not establish that these are the closest human skin data available for a GHRH analogue.

recheck.note: The cited study reports skin thickness measurements from a single-blind trial of [Nle27]GHRH(1-29), but the provided sources do not establish that these are the closest human skin data available for a GHRH analogue.

assertions.text: A 1997 single-blind study evaluated [Nle27]GHRH(1-29) in 19 older adults using a placebo lead-in without a parallel control group.
assertions.quote: Ten women and 9 men between the ages of 55-71 yr self-injected placebo (saline) s.c. nightly for 4 weeks followed by 16 weeks of [Nle27]GHRH-(1-29)-NH2 at a dose of 10 microg/kg.
assertions.note: Khorram et al. evaluated 19 participants (10 women and 9 men aged 55–71) who self-injected placebo for 4 weeks followed by 16 weeks of [Nle27]GHRH-(1-29)-NH2.

assertions.text: In the 1997 study of [Nle27]GHRH(1-29), caliper skin thickness rose significantly after treatment.
assertions.quote: Although blood pressure and body weight were unaffected, GHRH analog treatment resulted in a significant increase in skin thickness (P < 0.05) in both genders and increased lean body mass in men only (P < 0.05), with no other changes in body composition or bone mineral density in either gender.
assertions.note: Khorram et al. reported a statistically significant increase in skin thickness measured by Harpenden skin calipers in both genders.

units.text: CJC-1295 with DAC raised GH and IGF-1 for days in phase 1 trials in healthy adults, with no clinical endpoint; CJC-1295 without DAC ('Mod GRF 1-29') and IGF-1 LR3 have no peer-reviewed human studies. The Hormonaly guides rate CJC-1295/ipamorelin C ('anecdotal'); on the course rule the evidence for any clinical or skin benefit is D.

assertions.text: CJC-1295 with DAC raised GH and IGF-1 for days in phase 1 trials in healthy adults, with no clinical endpoint
assertions.quote: The best human evidence comes from randomised, placebo-controlled, double-blind ascending-dose trials conducted in healthy adults using CJC-1295 DAC administered subcutaneously. In these studies, a single injection produced dose-dependent increases in mean plasma GH (approximately 2- to 10-fold for ≥6 days) and mean plasma IGF-1 (approximately 1.5- to 3-fold for 9–11 days).
assertions.note: Phase 1 trials in healthy adults demonstrated dose-dependent increases in GH and IGF-1 lasting multiple days without clinical efficacy endpoints.

assertions.text: CJC-1295 without DAC ('Mod GRF 1-29') and IGF-1 LR3 have no peer-reviewed human studies
assertions.quote: At the opposite end, CJC-1295 without DAC, PEG-MGF, and IGF-1 LR3 (tier D) have no peer-reviewed human studies and are supported only by preclinical extrapolation and grey-literature user narratives.
assertions.note: A narrative review confirms that CJC-1295 without DAC and IGF-1 LR3 have no peer-reviewed human studies.

assertions.text: The Hormonaly guides rate CJC-1295/ipamorelin C ('anecdotal'); on the course rule the evidence for any clinical or skin benefit is D
assertions.quote: BPC-157, TB-500, CJC-1295/ipamorelin, epitalon, and thymalin have plausible mechanisms but only anecdotal human data (C); seven peptides go before the FDA's PCAC in July 2026 — but review is not approval, and there is no clear lawful compounding route yet.
assertions.note: The guide assigns grade C based on anecdotal human data, which supports grade D under the course rule given the lack of clinical trials.

units.text: Ipamorelin's only efficacy RCT (postoperative ileus, phase 2) showed no benefit over placebo; ibutamoren (MK-677) raised GH, IGF-1 and fat-free mass in a 2-year RCT in older adults without improving strength or function, raised fasting glucose and lowered insulin sensitivity, and a hip-fracture phase IIb trial was stopped early for a heart-failure signal.

assertions.text: The phase 2 RCT of ipamorelin for postoperative ileus showed no benefit over placebo.
assertions.quote: There were no significant differences between ipamorelin and placebo in the key and secondary efficacy analyses.
assertions.note: Beck et al. found no significant differences between ipamorelin and placebo across efficacy endpoints.

assertions.text: The postoperative ileus study is ipamorelin's only efficacy RCT.
assertions.note: The provided sources do not state that this was ipamorelin's only efficacy RCT.

recheck.note: The provided sources describe the postoperative ileus trial of ipamorelin and note a lack of controlled outcome trials for anti-aging, but none state that the postoperative ileus study is its only efficacy RCT.

assertions.text: In an RCT in older adults, ibutamoren (MK-677) raised GH, IGF-1, and fat-free mass.
assertions.quote: Daily MK-677 significantly increased GH and IGF-I levels to those of healthy young adults without serious adverse effects. With placebo, mean (95% Cl) FFM decreased -0.5 (-1.1 to 0.2) kg, however, FFM increased 1.1 (0.7 to 1.5) kg with MK-677 (P<0.001, MK-677 vs. placebo); body cell mass as reflected by intracellular water decreased -1.0 (-2.1 to 0.2) kg with placebo, but increased 0.8 (-0.1 to 1.6) kg with MK-677 (P=0.021).
assertions.note: MK-677 significantly increased GH, IGF-I, and fat-free mass compared to placebo.

assertions.text: MK-677 did not improve muscle strength or physical function in the RCT in older adults.
assertions.quote: Increased FFM did not result in changes in strength or function.
assertions.note: The study found that increases in fat-free mass did not lead to changes in strength or function.

assertions.text: MK-677 raised fasting glucose and lowered insulin sensitivity in older adults.
assertions.quote: Fasting blood glucose increased an average of 0.3 mmol/L (5 mg/dL) with MK-677 (P=0.015) and insulin sensitivity declined.
assertions.note: MK-677 significantly raised fasting blood glucose and reduced insulin sensitivity.

assertions.text: A phase IIb trial of MK-677 in hip-fracture patients was stopped early due to a heart-failure signal.
assertions.quote: Trial was terminated early due to a safety signal of congestive heart failure in a limited number of patients.
assertions.note: The phase IIb study in hip-fracture patients was terminated early because of a congestive heart failure safety signal.

units.text: In the US, sermorelin was approved as Geref (1990, diagnostic; 1997, idiopathic GH deficiency in children), discontinued in 2008, and its approvals withdrawn in 2009 at the maker's request; FDA determined in 2013 that this was not for safety or effectiveness reasons. As of 24 September 2026 no sermorelin product is marketed (Drugs@FDA), and sermorelin appears in no 503A category (FDA list of 14 May 2026).

units.text: Skin and soft-tissue signs of GH excess include puffiness and thickening of the face, hands and feet from glycosaminoglycan deposition and oedema, oily skin with large pores, hyperhidrosis, skin tags and acanthosis nigricans, with slow acral and jaw enlargement; the Endocrine Society recommends IGF-1 measurement for typical acral and facial features and suggests it when several associated conditions cluster (sleep apnoea, type 2 diabetes, debilitating arthritis, carpal tunnel syndrome, hyperhidrosis, hypertension).

assertions.text: Skin and soft-tissue signs of GH excess include puffiness and thickening of the face, hands, and feet from glycosaminoglycan deposition and oedema, oily skin with large pores, hyperhidrosis, skin tags, and acanthosis nigricans.
assertions.quote: Skin puffiness due to dermal glycosaminoglycan accumulation and edema are most prominent in the face, hands and feet. Oily skin with large pores, hypertrichosis, and excessive sweating are common features. Pigmented skin tags, acanthosis nigricans, and psoriasis are also encountered.
assertions.note: Supported by the review of cutaneous manifestations in acromegaly.

assertions.text: GH excess features insidious or slow acral and jaw enlargement.
assertions.quote: Characteristic changes in the face and head, including widening and malocclusion of the jaw and macroglossia, as well as enlarged hands, occur insidiously but are often apparent at initial assessment (HQ).
assertions.note: Supported by the consensus description of insidious physical changes.

assertions.text: The Endocrine Society recommends IGF-1 measurement for typical acral and facial features and suggests it when several associated conditions cluster (sleep apnoea, type 2 diabetes, debilitating arthritis, carpal tunnel syndrome, hyperhidrosis, hypertension).
assertions.note: The provided abstract of the Endocrine Society guideline does not include the specific testing recommendations or listed comorbid condition clusters.

units.text: GH-axis drugs commonly cause fluid retention (oedema, arthralgia, paraesthesia, carpal tunnel symptoms), usually transient and dose-related, and glucose intolerance; somatropin labelling asks that pre-existing nevi be monitored for growth or malignant change.

assertions.text: GH-axis drugs commonly cause fluid retention (manifested as oedema, arthralgia, paraesthesia, carpal tunnel symptoms), which is usually transient and dose-related.
assertions.quote: Fluid retention during somatropin replacement therapy in adults may occur. Clinical manifestations of fluid retention (e.g., edema, arthralgia, myalgia, nerve compression syndromes including carpal tunnel syndrome/paresthesia) are usually transient and dose dependent.
assertions.note: The prescribing information notes that fluid retention manifesting as edema, arthralgia, and nerve compression syndromes including carpal tunnel syndrome and paresthesia is usually transient and dose dependent.

assertions.text: GH-axis drugs can cause glucose intolerance.
assertions.quote: Treatment with somatropin may decrease insulin sensitivity, particularly at higher doses in susceptible patients. As a result, previously undiagnosed impaired glucose tolerance and overt diabetes mellitus may be unmasked during somatropin treatment.
assertions.note: Somatropin labelling states that treatment can reduce insulin sensitivity and unmask impaired glucose tolerance.

assertions.text: Somatropin labelling asks that pre-existing nevi be monitored for growth or malignant change.
assertions.quote: Monitor patients on somatropin therapy carefully for increased growth, or potential malignant changes, of preexisting nevi.
assertions.note: Genotropin labelling explicitly warns to monitor preexisting nevi for increased growth or potential malignant changes.

units.text: Observed human data on IGF-1 and cancer are associations: higher circulating IGF-1 is linked with modestly higher risks of prostate, breast, colorectal and thyroid cancer, with reverse causation not excluded; acromegaly shows a slightly raised cancer incidence in pooled studies (SIR 1.5) that a nationwide cohort did not confirm (SIR 1.1).

assertions.text: Higher circulating IGF-1 is linked with modestly higher risks of prostate, breast, colorectal, and thyroid cancer.
assertions.quote: Higher IGF-I concentration was associated with increased risks of thyroid cancer [HR per 5 nmol/L higher concentration 1.18; 95% confidence interval (CI), 1.01-1.37] in addition to colorectal (HR, 1.08; 95% CI, 1.03-1.13), breast (HR, 1.11; 95% CI, 1.07-1.15), and prostate cancer (HR, 1.08; 95% CI, 1.05-1.12), and reduced risks of ovarian and liver cancer.
assertions.note: UK Biobank analyses observed modestly increased risks for thyroid, colorectal, breast, and prostate cancer with higher IGF-I concentrations.

assertions.text: In the observed associations between IGF-1 and cancer, reverse causation is not excluded.
assertions.quote: Mean follow-up was 6.9 years and the possibility that the observed associations may be influenced by reverse causality bias cannot be excluded.
assertions.note: The UK Biobank study explicitly states that the possibility of reverse causality bias cannot be excluded.

assertions.text: Pooled studies of acromegaly show an overall cancer incidence standardized incidence ratio (SIR) of 1.5.
assertions.quote: The meta-analysis yielded an SIR of overall cancer of 1.5 (95% CI, 1.2 to 1.8).
assertions.note: The meta-analysis of 23 studies yielded an overall cancer SIR of 1.5.

assertions.text: A nationwide cohort of acromegaly patients showed an overall cancer incidence SIR of 1.1.
assertions.quote: The cohort study identified 81 cases of cancer after exclusion of cases diagnosed within the first year [SIR 1.1; 95% confidence interval (CI), 0.9 to 1.4].
assertions.note: The nationwide cohort study identified an overall cancer SIR of 1.1.

units.text: GH treatment cohorts are largely reassuring for replacement: no clear raised cancer risk in 23,984 GH-treated children with growth failure and no other major disease, and a 2022 consensus found no association between GH replacement and primary tumour or recurrence; people with GH-receptor deficiency have very little cancer. No long-term cancer data exist for secretagogues or IGF-1 LR3 used for ageing or skin — the mitogenic risk there is plausible and unmeasured.

assertions.text: In a cohort of 23,984 GH-treated children with growth failure and no other major disease, there was no clear raised cancer risk.
assertions.quote: After exclusions for high-risk diagnoses, data unavailability and lack of permission (see Supplemental data and Fig. 1), the cohort for mortality risk analyses comprised 23,984 patients and for cancer incidence 10,406 patients. Half the cohort were first treated at ages 10-14, and about half received GH for isolated growth failure (Table 1).
assertions.note: The total SAGhE cohort consisted of 23,984 patients, but only about half (12,468) had isolated growth failure without other major disease.

assertions.text: A 2022 consensus found no association between GH replacement and primary tumour or recurrence.
assertions.quote: Current evidence reviewed from the proceedings from the Workshop does not support an association between GH replacement and primary tumour or cancer recurrence.
assertions.note: The 2022 consensus concluded that current evidence does not support an association between GH replacement and primary tumour or cancer recurrence.

assertions.text: People with GH-receptor deficiency have very little cancer.
assertions.quote: The individuals with GHR deficiency (GHRD) exhibited only one non-lethal malignancy and no cases of diabetes, in contrast to 17% cancer and 5% diabetes prevalence in the controls.
assertions.note: A 22-year study found only one non-lethal malignancy in individuals with GHR deficiency compared to 17% cancer prevalence in controls.

assertions.text: No long-term cancer data exist for secretagogues or IGF-1 LR3.
assertions.quote: However, in the absence of high-quality randomized controlled trials and robust long-term safety data, oncologic risk remains a legitimate concern.
assertions.note: The review highlights the absence of long-term safety and oncologic data for off-label GH secretagogues and IGF-1 analogues.

assertions.text: The mitogenic risk from secretagogues or IGF-1 LR3 is plausible and unmeasured.
assertions.quote: We synthesise clinically relevant adverse effects with particular attention to hormonal imbalance, endocrine–metabolic risk, and biologically plausible but unproven mitogenic concerns.
assertions.note: The review characterizes mitogenic concerns from performance-enhancing peptides as biologically plausible but unproven in clinical data.

units.text: In the UK, somatropin (for example Genotropin) is a prescription-only medicine licensed in children for growth disturbance from growth hormone deficiency, Turner syndrome, chronic renal insufficiency, short stature after small-for-gestational-age birth and Prader-Willi syndrome, and in adults for pronounced growth hormone deficiency; somatropin is a Class C controlled drug under the Misuse of Drugs Act 1971.

assertions.text: In the UK, somatropin (for example Genotropin) is a prescription-only medicine.
assertions.quote:
About Medicine

Prescription only medicine
assertions.note: The SmPC lists Genotropin as a prescription-only medicine in the UK.

assertions.text: In children, somatropin is licensed for growth disturbance from growth hormone deficiency, Turner syndrome, or chronic renal insufficiency.
assertions.quote: Growth disturbance due to insufficient secretion of growth hormone (growth hormone deficiency, GHD) and growth disturbance associated with Turner syndrome or chronic renal insufficiency.
assertions.note: The SmPC approves somatropin for growth disturbance caused by growth hormone deficiency, Turner syndrome, or chronic renal insufficiency.

assertions.text: In children, somatropin is licensed for growth disturbance in short children born small for gestational age.
