units.text: A search of MHRA's products database on 25 September 2026 returned no summary of product characteristics, patient leaflet or public assessment report for tesamorelin, sermorelin or ipamorelin; supplied in the UK, any of them would be an unlicensed medicine, which MHRA guidance reserves for an individual patient's special need that no licensed product meets.

assertions.text: A search of MHRA's products database on 25 September 2026 returned no summary of product characteristics, patient leaflet or public assessment report for tesamorelin, sermorelin or ipamorelin.
assertions.note: The cited database search source is unavailable, so the absence of these records cannot be confirmed.

assertions.text: MHRA guidance reserves unlicensed medicines for an individual patient's special need that no licensed product meets.
assertions.quote: An unlicensed medicinal product may only be supplied in order to meet the special needs of an individual patient.  An unlicensed medicinal product should not be supplied where an equivalent licensed medicinal product can meet the special needs of the patient.
assertions.note: MHRA Guidance Note 14 confirms unlicensed products may only be supplied to meet an individual patient's special needs where licensed products cannot do so.

units.text: GRADE rates certainty in four levels (high, moderate, low, very low) for an outcome across a body of evidence, not for a single study or a molecule; randomized trials start high and observational studies start low.

assertions.text: GRADE rates certainty in four levels (high, moderate, low, very low) for an outcome across a body of evidence, not for a single study or a molecule.
assertions.quote: GRADE specifies four categories-high, moderate, low, and very low-that are applied to a body of evidence, not to individual studies.
assertions.note: The cited source confirms GRADE uses four levels applied to a body of evidence rather than individual studies, but does not mention rating per outcome or not for a molecule.

assertions.text: Under GRADE, randomized trials start high and observational studies start low.
assertions.quote: Randomized trials begin as high-quality evidence, observational studies as low quality.
assertions.note: The source confirms that randomized trials begin as high-quality evidence and observational studies as low-quality evidence.

units.text: Certainty is rated down for risk of bias, inconsistency (unexplained variability across studies), indirectness (study PICO differs from the question), imprecision (confidence interval crossing the important-difference threshold) and suspected publication bias — which a body of small, industry-funded studies should raise — and can be rated up for large effects.

assertions.text: In GRADE, certainty is rated down for risk of bias, inconsistency, indirectness, imprecision, and publication bias.
assertions.quote: "Quality" as used in GRADE means more than risk of bias and so may also be compromised by imprecision, inconsistency, indirectness of study results, and publication bias.
assertions.note: GRADE quality/certainty is compromised by risk of bias, imprecision, inconsistency, indirectness, and publication bias.

assertions.text: Inconsistency is defined as unexplained variability in results across studies.
assertions.quote: This third article in a seven part series presents the Core GRADE (Grading of Recommendations Assessment, Development and Evaluation) approach to deciding whether to rate down certainty of evidence due to inconsistency—that is, unexplained variability in results across studies.
assertions.note: Core GRADE defines inconsistency as unexplained variability in results across studies.

assertions.text: Indirectness occurs when the study PICO differs from the question/target PICO.
assertions.quote: When target and study PICOs differ substantially, studies provide indirect evidence and Core GRADE users may rate down the certainty of evidence as a result of this indirectness.
assertions.note: Core GRADE notes indirect evidence arises when study and target PICOs differ.

assertions.text: Certainty is rated down for imprecision when the confidence interval crosses the important-difference threshold.
assertions.quote: Users then rate down for imprecision if the 95% confidence interval crosses the MID for benefit or harm.
assertions.note: Core GRADE specifies rating down for imprecision if the 95% confidence interval crosses the minimal important difference (MID).

assertions.text: A body of small, industry-funded studies should raise suspicion of publication bias.
assertions.quote: For publication bias, a body of evidence comprising small studies funded by industry should raise suspicion.
assertions.note: Core GRADE states that a body of evidence comprising small industry-funded studies should raise suspicion of publication bias.

assertions.text: Certainty of evidence can be rated up for large effects.
assertions.quote: Core GRADE users appraising results from well conducted NSRI can consider rating up certainty of evidence when risk ratios from pooled estimates suggest large or very large effects.
assertions.note: Core GRADE allows rating up certainty when pooled estimates suggest large or very large effects.

units.text: Applied to this course: topical GHK-Cu's only indexed RCT measured post-laser healing (indirect for photoageing); BPC-157 wound data are rodent models (indirect); LL-37's 34-person positive trial and 148-person negative phase IIb disagree (inconsistent); oral collagen's benefit disappears in high-quality trials (risk of bias).

assertions.text: Topical GHK-Cu's only indexed RCT measured post-laser healing
assertions.quote: To evaluate the role of skin care products that contain a copper tripeptide complex, glycyl-l-histidyl-l-lysine-Cu(2+) (GHK-Cu), in treating carbon dioxide (CO(2)) laser-resurfaced skin.
assertions.note: Miller 2006 evaluated GHK-Cu in post-laser healing, but the provided text does not establish that it is the only indexed RCT of topical GHK-Cu.

assertions.text: BPC-157 wound healing data are rodent models
assertions.quote: A similar finding (i.e., rehabilitation of skin wound and maturation of granulation tissue markedly promoted by BPC 157) was obtained in small-type pigs.
assertions.note: While most wound healing studies reviewed are in rodents, the review also reports wound healing data in small-type pigs.

assertions.text: An initial clinical trial of LL-37 included 34 participants
assertions.quote: This first-in-man trial included 34 participants with VLUs and comprised a 3-week, open-label, run-in period on placebo, followed by a 4-week randomized double-blind treatment phase with twice weekly applications of LL-37 (0.5, 1.6, or 3.2 mg/mL) or placebo, and a 4-week follow-up.
assertions.note: Gronberg 2014 confirms that the initial trial included 34 participants.

assertions.text: The initial trial of LL-37 found significantly improved healing rates compared to placebo
assertions.quote: The healing rate constants for 0.5 and 1.6 mg/mL of LL-37 were approximately six- and threefold higher than for placebo (p = 0.003 for 0.5 mg/mL and p = 0.088 for 1.6 mg/mL).
assertions.note: Gronberg 2014 reports significantly higher healing rate constants for LL-37 compared to placebo.

assertions.text: LL-37's phase IIb trial was conducted in 148 patients
assertions.quote: This clinical trial HEAL LL‐37 was a phase IIb double‐blind, randomized, placebo‐controlled study, with the aim to evaluate the efficacy and safety of a new drug LL‐37 for topical administration, in combination with compression therapy, in 148 patients suffering from hard‐to‐heal venous leg ulcers.
assertions.note: Mahlapuu 2021 confirms that the phase IIb trial was conducted in 148 patients suffering from hard-to-heal venous leg ulcers.

assertions.text: LL-37's phase IIb trial found no significant improvement in healing compared with placebo in the full study population
assertions.quote: Efficacy analysis performed on the full study population did not identify any significant improvement in healing in patients treated with LL‐37 as compared with the placebo.
assertions.note: Mahlapuu 2021 reports that efficacy analysis on the full study population showed no significant improvement in healing with LL-37 over placebo.

assertions.text: Oral collagen's benefit disappears in high-quality trials
assertions.quote: Similarly, high-quality studies revealed no significant effect in all categories, while low-quality studies revealed a significant improvement in elasticity.
assertions.note: Myung 2025 finds that high-quality studies revealed no significant effect across all categories.

units.text: A Cochrane methodology review of 75 papers found industry-sponsored drug and device studies more often reported favourable efficacy results (RR 1.27, 95% CI 1.17–1.37; moderate-quality evidence) and favourable conclusions (RR 1.34) than non-industry studies, a bias not explained by standard risk-of-bias assessment.

assertions.text: The Cochrane methodology review included a total of 75 papers.
assertions.quote: Twenty-seven new papers were included in this update and in total the review contains 75 included papers.
assertions.note: The abstract confirms the review contains 75 included papers.

assertions.text: Industry-sponsored drug and device studies more often reported favourable efficacy results (RR 1.27, 95% CI 1.17–1.37; moderate-quality evidence) and favourable conclusions (RR 1.34) than non-industry studies.
assertions.quote: Industry sponsored studies more often had favorable efficacy results, RR: 1.27 (95% CI: 1.17 to 1.37) (25 papers) (moderate quality evidence), similar harms results RR: 1.37 (95% CI: 0.64 to 2.93) (four papers) (very low quality evidence) and more often favorable conclusions RR: 1.34 (95% CI: 1.19 to 1.51) (29 papers) (low quality evidence) compared with non-industry sponsored studies.
assertions.note: The review reports RR 1.27 for favourable efficacy results and RR 1.34 for favourable conclusions compared to non-industry studies.

assertions.text: This industry bias is not explained by standard risk-of-bias assessments.
assertions.quote: Our analyses suggest the existence of an industry bias that cannot be explained by standard 'Risk of bias' assessments.
assertions.note: The authors conclude that standard risk-of-bias assessments cannot explain the industry bias.

units.text: Both Hormonaly guides attach an A–D letter to the evidence for a specific use — adapted from GRADE's four levels — which rates evidence, not legality; mechanistic appeal never raises a grade, and grade and regulatory status are separate checks to clear.

assertions.text: GRADE specifies four categories for rating the quality of evidence.
assertions.quote: GRADE specifies four categories-high, moderate, low, and very low-that are applied to a body of evidence, not to individual studies.
assertions.note: GRADE specifies four categories (high, moderate, low, and very low) to rate evidence quality.

assertions.text: The Peptide Pocket Guide adapts the standard GRADE framework into an A–D letter rating for clinical evidence.
assertions.quote:
Every entry carries a GRADE letter rating derived from the Hormonaly.ai
evidence database, which adapts the standard GRADE framework to peptide
pharmacology.
assertions.note: The guide derives its A–D letter ratings from a database adapting the GRADE framework.

assertions.text: Mechanistic appeal never raises an evidence grade.
assertions.quote: Mechanistic appeal alone never raises a grade.
assertions.note: The Peptide Pocket Guide explicitly notes that mechanistic appeal alone never raises a grade.

assertions.text: Evidence grade and regulatory status are separate checks to clear.
assertions.quote: — Evidence grade and regulatory status are separate checks; clear both.
assertions.note: The Aesthetic & Regenerative Endocrinology guide lists checking evidence grade and regulatory status separately as a clinical principle.

units.text: In the US, 503A compounding by a licensed pharmacist or physician for an identified patient is exempt from new-drug approval, adequate directions for use and cGMP only if the bulk substance meets a USP/NF monograph, or failing that is a component of an approved drug, or failing that is on the 503A bulks list — and is made by an FDA-registered establishment and accompanied by a valid certificate of analysis. Quality is defined by reference to those standards and the certificate, not by a numerical purity threshold in the statute's text.

assertions.text: In the US, 503A compounding by a licensed pharmacist or physician for an identified patient is exempt from new-drug approval, adequate directions for use, and cGMP.
assertions.quote: (a) In general Sections 351(a)(2)(B) , 352(f)(1) , and 355 of this title shall not apply to a drug product if the drug product is compounded for an identified individual patient based on the receipt of a valid prescription order or a notation, approved by the prescribing practitioner, on the prescription order that a compounded product is necessary for the identified patient, if the drug product meets the requirements of this section, and if the compounding—
assertions.note: Section 503A exempts compounding for an identified individual patient from sections 351(a)(2)(B), 352(f)(1), and 355.

assertions.text: Bulk drug substances used under section 503A must meet an applicable USP/NF monograph, or failing that be a component of an approved drug, or failing that appear on the 503A bulks list.
assertions.quote: The Secretary , in consultation with the United States Pharmacopoeia Convention, Incorporated, shall promulgate regulations identifying drug substances that may be used in compounding under subsection (b)(1)(A)(i)(III) for which a monograph does not exist or which are not components of drug products approved by the Secretary.
assertions.note: The statute establishes that bulks list regulations apply when a monograph does not exist and the substance is not a component of an approved drug.

assertions.text: Bulk drug substances used in 503A compounding must be accompanied by a valid certificate of analysis and manufactured by an FDA-registered establishment.
assertions.quote: In addition, bulk drug substances must be accompanied by a valid certificate of analysis and must have been manufactured by an establishment registered with FDA under section 510 of the FD&C Act.
assertions.note: FDA guidance specifies that bulk drug substances must have a valid certificate of analysis and be manufactured by a registered establishment.

assertions.text: Quality is defined by reference to statutory standards and the certificate of analysis, not by a numerical purity threshold in the statute's text.
assertions.note: The provided sources do not mention or address a numerical purity threshold.

units.text: 503B outsourcing facilities compound sterile drugs, register with FDA, must meet cGMP, are inspected on a risk-based schedule, report adverse events and may compound without patient-specific prescriptions; their products are exempt from approval and adequate-directions requirements, so they remain unapproved.

assertions.text: 503B outsourcing facilities compound sterile drugs, register with FDA, and must meet current good manufacturing practice (cGMP) requirements.
assertions.quote: The law defines an outsourcing facility as a facility at one geographic location or address that is engaged in the compounding of sterile drugs; has elected to register as an outsourcing facility; and complies with all of the requirements of section 503B.
assertions.note: The law defines an outsourcing facility as engaged in compounding sterile drugs, registered as such, and required to meet CGMP.

assertions.text: 503B outsourcing facilities are inspected by FDA on a risk-based schedule and must report adverse events.
assertions.quote: Outsourcing facilities: must comply with CGMP requirements; are inspected by FDA according to a risk-based schedule; and must meet certain other conditions, such as reporting adverse events and providing FDA with certain information about the products they compound.
assertions.note: FDA explicitly lists risk-based inspections and adverse event reporting as requirements for outsourcing facilities.

assertions.text: 503B outsourcing facilities may compound without patient-specific prescriptions.
assertions.quote: An outsourcing facility may or may not obtain prescriptions for identified individual patients.
assertions.note: Section 503B explicitly provides that an outsourcing facility may or may not obtain prescriptions for identified individual patients.

assertions.text: Products from 503B outsourcing facilities are exempt from FDA approval and adequate-directions requirements, so they remain unapproved.
assertions.quote: Drugs compounded by an outsourcing facility can qualify for exemptions from FDA approval requirements and the requirement to label products with adequate directions for use, but not from current good manufacturing practice (CGMP) requirements.
assertions.note: FDA guidance confirms compounded drugs from outsourcing facilities can qualify for exemptions from approval and adequate-directions labeling.

units.text: As of 22 September 2026 the 503A bulks list (21 CFR 216.23) holds six substances, none a peptide, unchanged since 2019; listing carries no FDA endorsement of safety or efficacy.

assertions.text: The 503A bulks list (21 CFR 216.23) holds six substances, unchanged since 2019, none of which is a peptide.
assertions.quote: A final regulation was issued in February 2019, List of Bulk Drug Substances That Can Be Used To Compound Drug Products in Accordance with Section 503A of the FD&C Act , in which FDA placed six substances on the list, identified and did not place four other substances on the list, and established the criteria to evaluate substances for inclusion on the list.
assertions.note: The FDA page confirms that the final regulation issued in February 2019 placed six substances on the list.

assertions.text: Listing on the 503A bulks list carries no FDA endorsement of safety or efficacy.
assertions.quote: Any person who represents that a compounded drug made with a bulk drug substance that appears on this list is FDA approved, or otherwise endorsed by FDA generally or for a particular indication, will cause the drug to be misbranded under section 502(a) and/or 502(bb) of the Federal Food, Drug, and Cosmetic Act.
assertions.note: The regulation specifies that listing carries no endorsement of safety or efficacy and that representing FDA approval or endorsement misbrands the drug.

units.text: Categories 1–3 are FDA's interim enforcement posture while nominations are evaluated, not listing. As of 14 May 2026 Category 1 includes GHK-Cu except injectable routes and 503A Category 2 holds six substances; BPC-157, TB-500, KPV, injectable GHK-Cu, LL-37 and melanotan II sit in a table of withdrawn nominations whose safety concerns remain posted.

assertions.text: Categories 1–3 are FDA's interim enforcement posture while nominations are evaluated, rather than inclusion on the 503A bulks list.
assertions.quote: FDA developed an interim policy describing conditions under which the agency does not intend to take action against state-licensed pharmacies, federal facilities and licensed physicians for compounding drug products from certain bulk drug substances that cannot otherwise be used under section 503A. The agency issued this interim policy to avoid unnecessary disruption to patient treatment while FDA evaluates the bulk drug substances nominated for inclusion on the 503A bulks list .
assertions.note: FDA explains that the three categories are part of an interim enforcement policy while nominated substances are evaluated.

assertions.text: As of 14 May 2026, Category 1 includes GHK-Cu except for injectable routes of administration.
assertions.quote: FDA has added the following bulk drug substance to category 1 for the reason provided below: o “GHK-Cu (except for injectable routes of administration) ” - GHK-Cu (except for injectable routes of administration) was removed from c ategory 1 on April 22, 2026, because the nominations for GHK-Cu were withdrawn by the nominators.
assertions.note: The category list document updated May 14, 2026, confirms GHK-Cu (except for injectable routes) was added to Category 1.

assertions.text: As of 14 May 2026, 503A Category 2 contains six substances.
assertions.quote: 503A Category 2: Bulk Drug Substances that Raise Significant Safety Risks Visit Safety Risks Associated with Certain Bulk Drug Substances for Use in Compounding for a summary of the identified safety risks for bulk drug substances in category 2, as well as other bulk drug substances that were previously in category 2 but were withdrawn. • Cesium Chloride • Domperidone • Germanium Sesquioxide • Ibutamoren Mesylate • Kisspeptin-10 • Quinacrine Hydrochloride for intrauterine administration
assertions.note: The May 14, 2026 PDF lists exactly six substances under 503A Category 2.

assertions.text: BPC-157, TB-500, KPV, injectable GHK-Cu, LL-37, and melanotan II appear in an FDA table of withdrawn nominations whose potential safety concerns remain posted.
assertions.quote: Bulk drug substances nominated but withdrawn | Bulk drug substance | Potential significant safety risks | AOD-9604 | Compounded drugs containing AOD-9604 may pose significant risk for immunogenicity for certain routes of administration and may have complexities with regard to peptide-related impurities and API characterization.
assertions.note: All six listed substances appear in FDA's table of withdrawn nominations with posted safety risks.

units.text: The July 2026 Pharmacy Compounding Advisory Committee is advisory; FDA's review staff concluded the listing criteria weigh against BPC-157, and only rulemaking changes the bulks list, which no rule had changed as of September 2026.

assertions.text: The July 2026 Pharmacy Compounding Advisory Committee is advisory and makes non-binding recommendations.
assertions.quote: Advisory committees make non-binding recommendations to the FDA, which generally follows the recommendations but is not legally bound to do so.
assertions.note: The advisory committee meeting notice states that advisory committees make non-binding recommendations to the FDA.

assertions.text: FDA's review staff concluded the listing criteria weigh against BPC-157.
assertions.quote: On balance, the physicochemical characterization, information on historical use, lack of evidence of effectiveness, and safety information identified for both BPC-157 (free base) and BPC-157 acetate weigh against them being added to the 503A Bulks List.
assertions.note: The FDA briefing document concludes that the evaluation criteria weigh against adding BPC-157 to the 503A Bulks List.

assertions.text: Only rulemaking changes the 503A bulks list.
assertions.note: The provided excerpt of 21 CFR 216.23 does not state that rulemaking is the exclusive mechanism to change the list.

recheck.note: The provided sources do not address the procedural requirement that only rulemaking can modify the 503A bulks list.

assertions.text: No rule had changed the 503A bulks list as of September 2026.
assertions.quote: ( a ) The following bulk drug substances can be used in compounding under section 503A(b)(1)(A)(i)(III) of the Federal Food, Drug, and Cosmetic Act.
assertions.note: The eCFR text as of September 2026 shows that 21 CFR 216.23 remains unchanged from the 2019 rule and does not include BPC-157.

units.text: Since 23 March 2020 FDA defines a protein as an alpha amino acid polymer of more than 40 amino acids, chemically synthesized or not, so such products are biological products; tesamorelin and hyaluronidase were deemed biologics licences on that date, and biologics are not eligible for the 503A or 503B compounding exemptions.

assertions.text: Effective 23 March 2020, FDA defines a protein as an alpha amino acid polymer of more than 40 amino acids, classifying such products as biological products.
assertions.quote:
Under this final rule, the term protein means any alpha amino acid
polymer with a specific, defined sequence that is greater than 40 amino
acids in size.
This final rule is intended to clarify the statutory framework under
which such products are regulated.

DATES: This rule is effective March 23, 2020.
assertions.note: FDA's final rule defines a protein as an alpha amino acid polymer with a specific defined sequence greater than 40 amino acids effective March 23, 2020.

assertions.text: FDA's protein definition applies irrespective of whether the polymer is chemically synthesized.
assertions.quote:
Thus, in order to provide regulatory certainty and provide a bright-line
interpretation of the term ``protein,'' we are focusing on the number
of amino acids in the amino acid polymer (irrespective of the method of
manufacture).
assertions.note: FDA notes that the definition of protein focuses on the amino acid count regardless of the manufacturing method.

assertions.text: Tesamorelin was deemed an approved biologics license on 23 March 2020.
assertions.quote:
tesamorelin acetate Egrifta and 
Egrifta SV 
022505 Theratechnologies 
Inc. 
11/10/2010
assertions.note: Tesamorelin acetate is included in FDA's list of approved NDAs deemed to be BLAs on March 23, 2020.

assertions.text: Hyaluronidase was deemed an approved biologics license on 23 March 2020.
assertions.quote:
hyaluronidase Amphadase 021665 Amphastar 
Pharmaceuticals, 
Inc. 
10/26/2004
assertions.note: Hyaluronidase is listed among the approved NDAs transitioned to deemed BLAs on March 23, 2020.

assertions.text: Biological products are not eligible for the 503A or 503B compounding exemptions.
assertions.quote: This transition affects compounding under sections 503A and 503B of the FD&C Act because, beginning on March 23, these transitioning biological products will not be eligible for the exemptions for compounded drugs under sections 503A and 503B of the FD&C Act.
assertions.note: FDA states that biological products subject to licensure under section 351 are not eligible for 503A or 503B compounding exemptions.

units.text: How residues are counted can decide classification: a federal district court in 2025 upheld FDA's determination that retatrutide (39-alpha-amino-acid backbone plus a two-residue side chain) is not a protein, remanding only the 'analogous to a protein' question; the appeal was pending as of the latest filings found (June 2026).

assertions.text: Retatrutide consists of a 39-alpha-amino-acid backbone plus a two-residue side chain.
assertions.quote: Retatrutide is an alpha amino acid polymer that contains a specific, defined sequence of 41 amino acids cumulatively, comprising a backbone of 39 alpha amino acids and a second (associated) chain of one residue each of gamma-glutamate and 8-amino-3,6-dioxaoctanoic acid (ADO).
assertions.note: The district court order confirms retatrutide consists of a 39-alpha-amino-acid backbone and a two-residue associated chain.

assertions.text: A federal district court in 2025 upheld FDA's determination that retatrutide is not a protein, remanding only the 'analogous to a protein' question.
assertions.quote: The September 30, 2025 order split: the court upheld FDA's determination that retatrutide does not meet the regulatory definition of a protein, but vacated FDA's separate determination that it could not be "analogous to a protein" and remanded that question to the agency.
assertions.note: The reference guide summarizes the 2025 district court ruling upholding FDA's protein decision while vacating and remanding the analogous-to-a-protein issue.

assertions.text: The appeal was pending as of the latest filings found (June 2026).
assertions.quote: The court directs the parties to file supplemental memoranda addressing appellate jurisdiction.
assertions.note: The cited Seventh Circuit docket reflects filings and proceedings continuing through October 2026, not June 2026.

units.text: A certificate of analysis is the supplier's attestation for a named lot — mass spectrometry for identity (observed against expected mass), HPLC for purity, plus endotoxin, microbial, water, counter-ion, metal and solvent results. It cannot establish that the vial in hand is that lot, how it was stored since testing, or that the product is sterile and suitable to inject; lot-less, chromatogram-less, stale (over 12 months) and endotoxin-less certificates are warning signs.

assertions.text: A certificate of analysis is the supplier's attestation for a named lot, evaluating identity (observed against expected mass by mass spectrometry), purity by HPLC, counter-ion, endotoxin, and microbial results.
assertions.quote: A COA is the supplier's own quality attestation, not an independent certification. A serious COA tells you what the supplier found on a named lot: whether the mass matches the expected molecule, how pure the material was by HPLC, what counter-ion it carries, and what the endotoxin and microbial results were.
assertions.note: The guide confirms a COA is the supplier's attestation for a named lot indicating expected versus observed mass, HPLC purity, counter-ion, endotoxin, and microbial results.

assertions.text: A certificate of analysis cannot establish on its own that the vial in hand is that lot, how it was stored since testing, or that the product is sterile and suitable to inject.
assertions.quote: What it cannot establish on its own is that a product is safe to inject — that turns on sterility, the dose and route, the conditions the material was held in since testing, and whether the lot tested is the lot in hand.
assertions.note: The guide states that a COA cannot establish on its own whether the lot tested is the vial in hand, storage conditions since testing, or sterility and safety for injection.

assertions.text: Certificates of analysis lacking a chromatogram or lot number, or dated more than 12 months prior, are warning signs.
assertions.quote:
— A bare claim of "purity > 99%" with no chromatogram or supporting data.
— No mass spectrum, or a spectrum without a labelled expected mass.
— No batch or lot number; no manufacture date.
— A COA dated more than 12 months before purchase — peptides degrade in
  storage.
assertions.note: The guide lists lack of chromatogram, lack of batch/lot number, and being dated more than 12 months prior among items not to see on a serious COA.

assertions.text: Certificates of analysis lacking endotoxin testing for injectable preparations are warning signs.
assertions.quote: RUO peptides frequently have no endotoxin testing — a hard contraindication to injection.
assertions.note: The source identifies the absence of endotoxin testing on RUO peptides as a hard contraindication to injection.

units.text: There is no single universal endotoxin limit per milligram: FDA's guidance says the limit is calculated with the USP method from the product's dosage regimen and strength, and some routes (intrathecal, ophthalmic) differ.

assertions.text: There is no single universal endotoxin limit per milligram.
assertions.quote: There is no single universal per-milligram limit: the allowable endotoxin for a parenteral product is derived from the maximum human dose and the route, so the same concentration can pass for one product and fail for another.
assertions.note: Hannah-Shmouni confirms that there is no single universal per-milligram endotoxin limit.

assertions.text: FDA guidance states that endotoxin limits are established using calculation methods from USP or AAMI standards based on product dosage regimens and strengths.
assertions.quote: The endotoxins limit table is out of date due to the increase in numbers of dosage (regimes) and drug strengths since the publication of the 1987 Guidance.  The appropriate way to establish the endotoxins limit is to use the calculation methods provided in the USP or AAMI standards.
assertions.note: FDA guidance explains that endotoxin limits must be calculated using USP/AAMI standards to account for dosage regimens and drug strengths.

assertions.text: FDA guidance notes that products administered via intrathecal or ophthalmic routes may have endotoxin limits that differ from the standard parenteral calculation.
assertions.quote: Intrathecally-administered products, ophthalmics, or devices (see question 11 for devices) may have endotoxins limits that are not based on the calculation for parenterally administered products.
assertions.note: FDA guidance notes that intrathecal and ophthalmic products may have limits not based on the calculation for parenterally administered products.

units.text: FDA's July 2026 briefing on BPC-157 found the nominators' certificates described a different form (the acetate) from the one nominated, that publicly available BPC-157 certificates mostly report purity alone with no impurity limits, and that the nominator's certificate mentioned no endotoxin test.

assertions.text: FDA's July 2026 briefing on BPC-157 found that the nominators' certificates described a different form (the acetate) from the one nominated.
assertions.quote: Due to inconsistencies in the nomination packages, the nominated BDS is unclear from both nominators of BPC-157-related BDSs. For example, the nominated BDS is not consistent with what is listed in the Certificate of Analysis (CoA).
assertions.note: FDA noted that the nominated bulk drug substance matched BPC-157 free base but the provided certificates of analysis were for BPC-157 acetate.

assertions.text: Publicly available BPC-157 certificates mostly report purity alone with no impurity limits.
assertions.quote: We conducted  literature searches and found that most CoAs for BPC-157 (free base) only contain purity testing  results, an example of which is shown below (Figure 2).17 There is no information about the  impurity limits/testing results in the CoA to demonstrate control of the impurity profile of BPC- 157 (free base).
assertions.note: FDA's literature search found that most public CoAs contain purity results only and lack impurity limits.

assertions.text: The nominator's certificate mentioned no endotoxin test.
assertions.quote: No bioburden/endotoxin test is mentioned in the CoA provided by the nominator.
assertions.note: The briefing explicitly notes that no bioburden or endotoxin test was mentioned in the nominator's CoA.

units.text: Paperwork and contents can diverge: three semaglutide vials bought from illegal online pharmacies measured 7.7–14.4% purity against 99% on the label, 29–39% more peptide than labelled and endotoxin in every vial; a seized injection vial held an undocumented GHRP-2 analogue identifiable only by high-resolution mass spectrometry. Neither study concerns skin peptides.

assertions.text: Three semaglutide vials bought from illegal online pharmacies measured 7.7–14.4% purity against 99% on the label.
assertions.note: The study confirmed that the measured purity of the three semaglutide vials was 7.7% to 14.37%, compared with 99% on the label.

assertions.text: The semaglutide vials contained 29–39% more peptide than labelled, and endotoxin was detected in every vial.
assertions.note: The semaglutide content exceeded labeled amounts by 28.56% to 38.69% and bacterial endotoxin was detected in all three samples.

assertions.text: A seized injection vial contained an undocumented GHRP-2 analogue identifiable only by high-resolution mass spectrometry.
assertions.note: The authors used high-resolution tandem mass spectrometry to identify the novel GHRP-2 analogue, but do not state it was identifiable only by that method.

units.text: 'Not for use in humans' research labelling (21 CFR 312.160) permits shipment only for laboratory or in-vitro research, and FDA reads intended use objectively from claims, advertising and the circumstances of distribution (21 CFR 201.128); a research-use-only product therefore has no clinical route, and a certificate does not create one.

assertions.text: 'Not for use in humans' research labelling under 21 CFR 312.160 permits shipment only for laboratory or in-vitro research.
assertions.quote: The drug-side analogue, 21 C.F.R. 312.160, permits shipping an investigational drug without an IND for laboratory animal or in vitro use if the label reads "Not for use in humans" — and obliges the shipper to confirm the consignee runs such tests.
assertions.note: The source confirms that 21 CFR 312.160 permits shipping under 'Not for use in humans' labelling only for in vitro or laboratory animal research.

assertions.text: FDA reads intended use objectively from claims, advertising, and the circumstances of distribution under 21 CFR 201.128.
assertions.quote: The intent may be shown by such persons' expressions, the design or composition of the article, or by the circumstances surrounding the distribution of the article. This objective intent may, for example, be shown by labeling claims, advertising matter, or oral or written statements by such persons or their representatives.
assertions.note: The regulation specifies that intended use is determined objectively from labeling claims, advertising matter, and circumstances of distribution.

assertions.text: A research-use-only product has no clinical route.
assertions.quote: "Research-use-only" product is not a pathway to patient administration.
assertions.note: The guide explicitly notes that research-use-only products provide no lawful pathway to clinical patient administration.

assertions.text: A certificate of analysis does not create a clinical route for a research-use-only product.
assertions.quote: What it cannot establish on its own is that a product is safe to inject — that turns on sterility, the dose and route, the conditions the material was held in since testing, and whether the lot tested is the lot in hand.
assertions.note: The text confirms that a certificate of analysis cannot on its own establish that a product is safe or suitable for injection.

recheck.note: The text confirms that a certificate of analysis cannot on its own establish that a product is safe or suitable for injection.

units.text: In the US the regime follows intended use and route: appearance claims make a cosmetic (no premarket approval), while a claim to affect structure or function — such as 'regenerate cells' — makes a drug, and 'cosmeceutical' has no legal meaning; dietary supplements are not approved before sale, their makers being responsible for safety and labelling.

assertions.text: In the US, the regulatory regime follows intended use and route.
assertions.quote: Bottom line: route plus claim define the regime — the same peptide can be a lawful cosmetic, a prescription compound, or an unlawful "supplement" depending on how it is sold.
assertions.note: The guide confirms that the combination of route and claims determines the applicable regulatory regime.

assertions.text: Appearance claims make a product a cosmetic, which does not require premarket approval.
assertions.quote: Under the FD&C Act, cosmetic products and ingredients, with the exception of color additives, do not require FDA approval before they go on the market.
assertions.note: The FDA notes that cosmetics do not require FDA approval before going on the market.

assertions.text: A claim to affect structure or function, such as regenerating cells, makes a product a drug.
assertions.quote: Such claims establish the product as a drug because the intended use is to treat or prevent disease or otherwise affect the structure or functions of the human body. Some examples are claims that products will restore hair growth, reduce cellulite, treat varicose veins, increase or decrease the production of melanin (pigment) in the skin, or regenerate cells.
assertions.note: The FDA explains that claims to affect structure or function, including regenerating cells, establish a product as a drug.

assertions.text: The term 'cosmeceutical' has no legal meaning under US law.
assertions.quote: The FD&C Act does not recognize any such category as "cosmeceuticals." A product can be a drug, a cosmetic, or a combination of both, but the term "cosmeceutical" has no meaning under the law.
assertions.note: The FDA explicitly confirms that the term cosmeceutical has no meaning under the FD&C Act.

assertions.text: Dietary supplements are not approved before sale, with manufacturers responsible for safety and labelling.
assertions.quote: That means that these firms are responsible for evaluating the safety and labeling of their products before marketing to ensure that they meet all the requirements of the Federal Food, Drug, and Cosmetic Act as amended by DSHEA and FDA regulations.
assertions.note: Under DSHEA, manufacturers are responsible for evaluating safety and labeling before marketing rather than obtaining premarket approval.

units.text: 'Off-label' describes unapproved use of an approved drug; a never-approved peptide has no label to depart from, introducing an unapproved new drug into interstate commerce is a prohibited act under the FD&C Act, and FDA has warned a compounding pharmacy that its BPC-157 and GHK-Cu products did not qualify for the 503A exemptions.

assertions.text: 'Off-label' describes unapproved use of an approved drug.
assertions.quote: Unapproved use of an approved drug is often called “off-label” use.
assertions.note: FDA guidance explains that unapproved use of an approved drug is commonly termed off-label use.

assertions.text: A never-approved peptide has no label to depart from.
assertions.quote: Off-label prescribing presupposes an approved product to be off the label of; for a never-approved peptide the marketing prohibition is unrelieved and the adequate-directions exemption is unavailable.
assertions.note: The clinical reference notes that off-label prescribing presupposes an approved product to be off the label of.

assertions.text: Introducing an unapproved new drug into interstate commerce is a prohibited act under the FD&C Act.
assertions.quote: Under sections 505(a) and 301(d) of the FDCA [21 U.S.C. § 331(d)], a new drug may not be introduced into or delivered for introduction into interstate commerce unless an application approved by FDA under section 505 of the FDCA is in effect for the drug.
assertions.note: The FDA notes that introducing an unapproved new drug into interstate commerce violates sections 505(a) and 301(d) of the FD&C Act.

assertions.text: FDA has warned a compounding pharmacy that its BPC-157 and GHK-Cu products did not qualify for the 503A exemptions.
assertions.quote: During the inspection, the FDA investigators noted that drug products produced by your firm failed to meet the conditions of section 503A. For example, the investigators noted that your firm compounded drug products using Follistatin, GHRP-2, GHRP-6, Endurobal, AOD 9604, BPC 157, Bremelanotide (PT-141), Cerebrolysin, DSIP, Epitalon, GHK-Cu, IGF1-LR3, Ipamorelin, LL-37, Melanotan II, PEG-MGF, Selank, Semax, CJC 1295, SARMS, LGD-4033, and MK 677.
assertions.note: In a 2020 warning letter to Tailor Made Compounding, the FDA cited products compounded with BPC 157 and GHK-Cu for failing to satisfy section 503A conditions.

units.text: For an unapproved or compounded peptide the chart should name the article and its regulatory status in those terms; if compounded, the pathway, facility and certificate relied on; consent covering non-approval, foreseeable risks, approved alternatives (including doing nothing) and what happens if harm occurs — elements the Peptide Pocket Guide borrows from FDA's research-consent rule; the evidence grade quoted; monitoring and a stopping rule; and the date the FDA lists were checked.

assertions.text: For an unapproved or compounded peptide, chart documentation should name the article and its regulatory status in those terms, and if compounded, the pathway (503A or 503B), facility, and certificate of analysis relied on.
assertions.quote:
1.    Document the identity of the article and its regulatory status in the chart,
      in those terms — not as off-label use of an approved drug.
2. Where a compounded preparation is used, record the pathway (503A or
   503B), the facility, and the certificate of analysis relied on.
assertions.note: Supported by the regulatory chapter of The Peptide Pocket Guide.

assertions.text: Informed consent should cover non-approval, foreseeable risks, approved alternatives, and what happens if injury occurs, adopting elements from FDA's research-consent regulation.
assertions.quote:
3. Build consent around the elements FDA's research-consent regulation
   enumerates: that the therapy is not approved for the indication, the
   foreseeable risks, the approved alternatives, and what is available if injury
   occurs.
assertions.note: Supported by The Peptide Pocket Guide's consent guidelines.

assertions.text: Documentation should record the evidence grade quoted, a monitoring plan, and discontinuation criteria or a stopping rule.
assertions.quote:
Document the following:
— GRADE of evidence
— Regulatory status
— Alternatives offered
— Expected effects
— Monitoring plan
— Discontinuation criteria
assertions.note: Supported by Pearl 8 on documenting informed consent.

assertions.text: Prescribers should verify and document the category and listing status on FDA lists at the time of prescribing.
assertions.quote:
5. Verify category and listing status at the time of prescribing — these lists
   changed materially in April and May 2026 alone.
assertions.note: Supported by The Peptide Pocket Guide's instructions on verifying FDA lists at prescribing.

units.text: In the UK, regulation 167 of the Human Medicines Regulations 2012 lifts the marketing-authorisation requirement (regulation 46) for a 'special' supplied in response to an unsolicited order, manufactured to the specification of a doctor, dentist, nurse independent prescriber, pharmacist independent prescriber or supplementary prescriber, for a patient under that person's direct responsibility, to meet the patient's special needs; no advertisement may be published, and UK manufacture requires a manufacturer's licence for special medicinal products.

assertions.text: In the UK, regulation 167 of the Human Medicines Regulations 2012 provides an exemption from the marketing-authorisation requirement for a 'special'.
assertions.quote:
2.1  Regulation 167 of the Human Medicines Regulations 2012 sets out the exemption 
from the requirement for a medicinal product, placed on the market in the UK to hold 
a marketing authorisation.
assertions.note: Regulation 167 provides an exemption from the requirement for a medicinal product placed on the UK market to hold a marketing authorisation.

assertions.text: A 'special' is manufactured or imported to the specification of a doctor, dentist, nurse independent prescriber, pharmacist independent prescriber, or supplementary prescriber for the treatment of individual patients.
assertions.quote:
This Guidance Note provides advice on the manufacture, importation, distribution and 
supply of unlicensed medicinal products for human use (commonly described as 
“specials”) which have been specially manufactured or imported to the order of a 
doctor, dentist, nurse independent prescriber, pharmacist independent prescriber or 
supplementary prescriber for the treatment of individual patients.
assertions.note: Specials are unlicensed medicinal products manufactured or imported to the order of these specified prescribers for individual patients.

assertions.text: No advertisement relating to a special medicinal product may be published.
assertions.quote:
7.1  A “specials” manufacturer, importer or wholesaler may advertise the service he 
provides but particular “specials” must not be advertised as provided by condition B of 
regulation 167 of the Human Medicines Regulations 2012.
assertions.note: Condition B of regulation 167 prohibits the advertising of particular specials.

assertions.text: In the UK, manufacturing 'specials' requires a Manufacturer's Specials Licence.
assertions.quote:
4.1  The manufacturer or assembler of “specials” must hold a Manufacturer’s “Specials” 
Licence granted by the Licensing Authority.
assertions.note: Manufacturers or assemblers of specials must hold a Manufacturer's 'Specials' Licence granted by the Licensing Authority.

units.text: MHRA Guidance Note 14: specials are made in GMP-inspected facilities but are otherwise unassessed for safety, quality and efficacy; an unlicensed product should not be supplied where a licensed product can meet the patient's special need, and special need excludes cost, convenience and operational reasons; the order of preference is a UK-licensed product (even off-label), then a product licensed in its country of origin, then a UK special, with products that are not medicines in their country of origin, such as supplements, least acceptable.

assertions.text: Specials are manufactured in GMP-inspected facilities but are otherwise unassessed for safety, quality, and efficacy.
assertions.quote: If none of these options will suffice, then a completely unlicensed product may have to be used, for example, UK manufactured "specials", which are made in GMP inspected facilities, but which are otherwise un-assessed (GMP inspection of “specials” manufacturers is not product specific).
assertions.note: Guidance Note 14 notes that specials are made in GMP-inspected facilities but are otherwise unassessed.

assertions.text: An unlicensed product should not be supplied where an equivalent licensed medicinal product can meet the special needs of the patient.
assertions.quote: An unlicensed medicinal product should not be supplied where an equivalent licensed medicinal product can meet the special needs of the patient.
assertions.note: Guidance Note 14 confirms that an unlicensed product should not be supplied if a licensed equivalent is suitable.

assertions.text: The requirement for a special need excludes reasons of cost, convenience, or operational needs.
assertions.quote: The requirement for a “special need” relates to the special clinical needs of the individual patient. It does not include reasons of cost, convenience or operational needs (see Section 10 of this guide).
assertions.note: Guidance Note 14 explicitly excludes cost, convenience, and operational needs from the definition of special need.

assertions.text: Under the hierarchy for unlicensed medicines, a UK-licensed product should be used even off-label instead of an unlicensed product.
assertions.quote: Although MHRA does not recommend “off-label” (outside the licensed indications) use of products, if a UK licensed product can meet the clinical need, even off-label, it should be used instead of an unlicensed product (see Appendix 2).
assertions.note: Guidance Note 14 specifies that an available UK-licensed product should be used even off-label in preference to an unlicensed product.

assertions.text: If a UK-licensed product cannot meet the special need, an imported product licensed in its country of origin should be considered before a UK special.
assertions.quote: If the UK product cannot meet the special need, then another (imported) medicinal product should be considered, which is licensed in the country of origin.
assertions.note: The hierarchy places a product licensed in its country of origin ahead of completely unlicensed products such as UK specials.

assertions.text: Products that are not classed as medicines in their country of origin, such as supplements, are the least acceptable option in the hierarchy.
assertions.quote: The least acceptable products are those that are unlicensed in the country of origin, and which are not classed as medicines in the country of origin (but are in the UK).
assertions.note: Guidance Note 14 classifies products not treated as medicines in their country of origin, like supplements, as the least acceptable.

units.text: A pharmacist may also prepare or dispense a medicinal product in a registered pharmacy, hospital or health centre in accordance with a prescription without a marketing authorisation (Medicines Act 1968, s. 10); MHRA counts such pharmacy preparations among unlicensed medicines.

assertions.text: A pharmacist may prepare or dispense a medicinal product in a registered pharmacy, hospital, or health centre in accordance with a prescription without a marketing authorisation under Section 10 of the Medicines Act 1968.
assertions.quote: The restrictions imposed by [ F2 regulations 17(1) (manufacturing of medicinal products) and 46 (requirement for authorisation) of the 2012 Regulations ] do not apply to anything which is done in a registered pharmacy, a hospital [ F3 , a care home service ] or a health centre and is done there by or under the supervision of a pharmacist and consists of—
assertions.note: Section 10(1) exempts preparation or dispensing in these settings under the supervision of a pharmacist from the requirement for authorisation.

assertions.text: The MHRA classifies medicinal products prepared in a pharmacy under section 10 of the Medicines Act 1968 as unlicensed medicines.
assertions.quote: A holder of a Manufacturer’s “Specials” Licence may also be a registered pharmacy supplying unlicensed medicinal products prepared under the exemption provided by section 10 of the 1968 Medicines Act and regulation 4 of the Human Medicines Regulations 2012.
assertions.note: MHRA Guidance Note 14 explicitly categorises products prepared under section 10 of the 1968 Medicines Act as unlicensed medicinal products.

units.text: UK professional guidance puts responsibility for an unlicensed medicine on its prescriber: GMC — be satisfied there is sufficient evidence or experience of safety and efficacy, take responsibility for prescribing and for overseeing care and follow-up, record the reasons when not following common practice, and explain to the patient when the use is not routine or licensed alternatives exist; MHRA advises the same and names doctors, dentists, independent nurse and pharmacist prescribers and, in some circumstances, supplementary prescribers as able to prescribe unlicensed medicines; the GPhC asks pharmacist prescribers to be sure of sufficient evidence and to record discussions and reasons; the NMC Code limits prescribing to the registrant's training, competence, the law and guidance.

assertions.text: GMC guidance requires prescribers of unlicensed medicines to be satisfied there is sufficient evidence or experience of safety and efficacy, take responsibility for prescribing and overseeing follow-up, record reasons when not following common practice, and explain when use is not routine or licensed alternatives exist.
assertions.note: The cited GMC source is unavailable (HTTP 403) and its specific guidance is not provided.

recheck.note: The cited GMC guidance is not provided, and none of the provided source texts state what GMC guidance requires.

assertions.text: MHRA advises prescribers of unlicensed medicines to take responsibility for prescribing and follow-up, and be satisfied of sufficient evidence of safety and efficacy.
assertions.quote: The responsibility that falls on healthcare professionals when prescribing an unlicensed medicine or a medicine off-label may be greater than when prescribing a licensed medicine within the terms of its licence.
assertions.note: The MHRA guidance states prescribers carry greater responsibility when prescribing unlicensed medicines.

assertions.text: MHRA names doctors, dentists, independent nurse and pharmacist prescribers and, in some circumstances, supplementary prescribers as able to prescribe unlicensed medicines.
assertions.quote: At present, the following healthcare professionals can prescribe an unlicensed medicine: doctors; dentists; independent nurse and pharmacist prescribers and, in some circumstances, supplementary prescribers (who can be a pharmacist, nurse, midwife, community nurse, optometrist, physiotherapist, radiographer, or chiropodist/podiatrist).
assertions.note: The MHRA explicitly lists these healthcare professionals as able to prescribe unlicensed medicines.

assertions.text: The GPhC requires pharmacist prescribers to ensure there is sufficient evidence and experience of safety and effectiveness when prescribing an unlicensed medicine.
assertions.quote:
• in the case of an unlicensed or ‘off-label’ 
medicine, make sure there is sufficient 
evidence and experience of its safety and 
effectiveness, and of the appropriateness of 
its use to meet the needs of the person.
assertions.note: GPhC guidance instructs pharmacist prescribers to ensure sufficient evidence and experience of safety and effectiveness.

assertions.text: The GPhC requires pharmacist prescribers to record discussions and the reasons for their prescribing decisions when prescribing an unlicensed medicine.
assertions.quote:
This should include: 
– a record of discussions, especially when 
prescribing is outside the national 
guidelines or is for an unlicensed or ‘off-
label’ medicine 
– the reasons for their prescribing 
decisions, and 
– arrangements for follow-up and 
monitoring
assertions.note: GPhC guidance requires documenting discussions and reasons when prescribing unlicensed medicines.

assertions.text: The NMC Code limits prescribing to the registrant's training, competence, the law and guidance.
assertions.quote: 18 Advise on, prescribe, supply, dispense or administer medicines within the limits of your training and competence, the law, our guidance and other relevant policies, guidance and regulations
assertions.note: Standard 18 of the NMC Code restricts prescribing to the registrant's training, competence, law, and relevant guidance.

units.text: In the UK, MHRA decides whether a product is a medicinal product from all its claims (including websites and social media), its presentation, its product form (such as injection) and the way it is used; a medicinal product with no UK marketing authorisation may not be sold, supplied or offered for sale (Human Medicines Regulations 2012, reg. 46) or advertised (reg. 279).

assertions.text: In the UK, the MHRA decides whether a product is a medicinal product based on all its claims (including on websites and social media), its presentation, its product form (such as injection), and the way it is used.
assertions.quote:
The MHRA considers the following factors:  
• all claims made for the product, both explicit and implicit, including any made on 
websites, linked helplines, testimonials, linked publications, or in social media. Implicit 
claims may include product names   
• the context in which the claims are made, and the overall presentation
assertions.note: MHRA Guidance Note 8 lists claims across all media, context and presentation, product form, and intended use as factors determining medicinal product status.

assertions.text: Under regulation 46 of the Human Medicines Regulations 2012, an unauthorised medicinal product with no UK marketing authorisation may not be sold, supplied, or offered for sale.
assertions.quote: 46. —(1) A person may not sell or supply, or offer to sell or supply, an unauthorised medicinal product.
assertions.note: Regulation 46(1) states that a person may not sell, supply, or offer to sell or supply an unauthorised medicinal product.

assertions.text: Under regulation 279 of the Human Medicines Regulations 2012, a medicinal product without an appropriate authorisation in force may not be advertised.
assertions.quote:
(3)   A person may not publish an advertisement in the whole United Kingdom for a medicinal product unless, in relation to that product— 

(a) one of the authorisations or registrations specified in paragraph (1) is in force in Great Britain; and 

(b) one of the authorisations or registrations specified in paragraph (2) is in force in Northern Ireland. ]
assertions.note: Regulation 279 prohibits publishing an advertisement for a medicinal product in the UK unless valid authorisations or registrations are in force.

units.text: MHRA classifies injectable melanotan products as medicines and has removed melanotan products from the market (FOI 24/274, April 2024); its largest seizure of unlicensed weight-loss medicines, on 28 May 2026, included peptide products.

assertions.text: MHRA classifies injectable melanotan products as medicines.
assertions.quote: Products containing Melanotan II are classified as medicines if they are injectable or pens.
assertions.note: The MHRA response confirms that melanotan II products are classified as medicines if they are injectable or pens.

assertions.text: MHRA has taken action to remove melanotan products from the market.
assertions.quote: However, the MHRA has repeatedly taken action to remove Melanotan products from the market for over 10 years and will continue to do so where products fall within the definition of a medicinal product
assertions.note: The agency states that it has repeatedly taken action over more than a decade to remove melanotan products from the market.

assertions.text: The MHRA conducted its largest ever seizure of unlicensed weight-loss medicines.
assertions.quote: Officers from the Medicines and Healthcare products Regulatory Agency’s (MHRA) Criminal Enforcement Unit have arrested two people after raiding a country estate near Northampton, recovering around 12,000 doses of unlicensed weight loss medicines in the largest ever seizure of such products by the agency.
assertions.note: The MHRA reports recovering around 12,000 doses in the largest ever seizure of unlicensed weight loss medicines by the agency.

assertions.text: The unlicensed weight-loss medicines in the operation included peptide products.
assertions.quote: The property is believed to have been used as a large-scale facility to manufacture, assemble, and distribute unlicensed weight loss medicines, including retatrutide and tirzepatide, as well as peptide products.
assertions.note: The release confirms that the seized unlicensed weight-loss medicines included peptide products.

units.text: UK law prohibits publishing an advertisement likely to lead to the use of a prescription-only medicine (reg. 284), and CAP Code rule 12.12 bars advertising prescription-only medicines to the public; MHRA's Blue Guide lets clinics promote a service such as 'treatment for lines and wrinkles' provided they do not name a prescription-only medicine, and says unlicensed medicines should not be mentioned.

assertions.text: UK law prohibits publishing an advertisement likely to lead to the use of a prescription-only medicine (reg. 284).
assertions.quote: 284. —(1) A person may not publish an advertisement that is likely to lead to the use of a prescription only medicine.
assertions.note: Regulation 284(1) of the Human Medicines Regulations 2012 explicitly prohibits publishing advertisements likely to lead to the use of a prescription-only medicine.

assertions.text: CAP Code rule 12.12 bars advertising prescription-only medicines to the public.
assertions.quote: 12.12 Prescription-only medicines or prescription-only medical treatments may not be advertised to the public.
assertions.note: CAP Code rule 12.12 prohibits advertising prescription-only medicines or prescription-only treatments to the public.

assertions.text: MHRA's Blue Guide allows clinics to promote a service such as 'treatment for lines and wrinkles' provided they do not name a prescription-only medicine.
assertions.quote: As an example, advertising for cosmetic clinics and beauty salons may promote the service provided, e.g. “treatment for lines and wrinkles”, as this is non-specific and may include various procedures. Advertising materials such as magazine advertisements and flyers distributed to the public must not mention product names such as “Botox” or “botulinum toxin”.
assertions.note: The Blue Guide gives this specific example for cosmetic clinics provided product names are omitted.

assertions.text: MHRA's Blue Guide states that unlicensed medicines should not be mentioned.
assertions.quote: Unlicensed medicines should not be mentioned, to comply with regulation 279 of the Regulations which prohibits advertising of medicines for which no marketing authorisation or registration is in force.
assertions.note: The Blue Guide specifies in Appendix 6 that unlicensed medicines should not be mentioned.

units.text: On 11 February 2026 the ASA upheld a complaint that Instagram posts by customers of an online pharmacy's referral scheme, carrying discount codes and hashtags such as '#mounjaro', promoted a prescription-only medicine to the public.

assertions.text: On 11 February 2026 the ASA upheld a complaint that Instagram posts by customers of an online pharmacy's referral scheme, carrying discount codes and hashtags such as '#mounjaro', promoted a prescription-only medicine to the public.
assertions.quote: We therefore considered the references to “mounjaro” in the ads, whether or not such references were preceded by a hashtag or were part of larger references such as “mounjarojourney”, “mounjaroweightlossjourney”, “mounjarotribe” or “voymounjaro”, promoted POMs to the public.
assertions.note: The ASA ruling published on 11 February 2026 upheld that Instagram posts under Voy's referral scheme using discount codes and hashtags like #mounjaro unlawfully promoted prescription-only medicines to the public.

units.text: GMC guidance for doctors who offer cosmetic interventions requires a physical examination before prescribing injectable cosmetic medicines, which therefore may not be prescribed by telephone, video link or online for patients the doctor has not examined.
units.note: no cited source has readable text — nothing can be verified

units.text:
The skin as an endocrine organ, and how it ages
Lesson 1.1 The skin as a steroidogenic, endocrine organ · Lesson 1.2 Receptor maps and what they prove · Lesson 1.3 Senescence, the SASP and the ageing dermis.
Module 01 · The skin as an endocrine organ
The skin makes its own hormones.
This course starts with physiology, because every later question about a hormone or peptide for skin rests on it. Skin senses hormones from the blood, makes several of its own, and ages in ways that change both. In three lessons you will separate what happens locally in the skin from what the rest of the body sends in, and label each finding by the kind of evidence behind it.
1.2 Receptor maps: what a cell atlas can and cannot show
Your role
How will you use this course?
The evidence and grades are the same for everyone, and regulatory notes follow the country you choose. What changes with your role, in every…

Module 01 · Opening film
The skin as an endocrine organ, and how it ages
units.sourceNote: Slominski 2025 · Slominski & Wortsman 2000 · Zouboulis 2004 · Roosterman 2006 · Aesthetic & Regenerative Endocrinology, ch. 5–6

units.text:
Lesson 1.1 · Concept
Four units, one circuit.
Recent reviews describe the skin as a neuro-immuno-endocrine organ built from four units: epidermal, dermal, hypodermal and adnexal (hair follicles and glands). Each holds cells that can make hormones and mount an immune response. They signal to neighbouring cells, through sensory nerves, and through the blood. Most of this picture comes from cell, tissue and animal studies.
Four units: epidermal, dermal, hypodermal, adnexal
Three routes: neighbour to neighbour, nerve, bloodstream
Mechanism register: cell, tissue and animal work
Narration: Think of the skin as a sensing organ with its own hormone supply. Researchers who study it describe four units, epidermal, dermal, hypodermal and adnexal, the last meaning hair follicles and glands. Each unit holds cells that can make hormones and mount an immune response, such as keratinocytes, fibroblasts…
units.sourceNote: Slominski 2025 · Slominski & Wortsman 2000 · Zouboulis 2004 · Roosterman 2006 · Aesthetic & Regenerative Endocrinology, ch. 5–6

assertions.text: Recent reviews describe the skin as a neuro-immuno-endocrine organ built from four units: epidermal, dermal, hypodermal, and adnexal (hair follicles and glands).
assertions.quote: This skin neuro–immuno–endocrine system is compartmentalized through the formation of epidermal, dermal, hypodermal and adnexal regulatory units.
assertions.note: The review confirms that the cutaneous neuro-immuno-endocrine system is organized into epidermal, dermal, hypodermal, and adnexal regulatory units.

assertions.text: Each unit holds cells that can make hormones and mount an immune response, such as keratinocytes, fibroblasts, sebocytes, fat cells, and mast cells.
assertions.quote: Each contains resident cells with both hormone-making and immune capacity (keratinocytes, melanocytes, fibroblasts, sebocytes, adipocytes, mast cells, dendritic and Langerhans cells), wired together by sensory nerves that penetrate to the stratum corneum.
assertions.note: The text confirms that each unit contains resident cells with both hormone-making and immune capacity, citing these cell types.

assertions.text: Signaling moves through three routes: directly between neighbouring cells, via sensory nerves, and through the bloodstream to distant organs.
assertions.quote: Communication runs three ways: soluble factors between neighboring cells, rapid neural transmission, and release into the circulation that can reach distant organs.
assertions.note: The text explicitly describes these three routes of communication.

units.text:
Mechanism
A steroid factory with local axes.
Skin cells carry the enzymes to build steroids from cholesterol or to activate precursors arriving in the blood, and they run shortened copies of the body's central hormone axes. Each row names the evidence it rests on, because most of it comes from cells, tissue kept alive outside the body, or mice.
Steroid synthesis
Cholesterol to cortisol, androgens and estrogens
CYP11A1 starts the chain; 11β-HSD1, 5α-reductase and aromatase activate precursors from the blood. Cell and tissue studies.
HPA-like loop
CRH → ACTH → cortisol, with feedback
Human scalp follicles kept alive in culture. Ex vivo, human tissue.
Keratinocyte glucocorticoids
Set local immune tone
Genetic deletion in mouse keratinocytes. Animal evidence.
Thyroid-like loop
TRH, TSH and deiodinases → T3
Keratinocyte growth and the hair cycle. Mostly mouse models.
Somatotropic loop
GH and …
units.sourceNote: Slominski 2013 · Ito 2005 · Phan 2021 · Mancino 2021 · Horesh 2023 · Aesthetic & Regenerative Endocrinology, ch. 6

assertions.text: Skin cells contain the enzymatic apparatus to synthesize steroids from cholesterol or activate precursors arriving from the blood.
assertions.quote: Most recently it has been established that skin cells contain the entire biochemical apparatus necessary for production of glucocorticoids, androgens and estrogens either from precursors of systemic origin or, alternatively, through the conversion of cholesterol to pregnenolone and its subsequent transformation to biologically active steroids.
assertions.note: Supported by the review on cutaneous steroidogenesis.

assertions.text: CYP11A1 initiates the steroidogenic pathway from cholesterol.
assertions.quote: Steroid hormone biosynthesis is initiated upon mobilization of cholesterol, the substrate for steroid hormones, from cellular stores in cytoplasmic lipid granules to the mitochondrial inner membrane, the site of cytochrome P450scc (CYP11A1).
assertions.note: Supported by the source description of initial steroid biosynthesis.

assertions.text: Human scalp hair follicles cultured ex vivo display an HPA-like loop with CRH stimulating ACTH and cortisol production and responding to feedback.
assertions.quote: Thus, even in the absence of endocrine, neural, or vascular systemic connections, normal human scalp hair follicles directly respond to CRH stimulation in a strikingly similar manner to what is seen in the classical HPA axis, including synthesis and secretion of cortisol and activation of prototypic neuroendocrine feedback loops.
assertions.note: Supported by findings in organ-cultured human hair follicles.

assertions.text: De novo synthesized keratinocyte glucocorticoids set local immune tone, as shown by genetic deletion in mice.
assertions.quote: In line with 11β-hydroxylase deficiency in human inflammatory skin disorders, genetic in vivo Cyp11b1 ablation and long-term GC deficiency in keratinocytes primed the murine skin immune system resulting in spontaneous skin inflammation.
assertions.note: Supported by the mouse keratinocyte Cyp11b1 deletion study.

assertions.text: A cutaneous thyroid-like loop (TRH, TSH, deiodinases producing T3) regulates keratinocyte proliferation and the hair cycle, largely evidenced by mouse models.
assertions.quote: A cutaneous hypothalamic–pituitary–thyroid loop (local TRH and TSH, with deiodinases generating T3) modulates keratinocyte proliferation, the hair cycle, and mitochondrial function,[7]
assertions.note: Supported by the clinician's pocket guide and referenced review.

assertions.text: Human hair follicles maintain an autonomous somatotropic loop with GH and IGF-1 ex vivo.
assertions.quote: The human hair follicle runs functional peripheral equivalents of the central axes: it synthesizes cortisol and operates a local HPA-like loop,[11] and ex vivo it sustains a hypothalamic–pituitary–somatotropic equivalent (GHRH, GH, IGF-1) that paces its own growth.[12]
assertions.note: Supported by the clinician's pocket guide summarizing hair follicle ex vivo findings.

assertions.text: POMC cleavage generates α-MSH, ACTH, and β-endorphin to regulate skin pigment, barrier function, and local immune restraint.
assertions.quote: The skin makes and processes POMC into ACTH, α-MSH, and β-endorphin, acting on melanocortin receptors MC1–MC5 to govern pigment, barrier strength, sebum, and local immunosuppression.[8]
assertions.note: Supported by the clinician's pocket guide.

assertions.text: The Aesthetic & Regenerative Endocrinology pocket guide frames local cutaneous endocrine axes as mechanistic foundations rather than dosing rationales.
assertions.quote: It is a genuine steroidogenic and secosteroid factory (CYP11A1; vitamin D, lumisterol, tachysterol) and runs local HPA-, thyroid-, and GH/IGF-1-like axes — mechanistic foundation, not a dosing rationale.
assertions.note: Supported by chapter 6 of the pocket guide.

assertions.text: The sorting category for 'Keratinocytes make cortisol that restrains immune cells in the same patch of skin' is 'Local loop' (made and used in the skin).
assertions.quote: Our findings provide insights on how skin homeostasis and pathology are critically regulated by keratinocyte-derived GC, emphasizing the immunoregulatory potential of endogenous GC in the regulation of epithelial immune microenvironment.
assertions.note: Keratinocytes produce immunosuppressive glucocorticoids that locally regulate cutaneous immune homeostasis.

assertions.text: The sorting category for 'UVB turns 7-dehydrocholesterol into vitamin D3, which the blood carries to the liver' is 'Skin to body' (a skin product entering the circulation).
assertions.quote: Thus, UVB-exposed skin can generate a large number of biologically active sterol and secosteroidal photoproducts that regulate local and global homeostasis after entry into the circulation, explaining many of the beneficial effects of UVB that cannot be achieved by oral vitamin D delivery.
assertions.note: UVB photoproducts synthesized in the skin enter the circulation to regulate systemic homeostasis.

assertions.text: The sorting category for 'Violaceous striae, thin skin and easy bruising in Cushing syndrome' is 'Body to skin' (a circulating hormone acting on skin as part of a systemic disorder).
assertions.quote: The genuine endocrine entity is the moon facies of Cushing’s syndrome — a rounded, plethoric face with dorsocervical and supraclavicular fat pads, central adiposity, wide purple striae, proximal muscle weakness, and easy bruising — a referable diagnosis, not a cosmetic state.[5]
assertions.note: Cushing syndrome is a systemic endocrine disorder that produces cutaneous signs including purple striae and bruising.

assertions.text: The sorting category for 'Scalp hair follicles kept alive in culture secrete cortisol, then switch off their own CRH' is 'Local loop' (made and used in the skin).
assertions.quote: Thus, even in the absence of endocrine, neural, or vascular systemic connections, normal human scalp hair follicles directly respond to CRH stimulation in a strikingly similar manner to what is seen in the classical HPA axis, including synthesis and secretion of cortisol and activation of prototypic neuroendocrine feedback loops.
assertions.note: Organ-cultured human scalp hair follicles synthesize and secrete cortisol and engage local feedback loops independent of systemic connections.

assertions.text: The sorting category for 'Skin converts circulating precursors into androgens and estrogens that add to the body's supply' is 'Skin to body' (skin acting as an endocrine gland for other organs).
assertions.quote: The cutaneous steroidogenic system can also have systemic effects, which are emphasized by significant skin contribution to circulating androgens and/or estrogens.
assertions.note: Local steroidogenesis in skin contributes substantially to circulating levels of androgens and estrogens.

assertions.text: The sorting category for 'Dry, coarse skin and myxoedema in hypothyroidism' is 'Body to skin' (a circulating hormone deficiency acting on skin).
assertions.quote: Hypothyroidism gives dry, coarse, cool skin and myxedema; hyperthyroidism gives warm, moist skin and, in Graves' disease, pretibial myxedema.[8]
assertions.note: Systemic hypothyroidism causes cutaneous manifestations such as dry, coarse skin and myxedema.

assertions.text: The sorting category for 'Scalp follicles convert testosterone to DHT, which shrinks susceptible follicles' is 'Local loop' (made and used in the skin).
assertions.quote: Thyroid hormone and prolactin tune the cycle and estrogen withdrawal at menopause thins hair, but the dominant clinical lever is androgenic: 5α-reductase converts testosterone to DHT, which paradoxically miniaturizes genetically susceptible scalp follicles (androgenetic alopecia) while driving beard and body hair.
assertions.note: Local 5α-reductase in hair follicles converts testosterone to DHT, directly causing follicular miniaturization.
