assertions.text: Keratinocytes produce cortisol that restrains local skin immune cells in a local loop, demonstrated by mice lacking keratinocyte glucocorticoid synthesis developing spontaneous skin inflammation.
assertions.quote: In line with 11β-hydroxylase deficiency in human inflammatory skin disorders, genetic in vivo Cyp11b1 ablation and long-term GC deficiency in keratinocytes primed the murine skin immune system resulting in spontaneous skin inflammation.
assertions.note: Phan et al. report that genetic Cyp11b1 ablation in mouse keratinocytes leads to spontaneous skin inflammation.

assertions.text: UVB-mediated conversion of 7-dehydrocholesterol to vitamin D3 in the skin followed by release into the circulation and transport to the liver operates as a skin-to-body endocrine pathway.
assertions.quote: The skin is the unique site of cholecalciferol production and the liver is thought to be the main site of conversion to 25(OH)D 3.
assertions.note: Zouboulis confirms that cholecalciferol is uniquely produced in the skin and transferred to the liver for conversion.

assertions.text: The Aesthetic & Regenerative Endocrinology guide lists suspected Cushing syndrome, presenting with violaceous striae, thin skin, and easy bruising, as a condition requiring prompt referral.
assertions.quote: The genuine endocrine entity is the moon facies of Cushing’s syndrome — a rounded, plethoric face with dorsocervical and supraclavicular fat pads, central adiposity, wide purple striae, proximal muscle weakness, and easy bruising — a referable diagnosis, not a cosmetic state.[5]
assertions.note: The guide notes that Cushing syndrome presents with these signs and is a referable diagnosis.

assertions.text: Cultured human scalp hair follicles secrete cortisol and downregulate CRH expression through a local feedback loop in the absence of neural or vascular input.
assertions.quote: Thus, even in the absence of endocrine, neural, or vascular systemic connections, normal human scalp hair follicles directly respond to CRH stimulation in a strikingly similar manner to what is seen in the classical HPA axis, including synthesis and secretion of cortisol and activation of prototypic neuroendocrine feedback loops.
assertions.note: Ito et al. show that organ-cultured hair follicles secrete cortisol and operate local neuroendocrine feedback loops without systemic connections.

assertions.text: The skin synthesizes androgens and estrogens from circulating precursors and releases them into the circulation, especially in older individuals.
assertions.quote: Human skin produces, activates or inactivates metabolically numerous hormones which are probably important for skin functions but also for functions of the entire human organism, such as sex hormones, especially in aged individuals, insulin-like growth factor and -binding proteins, neuropeptides, prolactin, catecholamines, retinoids, steroids, vitamin D and eicosanoids.
assertions.note: Zouboulis notes that human skin releases hormones including sex steroids into the circulation, especially in aged individuals.

assertions.text: Circulating thyroid hormone regulates epidermal turnover and the dermal matrix, with hypothyroidism causing dry, coarse skin and myxedema.
assertions.quote: T3 and T4 govern epidermal turnover, sebum and sweat secretion, and hair cycling. Hypothyroidism gives dry, coarse, cool skin and myxedema; hyperthyroidism gives warm, moist skin and, in Graves' disease, pretibial myxedema.[8]
assertions.note: The guide confirms that thyroid hormones control epidermal turnover and that hypothyroidism causes dry, coarse skin and myxedema.

assertions.text: 5α-reductase in the pilosebaceous unit converts testosterone to DHT locally, providing the substrate for acne, androgenetic alopecia, and hirsutism.
assertions.quote: Androgens — testosterone and, more potently, DHT generated locally by 5α-reductase — enlarge sebaceous glands and raise sebum, making them central to acne, seborrhea, hirsutism, and androgenetic alopecia; the skin is itself a site of androgen metabolism.[4]
assertions.note: The guide notes that local DHT generated by 5α-reductase is central to acne, androgenetic alopecia, and hirsutism.

An HPA-like loop inside the follicle.

assertions.note: Ito et al. demonstrated that cultured human scalp hair follicles replicate the regulatory feedback and hormone synthesis of the classical HPA axis.

assertions.text: In the hair follicle, CRH stimulation up-regulates ACTH.

assertions.note: Ito et al. showed that the glucocorticoid receptor agonist hydrocortisone down-regulates follicular CRH expression.

units.text:
What changes in practice
Read the skin before the serum.
The Aesthetic & Regenerative Endocrinology guide treats the aesthetic exam as a systemic screen. Sudden thinning and easy bruising suggest cortisol excess; coarse, dry, cool skin suggests hypothyroidism; new acanthosis nigricans flags insulin resistance. It lists violaceous striae with new hypertension or diabetes, and rapidly progressive virilisation, among reasons to refer promptly to endocrinology. Local skin biology explains how skin behaves; it does not justify prescribing a hormone.
A skin sign can be the first sign of a systemic disorder
Some patterns need prompt endocrine referral
Local loops explain biology; they do not justify treatment
Narration: Picture the consultation where a patient asks about thinning, bruising skin. The Aesthetic and Regenerative Endocrinology guide asks you to read that skin as a window on the who…

— Rapidly progressive virilization (deepening voice, clitoromegaly, rapid hirsutism) — possible androgen-secreting tumor.

units.text:
Lesson 1.2 · Concept
A map of fourteen million cells.
The Hormone Cell Atlas, published in Science in 2026, read the RNA for 379 hormone and receptor genes in about 14 million single cells and nuclei from 47 human tissues, skin among them. From that RNA it predicted which cell types could make a hormone and which could respond to one. It is a map of predicted capacity; it did not measure hormone release.
About 14 million cells and nuclei, 47 tissues
Output: predicted producers and receivers
Narration: Fourteen million cells is the scale of the Hormone Cell Atlas, a Cambridge-led study published in Science in 2026. The team read the RNA for 379 hormone and receptor genes in single cells and nuclei from forty-seven human tissues, skin included. From those readings they scored each cell type for its predicted capacity to make or to receive a hormone, and they flagged unexpected sites, such …
units.sourceNote: Fei & Huang-Doran et al., Science 2026 · hormonecellatlas.org.uk · Aesthetic & Regenerative Endocrinology, ch. 7

assertions.text: The Hormone Cell Atlas, published in Science in 2026, analyzed the RNA expression of 379 hormone and receptor genes across approximately 14 million single cells and nuclei from 47 human tissues, including skin.
assertions.quote: Drawing inspiration from the Human Cell Atlas, we analyzed the expression of 379 hormone and receptor genes in a transcriptomic dataset comprising 14 million single cells and nuclei across 47 human tissues.
assertions.note: The abstract confirms profiling 379 hormone and receptor genes across 14 million single cells and nuclei in 47 human tissues.

assertions.text: The atlas mapped predicted hormone-producing and hormone-receiving cell capacity based on transcriptomic data rather than measuring functional hormone release.
assertions.quote: Important: these predictions are based on transcriptomic data and should be considered as putative and hypothesis-generating, rather than as functional hormones and receptors.
assertions.note: The portal explicitly clarifies that predictions are transcriptomic and putative rather than measurements of functional hormones and receptors.

assertions.text: The study identified unexpected sites of expression, including secretin in a type of immune cell.
assertions.quote: We predicted nonclassical sites of hormone expression, including secretin in plasmacytoid dendritic cells, inferred convergent hormone action and endocrine feedback loops, and implicated cell populations in monogenic endocrine disorders.
assertions.note: The study predicted nonclassical sites of hormone expression, specifically secretin in plasmacytoid dendritic cells.

assertions.text: The Aesthetic and Regenerative Endocrinology guide uses the atlas to argue that the skin, built from every major cell lineage, is plausibly one of the body's largest distributed endocrine signalling networks.
assertions.quote: Second, it follows that the skin — the body's largest organ, built from every major lineage (epithelial, mesenchymal, endothelial, adipocyte, immune, neural) in vast quantity — is plausibly one of the body's largest distributed endocrine signaling networks — an inference from transcriptomic prediction rather than direct measurement of secretion.[2]
assertions.note: Chapter 7 of the guide states that the skin is plausibly one of the body's largest distributed endocrine signaling networks based on transcriptomic prediction.

units.text:
What the atlas is
Prediction, in the authors' own words.
The atlas's own portal describes its scores as 'putative and hypothesis-generating'. A few predictions were tested in cells in the paper itself; the rest are left for users to validate. Across biology, the amount of RNA for a gene is often a poor guide to how much protein a cell makes, and protein is still a step short of secretion.
379
hormone and receptor genes read as RNA, cell by cell
Fei, Huang-Doran et al., Science 2026 · about 14 million cells and nuclei · 47 human tissues
What it means: The atlas shows which skin cells carry the RNA to make or sense a hormone. That is a well-founded hypothesis about where to look.
What it does not mean: It does not show that a skin cell secretes a hormone, how much, or that the hormone acts there. A receptor gene on the map is not evidence that a product aimed at it works.
units.sourceNote: Fei & Huang-Doran, Science 2026 · hormonecellatlas.org.uk About/FAQ, read 24 Sep 2026 · Liu 2016

assertions.note: The portal confirms that some predictions were tested in vitro in the paper while users take responsibility for validation.

assertions.text: Across biology, the amount of RNA for a gene is often a poor guide to cellular protein levels.
assertions.quote: We conclude that transcript levels by themselves are not sufficient to predict protein levels in many scenarios and to thus explain genotype-phenotype relationships and that high-quality data quantifying different levels of gene expression are indispensable for the complete understanding of biological processes.
assertions.note: The review concludes that transcript levels alone do not suffice to predict protein levels in many scenarios.

assertions.note: The abstract confirms the analysis of 379 hormone and receptor genes across 14 million cells/nuclei and 47 tissues.

assertions.quote: In line with 11β-hydroxylase deficiency in human inflammatory skin disorders, genetic in vivo Cyp11b1 ablation and long-term GC deficiency in keratinocytes primed the murine skin immune system resulting in spontaneous skin inflammation.
assertions.note: This finding represents experimental animal model research in mice with keratinocyte-specific Cyp11b1 knockout.

assertions.text: Sunlight on human skin forming vitamin D3 that enters the circulation is classified as human in vivo evidence.
assertions.quote: Photosynthesis of previtamin D3 can occur throughout the epidermis in the dermis when hypopigmented Caucasian skin is exposed to solar ultraviolet radiation. Once previtamin D3 is formed in the skin, it undergoes a temperature-dependent thermal isomerization that takes at least 3 days to complete. The vitamin D-binding protein preferentially translocates the thermal product, vitamin D3, into the circulation.
assertions.note: The cited study documents the photosynthesis of previtamin D3 in human skin under solar radiation and its subsequent translocation into circulation.

units.text:
How far up?
Tap the highest rung each finding reaches.
Sorting item (the learner sorts this statement; the course's claim is only the category): "A skin cell type scores high as a hormone producer in a single-cell RNA atlas" → Transcript prediction
Explanation: Transcript. The score comes from RNA; the atlas's authors call such predictions putative until validated.
Sorting item (the learner sorts this statement; the course's claim is only the category): "Scalp hair follicles kept alive in culture secrete cortisol and switch off their own CRH" → Function in tissue or animals
Explanation: Function in human tissue. The loop works ex vivo; whether it shapes hair growth in a living scalp is a further step.
Sorting item (the learner sorts this statement; the course's claim is only the category): "A brochure says skin 'has receptors for' a hormone, citing an RNA atlas" → Transcript prediction
E…

assertions.text: A skin cell type scoring high as a hormone producer in a single-cell RNA atlas constitutes a transcript prediction that is putative until validated.
assertions.quote: Important: these predictions are based on transcriptomic data and should be considered as putative and hypothesis-generating, rather than as functional hormones and receptors.
assertions.note: The Hormone Cell Atlas portal explicitly notes that predictions from transcriptomic data are putative and require functional validation.

assertions.text: Scalp hair follicles maintained in culture secrete cortisol and exhibit a negative feedback loop down-regulating CRH, representing function in ex vivo human tissue.
assertions.quote: Finally, human hair follicles display HPA axis-like regulatory feedback systems, since the glucocorticoid receptor agonist hydrocortisone down-regulates follicular CRH expression.
assertions.note: Isolated human hair follicles in culture were shown to secrete cortisol and down-regulate CRH expression in response to hydrocortisone.

assertions.text: Stating that skin has receptors for a hormone based solely on a single-cell RNA atlas represents a transcript-level prediction rather than demonstrated functional receptor activity.
assertions.quote: These predictions are based on transcriptomic data and should be considered as putative and hypothesis-generating, rather than as functional hormones and receptors.
assertions.note: The atlas portal specifies that its predictions are hypothesis-generating transcriptome scores rather than validated functional hormones and receptors.

assertions.text: Mice deficient in keratinocyte glucocorticoid production develop spontaneous skin inflammation, demonstrating function in animals.
assertions.quote: Most notably, long-term Cyp11b1 deficiency in the skin alone resulted in the development of a spontaneous skin inflammation involving type 1 and 17 cytokines, accompanied by mononuclear phagocyte infiltration.
assertions.note: Ablation of Cyp11b1 specifically in mouse keratinocytes led to spontaneous cutaneous inflammation.

assertions.text: Sunlight exposure to human skin generates vitamin D3 which is transported into the circulation, representing established human in vivo physiology.
assertions.quote: The vitamin D-binding protein preferentially translocates the thermal product, vitamin D3, into the circulation.
assertions.note: Solar radiation forms previtamin D3 in human skin, which thermally isomerizes to vitamin D3 and is carried into the circulation.

units.text:
What changes in practice
A map to confirm, then a trial.
Topical and transdermal treatments act through receptors the skin already carries, and the skin's own enzymes change how strongly a hormone acts, so the skin's response need not mirror the dose. A receptor on a map is where an efficacy question starts. The same caution applies to physiology you think you know: the guide says serum vitamin D falls with sunscreen use, yet field trials of daily sunscreen did not lower it.
A receptor on the map is a hypothesis
Local enzymes change potency in skin
Daily-sunscreen field trials did not lower vitamin D
Narration: Two habits follow from the atlas. The first concerns product claims. Topical and transdermal treatments act through receptors the skin already carries, and the skin's own enzymes change how strongly a hormone acts once it arrives, so the response in skin can differ from what the d…
units.sourceNote: Aesthetic & Regenerative Endocrinology, ch. 6–7 pearls · Neale 2019 · Fei 2026 · Bikle 2014

assertions.text: Topical and transdermal treatments act through receptors in the skin, and local enzymes alter hormone potency such that the cutaneous response need not mirror the dose.
assertions.quote: Therapy: topical and transdermal routes exploit the skin's native receptors — retinoids (RAR), vitamin D analogs (VDR), estrogens (ER), glucocorticoids (GR) — but local steroid-metabolizing enzymes modify potency, so the cutaneous response need not mirror the systemic dose.
assertions.note: Supported by the clinical pearl in chapter 7 of the guide.

assertions.text: The guide's testing pearl states that serum vitamin D falls with sunscreen use.
assertions.quote: CLINICAL PEARLS — TESTING & THERAPY — Testing: serum 25-OH vitamin D partly reflects cutaneous synthesis, so it falls with low UVB exposure and sunscreen use regardless of oral intake.
assertions.note: Supported by the testing pearl in chapter 7.

assertions.text: Randomized controlled field trials of daily sunscreen application did not lower blood vitamin D concentrations.
assertions.quote: The randomized controlled field trials found no effect of daily sunscreen application, but the sunscreens used had moderate protection [sun protection factor SPF) ~16].
assertions.note: Supported by Neale et al.'s systematic review findings.

assertions.text: The sunscreens evaluated in field trials had moderate protection, and high-SPF sunscreens have not been trialled.
assertions.quote: However, there have been no trials of the high-SPF sunscreens that are now widely recommended.
assertions.note: Supported by the review's conclusion on trial limitations.

A serum page, line by line.
A fictional product page that leans on the cell atlas.

units.text:
Where the page overreaches
A fictional product page. Find the lines this lesson's evidence does not support.
Sound line: The Hormone Cell Atlas (Science, 2026) read the RNA for 379 hormone and receptor genes in about 14 million cells and nuclei, skin among them.
Explanation: Accurate. The atlas read RNA in about 14 million cells and nuclei from 47 human tissues, skin among them; it did not measure hormone release.
Flagged line (the learner flags it; the course's claim is only that the evidence does not support it): "It proves your skin responds to the hormone in this serum."
Explanation: The atlas predicts from RNA, and its own portal calls the scores 'putative and hypothesis-generating'. It does not show that a hormone acts in skin.
Sound line: Treatments applied to the skin act through receptors the skin already carries.
Explanation: Supported. Receptors explain how a topical could act…

assertions.text: The Hormone Cell Atlas analyzed RNA expression for 379 hormone and receptor genes across roughly 14 million cells and nuclei from human tissues, including skin.
assertions.quote: The Hormone Cell Atlas profiled 379 hormone and receptor genes across roughly 14 million single cells from 47 human tissues — skin among them — and scored each cell type's predicted hormone-producing and hormone-receiving strength.[1]
assertions.note: The pocket guide confirms the atlas profiled 379 hormone and receptor genes across roughly 14 million cells from 47 human tissues, including skin.

assertions.text: The cited evidence does not support the claim that the Hormone Cell Atlas proves skin responds functionally to the hormone in a serum.
assertions.quote: Important: these predictions are based on transcriptomic data and should be considered as putative and hypothesis-generating, rather than as functional hormones and receptors.
assertions.note: The atlas portal explicitly states that its predictions are transcriptomic, putative, and hypothesis-generating rather than representing functional receptors.

assertions.text: Topical and transdermal treatments act via native receptors already carried by the skin.
assertions.quote: Therapy: topical and transdermal routes exploit the skin's native receptors — retinoids (RAR), vitamin D analogs (VDR), estrogens (ER), glucocorticoids (GR) — but local steroid-metabolizing enzymes modify potency, so the cutaneous response need not mirror the systemic dose.
assertions.note: The text states that topical and transdermal treatments exploit native cutaneous receptors.

assertions.text: The cited evidence does not support the claim that the presence of cutaneous receptors guarantees visible results.
assertions.quote: Important: these predictions are based on transcriptomic data and should be considered as putative and hypothesis-generating, rather than as functional hormones and receptors.
assertions.note: The atlas notes that predictions from transcriptomic data are putative and require validation rather than demonstrating functional efficacy.

assertions.text: The cited evidence does not support the claim that the skin's response always matches the strength on a product label.
assertions.quote: Therapy: topical and transdermal routes exploit the skin's native receptors — retinoids (RAR), vitamin D analogs (VDR), estrogens (ER), glucocorticoids (GR) — but local steroid-metabolizing enzymes modify potency, so the cutaneous response need not mirror the systemic dose.
assertions.note: The source notes that local steroid-metabolizing enzymes modify potency such that the cutaneous response need not mirror the dose.

assertions.text: The cited evidence does not support skipping sunscreen so that skin can synthesize vitamin D.
assertions.quote: There is little evidence that sunscreen decreases 25(OH)D concentration when used in real-life settings, suggesting that concerns about vitamin D should not negate skin cancer prevention advice.
assertions.note: The systematic review finds little evidence that real-life sunscreen use decreases vitamin D and states concerns should not negate sun protection.

units.text:
A brochure for a hormone-containing serum cites a single-cell atlas showing that dermal fibroblasts carry the RNA for that hormone's receptor. What does that finding establish?
Explanation: A receptor on the map is where the question starts.
Distractor (deliberately false, not a claim): That the serum reaches those fibroblasts and improves the skin.
Explanation: That needs penetration data and a clinical trial; an RNA map provides neither.
Distractor (deliberately false, not a claim): That skin secretes the hormone and needs it replaced when levels fall.
Explanation: The finding concerns a receptor, and RNA says nothing about secretion or deficiency.
Correct answer: That fibroblasts may respond to the hormone: a hypothesis to confirm at the protein, function and clinical level.
Explanation: Correct. The atlas's authors call such predictions putative and hypothesis-generating.

assertions.text: Finding receptor RNA in a cell type establishes only that the cells may respond to the hormone, which is a hypothesis that must be confirmed at the protein and functional level.
assertions.quote: We conclude that transcript levels by themselves are not sufficient to predict protein levels in many scenarios and to thus explain genotype-phenotype relationships and that high-quality data quantifying different levels of gene expression are indispensable for the complete understanding of biological processes.
assertions.note: Transcript levels alone cannot reliably predict protein levels or functional phenotype, necessitating multi-level validation.

assertions.text: The Hormone Cell Atlas authors describe predictions of hormone-receiving cells based on transcriptomic data as putative and hypothesis-generating.
assertions.quote: Important: these predictions are based on transcriptomic data and should be considered as putative and hypothesis-generating, rather than as functional hormones and receptors.
assertions.note: The atlas portal explicitly instructs users to treat transcriptome-derived receptor predictions as putative and hypothesis-generating.

units.text:
Lesson 1.3 · Concept
Cells that stop dividing and keep talking.
A senescent cell has stopped dividing for good but stays metabolically active, releasing cytokines, matrix-degrading enzymes and growth factors: the senescence-associated secretory phenotype, or SASP. The SASP was characterised in cultured cells. In human skin, cells carrying the senescence marker p16INK4a become more common with age in both epidermis and dermis.
Senescent: permanent arrest, still secreting
SASP (IL-6, IL-8, MMPs, growth factors): defined in culture
Human skin: p16-positive cells rise with age
Narration: Senescence begins as a safety mechanism. A cell that has taken enough damage stops dividing for good, which helps guard against cancer and is useful during wound repair. The problem is what the cell does next. It stays alive and metabolically busy and releases a mixture of inflammatory cytokines such as inte…
units.sourceNote: Coppé 2008 · Ressler 2006 · Ho & Dreesen 2021 · Wang & Dreesen 2018 · Haykal 2026 · Aesthetic & Regenerative Endocrinology, ch. 7

assertions.text: A senescent cell permanently stops dividing but remains metabolically active, secreting cytokines, matrix-degrading enzymes, and growth factors (the senescence-associated secretory phenotype, or SASP).
assertions.quote: With chronological time and cumulative UV exposure, dermal fibroblasts, keratinocytes, and endothelial cells accumulate as senescent cells — growth-arrested but metabolically active, broadcasting a senescence-associated secretory phenotype (SASP) of cytokines, matrix metalloproteinases, and growth factors.[5]
assertions.note: Aesthetic & Regenerative Endocrinology states that senescent skin cells are growth-arrested but metabolically active, secreting a SASP of cytokines, MMPs, and growth factors.

assertions.text: Senescence acts as a protective mechanism that helps guard against cancer and assists in wound repair.
assertions.quote: Initially evolved as a protective mechanism to prevent malignant transformation and facilitate wound repair, senescence becomes maladaptive when senescent cells persist.
assertions.note: Haykal et al. confirm that senescence evolved as a protective mechanism to prevent malignant transformation and facilitate wound repair.

assertions.text: The SASP profile was characterized in cultured human cells following genotoxic stress or DNA damage.
assertions.quote: We show that human cells induced to senesce by genotoxic stress secrete myriad factors associated with inflammation and malignancy. This senescence-associated secretory phenotype (SASP) developed slowly over several days and only after DNA damage of sufficient magnitude to induce senescence.
assertions.note: Coppé et al. report defining the SASP in cultured human cells following genotoxic stress and DNA damage.

assertions.text: In human skin, cells carrying the senescence marker p16INK4a become more frequent with age in both the epidermis and the dermis.
assertions.quote: We show that the number of p16INK4A positive cells is significantly higher in elderly individuals compared to the younger age groups. The number of p16INK4A positive cells was found to be increased in both epidermis and dermis, compartments with strictly different proliferative activities.
assertions.note: Ressler et al. found that p16INK4a-positive cells increase significantly with age in both epidermal and dermal compartments.

assertions.text: Fibroblasts, keratinocytes, and melanocytes in skin can all become senescent.
assertions.quote: Senescent keratinocytes, fibroblasts, and melanocytes can secrete pro-inflammatory mediators and other factors, collectively termed the senescence-associated secretory phenotype (SASP), which may degrade extracellular matrix components, disrupt pigmentary balance, and impair barrier function.
assertions.note: Haykal et al. describe senescent keratinocytes, fibroblasts, and melanocytes in skin.

assertions.text: No single universal biomarker unequivocally identifies senescent cells.
assertions.quote: However, a significant hurdle in the aging field has been the identification of a universal biomarker that facilitates the unequivocal detection and quantification of senescent cell types in vitro and in vivo .
assertions.note: Wang and Dreesen note that identifying a universal biomarker for unequivocal detection of senescent cells remains a major hurdle.

units.text:
Practice
Stopped for good, still secreting.
A senescent cell beside one that still divides.
units.sourceNote: Coppé 2008 · Ho & Dreesen 2021 · Wang & Dreesen 2018 · Aesthetic & Regenerative Endocrinology, ch. 7

assertions.text: Senescent cells undergo permanent growth arrest while continuing to secrete active factors.
assertions.quote: Senescent cells are characterized by their inability to proliferate, resistance to apoptosis, and secretion of factors that promote inflammation and tissue deterioration ( Campisi and d’Adda di Fagagna, 2007 ; Kuilman et al., 2010 ; He and Sharpless, 2017 ).
assertions.note: The source confirms that senescent cells permanently lose the ability to proliferate while secreting inflammatory and tissue-modifying factors.

units.text:
Dividing, senescent, secreting
Find the cell that still divides, the senescent cell and the SASP it releases.
A dividing cell
A senescent cell
The SASP

Human evidence
Three years of perceived age.
In a Dutch cohort, people with more p16-positive cells in sun-protected arm skin had more ageing-type elastic fibres, more facial wrinkles and looked older, after allowing for their actual age. The epidermal p16-positive cells were mostly melanocytes. The study was publicly funded; one co-author worked for Unilever.
3 years
younger-looking: fewest versus most p16-positive epidermal cells, at the same chronological age
Waaijer et al., 2016 — 178 adults aged 45–81, Leiden Longevity Study, sun-protected arm biopsies
What it means: Senescent-cell burden in human skin tracks visible ageing, even in skin that sees little sun.
What it does not mean: It does not show that senescent cells cause wrinkles, or that removing them would reverse any. One observational cohort shows an association.
units.sourceNote: Waaijer 2016 (Leiden Longevity Study) · Ressler 2006

assertions.text: In a Dutch cohort, people with more p16-positive cells in sun-protected arm skin had more ageing-type elastic fibres.
assertions.quote: The numbers of epidermal and dermal p16INK4a positive cells were significantly associated with age-associated elastic fiber morphologic characteristics, such as longer and a greater number of elastic fibers.
assertions.note: Higher numbers of p16-positive cells were significantly associated with age-associated elastic fiber morphology.

assertions.text: People with more p16-positive cells in sun-protected arm skin had more facial wrinkles and looked older after adjusting for actual age.
assertions.quote: The p16INK4a positive epidermal cells (identified as primarily melanocytes) were also significantly associated with more facial wrinkles and a higher perceived age.
assertions.note: Epidermal p16-positive cells were significantly associated with more facial wrinkles and higher perceived age.

assertions.text: The epidermal p16-positive cells were mostly melanocytes.
assertions.quote: The p16INK4a positive epidermal cells (identified as primarily melanocytes) were also significantly associated with more facial wrinkles and a higher perceived age.
assertions.note: The abstract explicitly notes the p16-positive epidermal cells were identified primarily as melanocytes.

assertions.text: The study was publicly funded; one co-author worked for Unilever.
assertions.note: The provided abstract does not contain funding information or author affiliations.

assertions.text: Participants with the fewest p16-positive epidermal cells looked 3 years younger than those with the most, at the same chronological age.
assertions.quote: Participants in the lowest tertile of epidermal p16INK4a counts looked 3 years younger than those in the highest tertile, independently of chronological age and elastic fiber morphology.
assertions.note: Participants in the lowest tertile of p16 counts looked 3 years younger than those in the highest tertile independently of chronological age.

assertions.text: Waaijer et al. analyzed sun-protected arm biopsies from 178 adults aged 45–81 from the Leiden Longevity Study.
assertions.quote: We counted cells positive for the tumor suppressor and senescence associated protein p16INK4a in sun-protected upper-inner arm skin biopsies from 178 participants (aged 45-81 years) of the Leiden Longevity Study.
assertions.note: The study included sun-protected arm skin biopsies from 178 participants aged 45 to 81 years in the Leiden Longevity Study.

units.text:
Four registers
Human, mouse or dish?
Senescence research mixes human tissue, mice and cultured cells. For the ageing dermis the four answers point in different directions, which is why they belong in separate sentences.
Mechanism
A collagen-fragmentation loop
Skin collagen falls with age. Aged human dermis shows more fibroblast MMP-1 and fragmented collagen; in culture, fragmentation raises MMP-1 further. That senescent cells drive this in living skin is plausible, not shown.
Human evidence
Association
p16-positive cells rise with age and track with wrinkles and perceived age
Animal evidence
Causation, in mice
Clearing p16-positive cells, or giving senolytic drugs, extends healthy lifespan in mice. Skin was checked only for safety, and clearing these cells during healing slowed wound closure.
Open question
Do senotherapies change human skin?
Small pilots measuring tissue markers. One exp…
units.sourceNote: Shuster 1975 · Varani 2006 · Fisher 2009 · Waaijer 2016 · Baker 2016 · Xu 2018 · Hickson 2019 · Chung 2019

assertions.text: Skin collagen falls with age.
assertions.quote: Skin collagen decreased with age and was less in the females at all ages.
assertions.note: Shuster et al. found that skin collagen decreased with advancing age.

assertions.text: Aged human dermis shows more fibroblast MMP-1 and fragmented collagen.
assertions.quote: We report here that dermal fibroblasts express increased levels of collagen-degrading matrix metalloproteinases-1 (MMP-1) in aged (>80 years old) compared with young (21 to 30 years old) human skin in vivo.
assertions.note: Fisher et al. showed increased MMP-1 and fragmented collagen fibrils in aged human skin.

assertions.text: In culture, collagen fragmentation raises fibroblast MMP-1 further.
assertions.quote: Furthermore, fibroblasts cultured in fragmented collagen lattices express elevated levels of MMP-1, AP-1, and alpha2beta1 integrin.
assertions.note: Culturing fibroblasts in fragmented collagen lattices elevated MMP-1 expression.

assertions.text: p16-positive cells rise with age and track with wrinkles and perceived age.
assertions.quote: The p16INK4a positive epidermal cells (identified as primarily melanocytes) were also significantly associated with more facial wrinkles and a higher perceived age.
assertions.note: Waaijer et al. demonstrated that p16-positive cells correlate with facial wrinkling and perceived facial age.

assertions.text: Clearing p16-positive cells, or giving senolytic drugs, extends healthy lifespan in mice.
assertions.quote: Here we show that compared to vehicle alone, AP20187 treatment extended median lifespan in both male and female mice of two distinct genetic backgrounds.
assertions.note: Baker et al. demonstrated that clearing p16-positive cells with AP20187 extends median lifespan in mice.

assertions.text: Clearing p16-positive cells during healing slowed wound closure in mice.
assertions.quote: When AP was administered during wound closure, healing was delayed with similar kinetics as 4- or 18-month-old ATTAC mice without prior AP treatment, indicating that acute senescence mechanisms are preserved with aging and not influenced by constitutive clearance of senescent cells 3 .
assertions.note: Administering AP to clear p16-positive cells during wound repair delayed wound closure.

assertions.text: An exploratory randomized trial of topical rapamycin (36 enrolled, 19 dropped out) lowered skin p16.
assertions.quote: Thirty-six participants were enrolled in the study, and nineteen discontinued or were lost to follow-up. A significant (P = 0.008) reduction in p16INK4A protein levels and an increase in collagen VII protein levels (P = 0.0077) were observed among participants at the end of the study.
assertions.note: Chung et al. enrolled 36 participants with 19 discontinuing and reported a significant reduction in p16INK4A.

assertions.text: No adequately sized trial with clinical skin-ageing outcomes was found as of 2026.
assertions.quote: Senolytic and senomorphic strategies to clear or quiet them (Ch. 17) are an active dermatologic frontier, though skin-specific human evidence is still early.
assertions.note: The clinical guide notes that skin-specific human evidence for senotherapeutics remains early.

units.text:
Where the evidence is strongest
The levers with trials behind them.
Two ways of protecting or rebuilding the dermal matrix have randomized human trials. In a community trial of 903 adults, daily sunscreen for four and a half years slowed photoageing compared with discretionary use (GRADE B). Topical tretinoin improves photoageing consistently across randomized trials, and the Aesthetic & Regenerative Endocrinology guide rates topical retinoids first-line, GRADE A. Retinol improved fine wrinkles in very old skin in a small trial (C), and within a week it raised collagen synthesis and lowered MMPs in biopsies of aged human skin.
Daily sunscreen: one large RCT (B)
Topical retinoids for photoageing: GRADE A
Senolytics for skin: no clinical-outcome trials yet
Narration: Set the senescence story beside the interventions that have been tested in people. In Nambour, Australia, a publicly funded …
units.sourceNote: Hughes 2013 · Sitohang 2022 · Kafi 2007 · Varani 2000 · Fisher 2002 · Aesthetic & Regenerative Endocrinology, ch. 5

assertions.text: In a randomized community trial of 903 adults in Nambour, Australia, daily sunscreen use over 4.5 years resulted in 24% less skin aging compared with discretionary use.
assertions.quote: Skin aging from baseline to the end of the trial was 24% less in the daily sunscreen group than in the discretionary sunscreen group (relative odds, 0.76 [95% CI, 0.59 to 0.98]).
assertions.note: Hughes et al. reported that skin aging was 24% less in the daily sunscreen group compared with discretionary use over 4.5 years.

assertions.text: Topical tretinoin improves clinical photoaging consistently across randomized controlled trials.
assertions.quote: With regard to efficacy, all studies consistently reported that topical tretinoin was efficacious in improving clinical appearance of photoaging in terms of wrinkling, mottled hyperpigmentation, sallowness, and lentigines as early as 1 month and lasted after 24 months.
assertions.note: A systematic review of RCTs found that all included studies consistently reported tretinoin was efficacious in improving signs of photoaging.

assertions.text: The Aesthetic & Regenerative Endocrinology pocket guide rates topical retinoids first-line for photoaging with GRADE A evidence.
assertions.quote: Among topical agents, retinoids have the strongest dermatologic evidence for reversing measurable signs of photoaging and remain first-line GRADE A.
assertions.note: The guide rates retinoids as first-line GRADE A for reversing measurable signs of photoaging.

assertions.text: Topical retinol improved fine wrinkles and increased procollagen I in a trial of elderly nursing-home residents (mean age 87).
assertions.quote: After 24 weeks, an intent-to-treat analysis using the last-observation-carried-forward method revealed that there were significant differences between retinol-treated and vehicle-treated skin for changes in fine wrinkling scores (-1.64 [95% CI, -2.06 to -1.22] vs -0.08 [95% CI, -0.17 to 0.01]; P<.001).
assertions.note: Kafi et al. observed significant fine wrinkle improvement and increased procollagen I immunostaining in elderly residents treated with retinol.

assertions.text: Topical application of retinol for 7 days increased collagen synthesis and lowered matrix metalloproteinases in aged human skin biopsies.
assertions.quote: In a separate group of 53 individuals (80+ y of age), topical application of 1% vitamin A for 7 d increased fibroblast growth and collagen synthesis, and concomitantly reduced the levels of matrix-degrading matrix metalloproteinases.
assertions.note: Varani et al. showed 7 days of topical vitamin A increased collagen synthesis and reduced MMPs in skin biopsies of adults aged 80+.

assertions.text: There are no clinical-outcome trials of senolytics for skin aging yet.
assertions.quote: Senolytic and senomorphic strategies to clear or quiet them (Ch. 17) are an active dermatologic frontier, though skin-specific human evidence is still early.
assertions.note: The guide indicates that human clinical outcome evidence for senolytics in skin aging is still lacking.

assertions.text: The finding that daily sunscreen for four and a half years slowed photoageing is supported by randomized controlled trials with clinical skin outcomes.
assertions.quote: The daily sunscreen group showed no detectable increase in skin aging after 4.5 years. Skin aging from baseline to the end of the trial was 24% less in the daily sunscreen group than in the discretionary sunscreen group (relative odds, 0.76 [95% CI, 0.59 to 0.98]).
assertions.note: A randomized trial confirmed that regular sunscreen use for 4.5 years retarded skin aging measured by microtopography.

assertions.text: The finding that topical tretinoin improves photoageing is supported by randomized controlled trials with clinical skin outcomes.
assertions.quote: With regard to efficacy, all studies consistently reported that topical tretinoin was efficacious in improving clinical appearance of photoaging in terms of wrinkling, mottled hyperpigmentation, sallowness, and lentigines as early as 1 month and lasted after 24 months.
assertions.note: A systematic review of randomized controlled trials demonstrated that topical tretinoin consistently improves clinical signs of photoaging.

assertions.text: The finding that more p16-positive cells in arm skin correlate with more facial wrinkles and an older look belongs to the category of human association or biomarker pilots.
assertions.quote: The p16INK4a positive epidermal cells (identified as primarily melanocytes) were also significantly associated with more facial wrinkles and a higher perceived age.
assertions.note: In a human cohort study, p16-positive epidermal cells in sun-protected arm biopsies were significantly associated with facial wrinkles and perceived age.

assertions.text: The finding that topical rapamycin lowered p16 in human skin belongs to the category of human association or biomarker pilots.
assertions.quote: A significant (P = 0.008) reduction in p16INK4A protein levels and an increase in collagen VII protein levels (P = 0.0077) were observed among participants at the end of the study.
assertions.note: An exploratory human interventional trial evaluated topical rapamycin and demonstrated a significant reduction in cutaneous p16 protein expression.

assertions.text: The finding that clearing p16-positive cells or giving senolytic drugs extends healthy lifespan is demonstrated in mice or cultured cells only.
assertions.quote: Senolytics (dasatinib plus quercetin; fisetin) clear senescent cells and extend healthspan in mice; first-in-human pilots in pulmonary fibrosis and diabetic kidney disease show feasibility and reduced senescent-cell burden but are small, surrogate-only, and not outcome-powered, so any human healthspan claim remains GRADE C.
assertions.note: Lifespan and healthspan extension through senescent cell clearance or senolytics has been shown in mice, whereas human studies remain small surrogate pilots without outcome proof.

assertions.text: The finding that senescent cells release IL-6, IL-8, matrix-degrading enzymes, and growth factors is categorized under mice or cultured cells only.
assertions.quote: SASP components included inflammatory and immune-modulatory cytokines and chemokines (e.g., IL-6, −7, and −8, MCP-2, and MIP-3a). They also included growth factors (e.g., GRO, HGF, and IGFBPs), shed cell surface molecules (e.g., ICAMs, uPAR, and TNF receptors), and survival factors ( Figure 1 A and Table S2 ).
assertions.note: The SASP profile consisting of cytokines like IL-6 and IL-8 and growth factors was characterized in cultured senescent cells.

units.text:
What stands behind it?
Sort each finding by the strongest evidence behind it.
Sorting item (the learner sorts this statement; the course's claim is only the category): "Daily sunscreen for four and a half years slowed photoageing" → Randomized trials with clinical skin outcomes
Explanation: GRADE B. A community trial randomized 903 adults to daily or discretionary sunscreen, and skin ageing was about a quarter lower with daily use.
Sorting item (the learner sorts this statement; the course's claim is only the category): "Topical tretinoin improves photoageing" → Randomized trials with clinical skin outcomes
Explanation: Randomized trials of tretinoin in photoaged skin agree with one another, and the guide rates topical retinoids first-line, GRADE A.

assertions.text: The strongest evidence that daily sunscreen slows photoageing comes from randomized controlled trials with clinical skin outcomes, including a trial randomizing 903 adults where daily use resulted in approximately 24% less skin ageing over 4.5 years.
assertions.quote: The daily sunscreen group showed no detectable increase in skin aging after 4.5 years. Skin aging from baseline to the end of the trial was 24% less in the daily sunscreen group than in the discretionary sunscreen group (relative odds, 0.76 [95% CI, 0.59 to 0.98]).
assertions.note: A community-based trial of 903 adults showed 24% less skin aging over 4.5 years with daily sunscreen compared to discretionary use.

assertions.text: The strongest evidence that topical tretinoin improves photoageing comes from randomized trials with clinical skin outcomes, and clinical reference guidance rates topical retinoids first-line with GRADE A evidence.
assertions.quote: Among topical agents, retinoids have the strongest dermatologic evidence for reversing measurable signs of photoaging and remain first-line GRADE A.
assertions.note: The clinical pocket guide states retinoids have the strongest evidence for photoaging and remain first-line GRADE A.

assertions.text: The finding that increased p16-positive cells in arm skin correlate with increased facial wrinkles and an older perceived age is based on a human observational cohort of 178 adults.
assertions.quote: We counted cells positive for the tumor suppressor and senescence associated protein p16INK4a in sun-protected upper-inner arm skin biopsies from 178 participants (aged 45-81 years) of the Leiden Longevity Study.
assertions.note: The study assessed p16-positive cells in upper-inner arm skin biopsies from 178 participants and found an association with facial wrinkling and perceived age.

assertions.text: Evidence that topical rapamycin lowers p16 in human skin comes from an exploratory randomized trial measuring tissue biomarkers, where 36 participants enrolled and 19 dropped out.
assertions.quote: Thirty-six participants were enrolled in the study, and nineteen discontinued or were lost to follow-up. A significant (P = 0.008) reduction in p16INK4A protein levels and an increase in collagen VII protein levels (P = 0.0077) were observed among participants at the end of the study.
assertions.note: The exploratory randomized trial enrolled 36 participants, observed 19 discontinuations or losses to follow-up, and showed reduced p16 protein expression.

assertions.text: Evidence that clearing p16-positive cells or administering senolytics extends healthy lifespan comes from mouse models, where clearing p16-positive cells during healing slowed wound closure.
assertions.quote: AP administration during the wound healing process significantly attenuates the rate of wound closure independently of whether senescent cell removal had occurred prior to wounding.
assertions.note: Mouse experiments showed senescent cell clearance extended lifespan, but administering clearance treatment during wound repair attenuated the rate of wound closure.

assertions.text: The finding that senescent cells secrete IL-6, IL-8, matrix metalloproteinases, and growth factors was characterized in cultured human cells following DNA damage.
assertions.quote: We show that human cells induced to senesce by genotoxic stress secrete myriad factors associated with inflammation and malignancy. This senescence-associated secretory phenotype (SASP) developed slowly over several days and only after DNA damage of sufficient magnitude to induce senescence.
assertions.note: The SASP profile was characterized in cultured human cells induced to senesce following genotoxic stress.

units.text:
Fictional case
'Can a senolytic fix my skin?'
A 58-year-old patient has read that senolytic supplements 'clear zombie cells' and reverse skin ageing, and asks whether to start one she found online. She does not use sunscreen daily. The case is fictional and built from the lesson's evidence; decide your first move.
Senescent cells in human skin: real, and linked with visible ageing
Clearing them: mouse evidence and small human biomarker pilots
Sunscreen and retinoids: randomized human trials
Narration: Consider a fifty-eight-year-old patient, fictional and built from this lesson's evidence. She has read that senolytic supplements clear so-called zombie cells and reverse skin ageing, and she asks whether to start one she found online. She does not wear sunscreen every day. Three facts frame the conversation. Senescent cells really do accumulate in human skin, and their number tracks with w…
units.sourceNote: Fictional case · Waaijer 2016 · Baker 2016 · Hickson 2019 · Hughes 2013 · Sitohang 2022 · Aesthetic & Regenerative Endocrinology, ch. 17

assertions.text: Senescent cells accumulate in human skin, and their number tracks with wrinkles and perceived facial age.
assertions.quote: The p16INK4a positive epidermal cells (identified as primarily melanocytes) were also significantly associated with more facial wrinkles and a higher perceived age.
assertions.note: Waaijer et al. demonstrated that p16INK4a-positive epidermal cells in human skin significantly associate with facial wrinkling and higher perceived age.

assertions.text: Evidence that clearing senescent cells helps comes from mice, whereas human studies are small pilots measuring surrogate tissue markers.
assertions.quote: Senolytics (dasatinib plus quercetin; fisetin) clear senescent cells and extend healthspan in mice;[1] first-in-human pilots in pulmonary fibrosis and diabetic kidney disease show feasibility and reduced senescent-cell burden but are small, surrogate-only, and not outcome-powered, so any human healthspan claim remains GRADE C.[2,3]
assertions.note: The guide notes senolytic clearance extends healthspan in mice, but human trials remain small biomarker pilots.

assertions.text: Daily sunscreen has randomized controlled trial evidence demonstrating visible reductions in skin aging.
assertions.quote: Skin aging from baseline to the end of the trial was 24% less in the daily sunscreen group than in the discretionary sunscreen group (relative odds, 0.76 [95% CI, 0.59 to 0.98]).
assertions.note: A randomized trial confirmed daily sunscreen significantly reduced skin aging compared with discretionary use.

assertions.text: Topical retinoids have randomized controlled trials demonstrating visible improvements in photoaged skin.
assertions.quote: With regard to efficacy, all studies consistently reported that topical tretinoin was efficacious in improving clinical appearance of photoaging in terms of wrinkling, mottled hyperpigmentation, sallowness, and lentigines as early as 1 month and lasted after 24 months.
assertions.note: A systematic review of randomized trials showed topical tretinoin consistently improved visible signs of photoaging.

assertions.text: The Aesthetic and Regenerative Endocrinology guide advises keeping senolytics within clinical trials.
assertions.quote: PEARL 10 — Senolytics belong in trials. The preclinical story is compelling; human outcome evidence is not yet there. Intermittent dasatinib + quercetin and similar regimens should generally stay within registered studies.
assertions.note: The clinical pocket guide states that senolytic regimens should generally stay within clinical trials.

Distractor (deliberately false, not a claim): Support a trial of the supplement: senescent cells clearly age skin, so clearing them should help.
Explanation: The human evidence is an association and the clearing evidence is in mice. No trial has tested senolytics on skin-ageing outcomes.
Correct answer: Explain what is known in people and what only in mice, point her to the measures with trials (daily sunscreen, and a topical retinoid discussed with a prescriber), and mention that senolytics are being studied in trials.
Explanation: Right. It keeps the registers apart and moves her toward the levers with human outcome data. The guide advises that senolytics generally be confined to clinical trials.
Distractor (deliberately false, not a claim): Tell her senescence is a mouse phenomenon with no relevance to human skin.

assertions.text: Evidence for the clearance of senescent cells delaying age-related deterioration comes from mouse studies.
assertions.quote: Clearance of p16 Ink4a -positive cells delayed tumorigenesis and attenuated age-related deterioration of several organs without apparent side effects, including kidney, heart and fat, where clearance preserved the functionality of glomeruli, cardio-protective K ATP channels, and adipocytes, respectively.
assertions.note: A mouse study confirms that clearing p16-positive senescent cells attenuated age-related deterioration across multiple organs.

assertions.text: No clinical trial has tested senolytics on skin-aging outcomes.
assertions.quote: senolytics remain investigational with no human outcome data (D).
assertions.note: The guide notes that senolytics remain investigational with no human outcome data.

assertions.text: Daily sunscreen use has randomized controlled trial evidence demonstrating that it slows skin aging.
assertions.quote: Skin aging from baseline to the end of the trial was 24% less in the daily sunscreen group than in the discretionary sunscreen group (relative odds, 0.76 [95% CI, 0.59 to 0.98]).
assertions.note: A randomized trial showed that daily sunscreen significantly reduced skin aging compared with discretionary use.

assertions.text: Topical retinoids have randomized trial evidence for improving signs of photoaging.
assertions.quote: With regard to efficacy, all studies consistently reported that topical tretinoin was efficacious in improving clinical appearance of photoaging in terms of wrinkling, mottled hyperpigmentation, sallowness, and lentigines as early as 1 month and lasted after 24 months.
assertions.note: A systematic review of randomized controlled trials confirmed that topical tretinoin consistently improved clinical signs of photoaging.

assertions.text: The guide advises that senolytics generally be confined to clinical trials.
assertions.quote: Senolytics in particular should generally be confined to clinical trials.
assertions.note: The pocket guide explicitly recommends confining senolytics to clinical trials.

assertions.text: Senescent cells are measurable in human skin and track with wrinkles and perceived age.
assertions.quote: The p16INK4a positive epidermal cells (identified as primarily melanocytes) were also significantly associated with more facial wrinkles and a higher perceived age.
assertions.note: Biopsy analysis in humans showed epidermal senescent cell markers were significantly associated with facial wrinkles and perceived age.

units.text:
Which statement about senescence and skin ageing matches the evidence?
Explanation: Name the species before you weigh the finding.
Distractor (deliberately false, not a claim): Randomized trials show that senolytics reverse human skin ageing.
Explanation: No randomized trial of a senolytic with clinical skin-ageing outcomes was found. Human data are small pilots measuring tissue markers.
Distractor (deliberately false, not a claim): Senescence has been seen only in mice and cultured cells.
Explanation: p16-positive cells are measurable in human skin and become more common with age.
Correct answer: In human skin, senescent cells increase with age and track with wrinkles; the evidence that clearing them improves ageing comes from mice.
Explanation: Correct. Human association, mouse causation: two registers, kept apart.

assertions.text: p16-positive cells are measurable in human skin and become more common with age.
assertions.quote: We show that the number of p16INK4A positive cells is significantly higher in elderly individuals compared to the younger age groups.
assertions.note: Ressler et al. confirmed that p16INK4A-positive cells were significantly higher in elderly individuals compared to younger groups.

assertions.text: In human skin, senescent cells track with wrinkles.
assertions.quote: The p16INK4a positive epidermal cells (identified as primarily melanocytes) were also significantly associated with more facial wrinkles and a higher perceived age.
assertions.note: Epidermal p16INK4a-positive cell counts were significantly associated with facial wrinkling in human participants.

assertions.text: The evidence that clearing senescent cells improves ageing comes from mice.
assertions.quote: Clearance of p16 Ink4a -positive cells delayed tumorigenesis and attenuated age-related deterioration of several organs without apparent side effects, including kidney, heart and fat, where clearance preserved the functionality of glomeruli, cardio-protective K ATP channels, and adipocytes, respectively.
assertions.note: Genetic clearance of senescent cells in mice was shown to delay organ deterioration and improve healthspan.

assertions.text: Human data on senolytics come from small pilot studies measuring tissue markers.
assertions.quote: Here, in an open-label Phase 1 pilot study, we show for the first time that senolytic drugs decrease senescent cell abundance in humans.
assertions.note: Initial human trials of senolytics are phase 1 pilot studies assessing changes in senescent cell burden in human tissues.

units.text:
Mechanism
The skin regenerates its own cortisol.
Skin expresses the machinery of a local stress axis, including CRH and POMC with its product ACTH. Keratinocytes and dermal fibroblasts also carry 11β-HSD1, the enzyme that turns inactive cortisone back into active cortisol inside the cell. In human skin samples its activity is higher with age and in sun-exposed skin, and local cortisol availability is set independently of blood levels. Cortisol slows collagen production in dermal fibroblasts, and mice lacking the enzyme kept their dermal thickness with age.
Local axis: CRH, POMC and ACTH are made in skin
11β-HSD1 regenerates cortisol inside skin cells
Mechanism register: human samples, cultured cells and mice
Narration: Picture the skin as a small endocrine organ with its own stress axis. Skin cells make CRH and ACTH, the same signals that drive the adrenal glands, and they carry the rece…
units.sourceNote: Slominski & Wortsman 2000 · Tiganescu 2011, 2013 · Aesthetic & Regenerative Endocrinology, ch. 8

assertions.text: Skin expresses the machinery of a local stress axis, including CRH and POMC with its product ACTH.
assertions.quote: In fact, all of the elements controlling the activity of the hypothalamus-pituitary-adrenal axis are expressed in the skin including CRH, urocortin, and POMC, with its products ACTH, alpha-MSH, and beta-endorphin.
assertions.note: The source confirms that elements of the HPA axis, including CRH and POMC with its product ACTH, are expressed in the skin.

assertions.text: Keratinocytes and dermal fibroblasts carry 11β-HSD1, which regenerates active cortisol from inactive cortisone inside the cell.
assertions.quote: 11β-HSD1 (which activates cortisol), but not 11β-HSD2 (which inactivates cortisol), was expressed in epidermal keratinocytes and dermal fibroblasts in human skin and also in outer hair follicle root sheath cells in murine skin.
assertions.note: The source confirms expression of 11β-HSD1, which activates cortisol, in epidermal keratinocytes and dermal fibroblasts.

assertions.text: In human skin samples, 11β-HSD1 activity is elevated with age and in sun-exposed skin.
assertions.quote: 11β-HSD1 activity was elevated in aged human and mouse skin and in PE compared with donor-matched photo-protected human biopsies.
assertions.note: The study confirms 11β-HSD1 activity was elevated in aged human skin and in photoexposed biopsies compared with photoprotected biopsies.

assertions.text: Local cortisol availability in skin is regulated independently of systemic blood levels.
assertions.quote: Within target tissues, GC availability is regulated at a prereceptor level, independently of systemic levels, by isozymes of 11β-hydroxysteroid dehydrogenase (11β-HSD) that interconvert active cortisol and inactive cortisone.
assertions.note: The source reports that glucocorticoid availability in target tissues is regulated independently of systemic levels by 11β-HSD.

assertions.text: Cortisol slows collagen production in dermal fibroblasts.
assertions.quote: We found that treatment of HDFs with physiological concentrations of cortisol inhibited rate-limiting steps in collagen biosynthesis and processing.
assertions.note: The study found that physiological concentrations of cortisol inhibited rate-limiting steps in collagen biosynthesis and processing in human dermal fibroblasts.

assertions.text: Mice lacking 11β-HSD1 maintain dermal thickness as they age.
assertions.quote: Age-induced dermal atrophy with deranged collagen structural organization was prevented in 11β-HSD1 KO mice, which also exhibited increased collagen density.
assertions.note: The study reports that age-induced dermal atrophy was prevented in 11β-HSD1 knockout mice.

units.text:
Four registers
11β-HSD1: four separate answers.
Local cortisol regeneration is a real and interesting mechanism. Each register below answers a different question, and blending them produces the line you will hear online: that blocking cortisol in the skin reverses ageing.
Mechanism
Plausible
Enzyme activity rises with age and sun exposure in human skin samples; knockout mice resist age-related dermal thinning
Human evidence
One pilot RCT · GRADE C
28 adults with type 2 diabetes took an oral inhibitor: the primary outcome was missed, wounds closed faster in an exploratory analysis, and barrier function was modestly worse
Regulatory status (US, 24 September 2026)
Investigational only
The inhibitor tested in human skin is a research compound with no FDA approval

Does it drive visible ageing?

units.text:
The evidence
Rare, and usually from a prescription.
Endogenous Cushing's syndrome is uncommon: European population studies put it at two to three new cases per million people a year. The commonest cause of Cushing's syndrome is iatrogenic, from glucocorticoids given as medicine. The Endocrine Society therefore asks for a drug history first, covering tablets, inhalers, injections and creams, including skin-bleaching products, and recommends testing when features are multiple and progressive.
2–3
new cases of endogenous Cushing's syndrome per million people per year (European population studies)
As cited in the Endocrine Society diagnostic guideline, 2008
What it means: A round, puffy face in an aesthetic clinic is almost always something other than Cushing's syndrome, and when cortisol excess is real it most often comes from a glucocorticoid the patient is already using.

units.text:
What changes in practice
Reassure the many, refer the few.
When a patient asks about 'cortisol face', start with the drug history: steroid creams, skin-lighteners, herbal tonics and injections. Then look for the discriminating features. Without them, the Aesthetic & Regenerative Endocrinology guide reads most puffiness as sleep, alcohol, salt and fluid, and the Endocrine Society recommends against widespread testing. With them, especially when they are progressing, the next step is formal testing and an endocrinologist. A cortisol supplement or a consumer cortisol panel answers the wrong question.
Drug history first, including creams and injections
Look for bruising, plethora, proximal weakness, wide purple striae
Refer for testing; skip supplements and consumer panels

units.text:
Lesson 2.2 · Concept
Estrogen and the dermis.
Skin carries estrogen receptors (ERα, ERβ and the membrane receptor GPER) in both sun-protected and sun-damaged sites. In postmenopausal women, two weeks of topical estradiol raised collagen production in sun-protected hip skin; photoaged facial skin showed no such response. After menopause, small biopsy studies found skin collagen and thickness falling year by year, following years since menopause more closely than age. That is mechanism and natural history. What hormone therapy does to a face is a separate question.
Receptors: ERα, ERβ and GPER in aged and photoaged skin
Topical estradiol raises collagen in sun-protected skin only
Collagen loss follows years since menopause
Narration: Estrogen is the hormone the guide says dominates the visible ageing of women's skin, so start with what it does in the dermis. Skin carries estrogen receptors…

units.text:
The evidence
One to two per cent a year.
In small biopsy studies of postmenopausal women, skin collagen content and skin thickness fell by about 1–2% a year, in step with bone mass, and followed years since menopause more than age. Reviews, and the Aesthetic & Regenerative Endocrinology guide, quote a steeper early loss of up to 30% in the first five years. That figure traces to the same small studies, and a check of their abstracts in September 2026 did not find it stated.
fall in skin collagen content and thickness per year after menopause (small biopsy studies)
Brincat et al., 1987 — in parallel with bone mass
What it means: Estrogen withdrawal is a measurable contributor to dermal thinning, and it follows the menopause clock rather than age alone.
What it does not mean: It does not show that hormone therapy restores a younger-looking face. These are small observational studies, mostl…

units.text:
Human evidence
Biopsy gains, mirror results.
Hormone therapy has two kinds of trial behind it. Small trials measure the dermis; larger trials measure the face. They point in different directions, so read them separately. The Aesthetic & Regenerative Endocrinology guide grades the skin benefit B; the North American Menopause Society rates the same evidence 'limited or inconsistent'. This course grades the structural gains C and teaches the negative wrinkle trials alongside them.

assertions.quote: Surprisingly, no significant changes in production were observed in women or men after 2-week estradiol treatment of photoaged forearm or face skin, despite similar expression of estrogen receptors (ER-alpha, ER-beta, and GPR30) in aged and photoaged skin.
assertions.note: Topical estradiol stimulated collagen in sun-protected hip skin but not in photoaged face or forearm skin.

assertions.text: A small randomized study in healthy older adults found that topical estrogen accelerated cutaneous wound healing.
assertions.quote: Compared to placebo, estrogen treatment increased the extent of wound healing in both males and females with a decrease in wound size at day 7, increased collagen levels at both days 7 and 80, and increased day 7 fibronectin levels.
assertions.note: A study in healthy elderly subjects found topical estrogen increased the extent and rate of wound healing at day 7.

assertions.text: The finding that low-dose hormone therapy made no difference to facial wrinkles is based on a randomized trial in people.

assertions.note: Tiganescu et al. demonstrated in human dermal fibroblasts in vitro that physiological concentrations of cortisol inhibited collagen biosynthesis.

assertions.note: Tiganescu et al. demonstrated prevention of age-induced dermal atrophy in 11β-HSD1 knockout mice.

units.text:
Regulatory status and indications
Symptoms and bone. Skin is a bystander.
In the US, as of February 2026, FDA-approved menopausal hormone therapy is for moderate-to-severe hot flashes, vaginal and vulvar symptoms and, for some products, preventing bone loss. FDA's 2025–26 labeling changes removed cardiovascular, breast-cancer and dementia statements from the boxed warning; skin did not become an indication. The North American Menopause Society's 2022 statement finds benefit outweighs risk for bothersome symptoms and bone protection when therapy starts before 60 or within 10 years of menopause, and finds insufficient evidence for compounded 'bioidentical' hormones. Under US rules an over-the-counter 'hormone cream' is an unapproved drug. For the skin itself, daily sunscreen has a large randomized trial behind it, and one tretinoin cream is FDA-approved as an adjunct for fine facial wrinkl…
units.sourceNote: FDA, 10 Nov 2025 and 12 Feb 2026 · 21 CFR 310.530 · NAMS 2022, 2020 · Manson 2013 · Hughes 2013 · Renova label · UK: Evorel and Sandrena SmPCs, MHRA Guidance Note 14, medicines compendium (checked 25 Sep 2026)

assertions.text: In the United States, FDA-approved indications for menopausal hormone therapy include moderate-to-severe hot flashes, vaginal and vulvar symptoms, and for some products, the prevention of bone loss.
assertions.quote: The FDA has approved multiple hormone therapies for moderate-to-severe hot flashes, vaginal dryness and discomfort, and preventing bone loss.
assertions.note: FDA announcements confirm these approved indications for menopausal hormone therapy.

assertions.text: FDA's 2025–26 labeling changes removed statements concerning cardiovascular disease, breast cancer, and probable dementia from the boxed warning of menopausal hormone therapy products.
assertions.quote: Specifically, risk statements related to cardiovascular disease, breast cancer and probable dementia were removed from the “boxed warning,” the agency’s most prominent safety-related warning.
assertions.note: The FDA press release confirms the removal of these risk statements from the boxed warning.

assertions.text: The FDA initiated the removal of these boxed warnings in late 2025 and approved the first batch of revised labels in February 2026.
assertions.quote: The FDA initiated the removal of these warnings in November 2025, following a comprehensive review of the scientific literature. At the FDA’s request, 29 drug companies have submitted proposed labeling changes. This first batch of six products with approved labeling changes includes products from each of the four categories of HRT for menopausal women:
assertions.note: The FDA news release documents initiation in November 2025 and approval of the first six revised labels on February 12, 2026.

assertions.text: The North American Menopause Society's 2022 position statement concludes that the benefit-risk balance is favorable for bothersome vasomotor symptoms and bone loss prevention when therapy starts before age 60 or within 10 years of menopause onset.
assertions.quote: For women aged younger than 60 years or who are within 10 years of menopause onset and have no contraindications, the benefit-risk ratio is favorable for treatment of bothersome VMS and prevention of bone loss.
assertions.note: The NAMS 2022 position statement abstract confirms this benefit-risk conclusion for women meeting these timing criteria.

assertions.text: The North American Menopause Society's 2022 position statement finds insufficient evidence for compounded bioidentical hormones.
assertions.note: The provided abstract of the NAMS 2022 position statement does not mention compounded bioidentical hormones.

assertions.text: Under US regulations, topically applied over-the-counter hormone creams are regarded as new drugs requiring an approved application to be marketed.
assertions.quote: Any OTC drug product that is labeled, represented, or promoted as a topically applied hormone-containing product for drug use, with the exception of those hormones identified in paragraph (e) of this section, is regarded as a new drug within the meaning of section 201(p) of the act, for which an approved application or abbreviated application under section 505 of the act and part 314 of this chapter is required for marketing.
assertions.note: 21 CFR 310.530 specifies that OTC topical hormone products are considered new drugs requiring approved applications.

assertions.text: Daily sunscreen use has a randomized controlled trial demonstrating that it retards skin aging compared to discretionary use.
assertions.quote: Skin aging from baseline to the end of the trial was 24% less in the daily sunscreen group than in the discretionary sunscreen group (relative odds, 0.76 [95% CI, 0.59 to 0.98]).
assertions.note: The Hughes et al. trial demonstrated 24% less skin aging over 4.5 years with daily broad-spectrum sunscreen compared to discretionary use.

assertions.note: The NAMS 2022 position statement abstract recommends low-dose vaginal estrogen for bothersome GSM symptoms not relieved by over-the-counter therapies.

units.text:
Hormones, symptoms and skin
A 51-year-old asks you for 'hormones for my skin'. Her last period was two years ago.
Where do you start?
Correct answer: Ask about hot flashes, sleep and vaginal symptoms, and record what she says.
Explanation: Right. Treat symptoms on their merits; the skin concern stays with skin-directed care.
Distractor (deliberately false, not a claim): Ask which estrogen cream she would like for her face.
Explanation: That starts from the skin, and systemic or topical estrogen is not prescribed for wrinkles alone.
Distractor (deliberately false, not a claim): Tell her hormone therapy is too risky to discuss.
Explanation: The 2022 position statement finds benefit outweighs risk for bothersome symptoms and bone when therapy starts before 60 or within 10 years of menopause, so hear her symptoms first.
Hot flashes wake her most nights. What do you do with them?
Correct answ…

assertions.text: The 2022 position statement finds benefit outweighs risk for bothersome symptoms and bone when hormone therapy starts before age 60 or within 10 years of menopause.
assertions.quote: For women aged younger than 60 years or who are within 10 years of menopause onset and have no contraindications, the benefit-risk ratio is favorable for treatment of bothersome VMS and prevention of bone loss.
assertions.note: The NAMS 2022 statement confirms a favorable benefit-risk ratio for bothersome VMS and bone loss prevention within this window.

assertions.text: The position statement finds compounded 'bioidentical' preparations lack efficacy and safety data and finds too little evidence for them.
assertions.note: The provided abstract of the 2022 position statement does not address compounded bioidentical hormone preparations.

assertions.text: The largest trial on facial skin, including 485 women followed for 48 weeks, found no significant difference in facial wrinkles.
assertions.quote: Low-dose hormone therapy for 48 weeks in postmenopausal women did not significantly alter mild to moderate age-related facial skin changes.
assertions.note: A 48-week trial of 485 women found hormone therapy did not significantly improve facial wrinkling compared to placebo.

assertions.text: A four-year randomized trial in recently menopausal women found no difference in skin wrinkles with hormone therapy.
assertions.quote: Neither total wrinkle score nor total rigidity score was significantly different at baseline or over the 4-year follow-up among patients randomized to CEE, E 2 , or placebo.
assertions.note: The KEEPS ancillary skin study found no significant difference in total wrinkle score over 4 years among hormone therapy arms and placebo.

assertions.text: Daily sunscreen has a large randomized trial behind it demonstrating retarded skin aging.
assertions.quote: Skin aging from baseline to the end of the trial was 24% less in the daily sunscreen group than in the discretionary sunscreen group (relative odds, 0.76 [95% CI, 0.59 to 0.98]).
assertions.note: The randomized trial in over 900 adults demonstrated that daily sunscreen reduced skin aging by 24% compared to discretionary use.

assertions.text: A 24-week trial of topical conjugated estrogen cream found improvement in facial skin thickness and fine wrinkles.
assertions.quote: In conclusion, Premarin cream produced better results than the placebo cream; the difference was statistically significant for skin thickness and fine wrinkles.
assertions.note: A 24-week randomized study showed statistically significant improvements in skin thickness and fine wrinkles with Premarin cream.

assertions.text: A biopsy study found no collagen response following topical estradiol application on photoaged facial skin.
assertions.quote: Surprisingly, no significant changes in production were observed in women or men after 2-week estradiol treatment of photoaged forearm or face skin, despite similar expression of estrogen receptors (ER-alpha, ER-beta, and GPR30) in aged and photoaged skin.
assertions.note: Biopsy analysis revealed topical estradiol did not induce significant changes in collagen synthesis in photoaged forearm or facial skin.

assertions.text: Under US regulations, an over-the-counter 'hormone cream' is classified as an unapproved new drug requiring an approved NDA to be lawfully marketed.

Explanation: Symptoms decide hormone therapy; skin gets skin-directed care.

Explanation: That is the mechanism talking. Small trials show thicker skin, the largest trials found no difference in wrinkles, and skin is not an approved indication.
Distractor (deliberately false, not a claim): A compounded 'bioidentical' estrogen face cream avoids the risks of systemic therapy.
Explanation: Compounded 'bioidentical' preparations lack efficacy and safety data and carry quality concerns; the menopause society says preference alone should not justify them.
