units.text:
Concept
What a certificate can and cannot prove.
A certificate of analysis is the supplier's own report on a named lot. Mass spectrometry checks identity, and a careful certificate prints the expected mass beside the observed one. HPLC gives purity as a percentage, which says nothing about what the impurities are. Endotoxin, microbial, water, counter-ion, metal and solvent results complete it. A certificate cannot prove that the vial in your hand came from that lot, how it was stored since, or that it is sterile and suitable to inject.
Identity: mass spectrometry, observed against expected
Purity: an HPLC percentage, impurities unnamed
Suitability to inject needs sterility, endotoxin and the right lot
Narration: Picture the certificate a patient hands you, and read it line by line, asking what each line actually tests. Mass spectrometry checks identity, and a careful certificate shows th…
units.sourceNote: Peptide Pocket Guide, peptide fundamentals · FDA PCAC briefing, BPC-157 (July 2026) · FDA endotoxin guidance (2026) · Popławska 2019

assertions.text: A certificate of analysis is the supplier's own report on a named lot.
assertions.quote: A COA is the supplier's own quality attestation, not an independent certification. A serious COA tells you what the supplier found on a named lot: whether the mass matches the expected molecule, how pure the material was by HPLC, what counter-ion it carries, and what the endotoxin and microbial results were.
assertions.note: The guide notes a certificate of analysis is the supplier's own attestation reporting findings on a named lot.

assertions.text: Mass spectrometry checks identity, and a certificate displays the expected theoretical mass beside the observed mass.
assertions.quote: Mass spectrometry confirms the molecular weight matches the expected peptide. The theoretical monoisotopic mass should be reported alongside the observed mass.
assertions.note: The guide states mass spectrometry confirms molecular weight and the theoretical mass should be reported alongside the observed mass.

assertions.text: HPLC reports purity as a percentage, which does not identify or specify what the impurities are.
assertions.quote: However, the impurity profiles are unclear because the impurities were not identified or specified. In the CoA provided by nominator 2, there is only a purity test with the testing result of 98.34%.
assertions.note: The FDA briefing document notes that a CoA reporting HPLC purity alone leaves impurity profiles unclear because impurities are not identified or specified.

assertions.text: A certificate of analysis cannot prove that a vial in hand came from that lot, how it was stored since, or that it is sterile and suitable to inject.
assertions.quote: What it cannot establish on its own is that a product is safe to inject — that turns on sterility, the dose and route, the conditions the material was held in since testing, and whether the lot tested is the lot in hand.
assertions.note: The guide confirms a CoA cannot establish that a product is safe to inject, as that depends on storage conditions, sterility, and lot verification.

assertions.text: FDA's guidance states that endotoxin limits are calculated based on dose and route.
assertions.quote: The appropriate way to establish the endotoxins limit is to use the calculation methods provided in the USP or AAMI standards. Monograph limits may also not account for current product strengths or dosage regimes; these should also be checked using the calculations recommended in the standards.
assertions.note: FDA guidance specifies that endotoxin limits are established using calculation methods that account for product dosage regimes, strengths, and routes of administration.

assertions.text: When FDA reviewed BPC-157 for its advisory committee, most public certificates listed purity alone, and the nominator's CoA omitted endotoxin testing.
assertions.quote: No bioburden/endotoxin test is mentioned in the CoA provided by the nominator. Endotoxin test is considered a critical quality attribute to control microbiological quality of a BDS intended for an injection product.
assertions.note: The FDA briefing document observed that most public CoAs for BPC-157 contained purity testing only and the nominator's CoA mentioned no endotoxin test.

assertions.note: A bare claim of purity over 99% without a chromatogram or supporting data is specifically identified as something that should not appear on a serious COA.

assertions.text: Reporting both expected and observed mass with an attached spectrum for identity verification is useful evidence on a certificate of analysis.
assertions.quote: The theoretical monoisotopic mass should be reported alongside the observed mass.
assertions.note: The reference guide states that theoretical and observed mass should be reported together via mass spectrometry.

assertions.text: Failing to list impurity limits or results on a certificate of analysis is a red flag.
assertions.quote: There is no information about the impurity limits/testing results in the CoA to demonstrate control of the impurity profile of BPC- 157 (free base).
assertions.note: The FDA briefing highlights that a lack of impurity limits or test results fails to demonstrate control over the impurity profile.

assertions.text: A certificate of analysis lacking endotoxin testing for a product sold for injection is a red flag.
assertions.quote: — No endotoxin or microbial data on a product marketed for injection.
assertions.note: Missing endotoxin or microbial data on an injectable product is listed among serious COA defects.

assertions.text: A certificate of analysis reflecting testing performed 20 months before purchase is a red flag.
assertions.quote: — A COA dated more than 12 months before purchase — peptides degrade in storage.
assertions.note: A COA dated more than 12 months prior to purchase is flagged because peptides degrade during storage.

assertions.text: A clean certificate cannot establish that a research-use-only vial is sterile, lawful, or from the intended lot.
assertions.quote: What it cannot establish on its own is that a product is safe to inject — that turns on sterility, the dose and route, the conditions the material was held in since testing, and whether the lot tested is the lot in hand.
assertions.note: The guide explains that a COA alone cannot confirm injectable safety, sterility, holding conditions, or that the lot matches.

assertions.text: A lot number printed on a Certificate of Analysis that matches the vial label links the documentation to the product in hand, though it remains the supplier's own claim.
assertions.quote: Ask which testing laboratory ran the analysis, the date of testing, the USP-797 / 800 compliance status of the facility, and the lot number that links the COA to the vial in hand.
assertions.note: The guide notes that the lot number links the COA to the vial and that a COA is the supplier's own attestation.

assertions.quote: A bare claim of "purity > 99%" with no chromatogram or supporting data.
assertions.note: The guide lists a bare purity claim over 99% without a chromatogram under what should not be seen on a serious COA.

assertions.text: Reporting expected and observed mass with a mass spectrum attached confirms peptide identity.
assertions.quote: Mass spectrometry confirms the molecular weight matches the expected peptide. The theoretical monoisotopic mass should be reported alongside the observed mass.
assertions.note: The guide states mass spectrometry confirms molecular weight matches the expected peptide when expected and observed masses are reported.

assertions.text: FDA reviewers flagged for BPC-157 that when purity was reported without an impurity profile, immunogenic impurities and aggregates could not be ruled out.
assertions.quote: Because there is a lack of information regarding potential impurities that can be present in BPC-157 acetate and the potential of peptide aggregation, we cannot rule out the potential for immunogenicity associated with these impurities and peptide-related aggregates.
assertions.note: FDA reviewers noted that lack of information on impurities and aggregation prevents ruling out immunogenicity.

assertions.text: Lack of endotoxin testing on a product sold for injection is a red flag and hard contraindication, as allowable endotoxin depends on dose and route.
assertions.quote: RUO peptides frequently have no endotoxin testing — a hard contraindication to injection.
assertions.note: The guide describes lack of endotoxin testing as a hard contraindication to injection.

assertions.text: The Peptide Pocket Guide considers a Certificate of Analysis dated more than 12 months before purchase a warning sign because peptides degrade in storage.
assertions.quote: A COA dated more than 12 months before purchase — peptides degrade in storage.
assertions.note: The guide includes a COA dated more than 12 months before purchase among the red flags due to degradation in storage.

units.text:
Label against laboratory
99% on the label.
Researchers made test purchases of semaglutide from illegal online pharmacies and analysed what arrived. The three vials that were delivered were all judged probably substandard or falsified: purity measured 7.7–14.4% against the 99% printed on the label, peptide content ran 29–39% above the labelled amount, and endotoxin was found in every vial, although none grew microorganisms.
measured purity of online semaglutide vials labelled 99%
Ashraf et al., J Med Internet Res 2024 · three delivered vials · endotoxin detected in all three
What it means: Purity printed on a label can be wildly wrong, and a vial that grows nothing can still carry endotoxin. Independent testing found what the paperwork hid.
What it does not mean: Three vials of one drug give no market-wide failure rate, and semaglutide is outside the skin-peptide shelf. It documents the g…
units.sourceNote: Ashraf et al., J Med Internet Res 2024 · Peptide Pocket Guide

assertions.text: Three semaglutide vials delivered from test purchases from illegal online pharmacies were all judged probably substandard or falsified.
assertions.quote: All purchased vials were considered probable substandard and falsified products, as visual inspection indicated noncompliance in more than half (59%-63%) of the evaluated criteria.
assertions.note: Ashraf et al. report that all three delivered vials were evaluated as probable substandard and falsified products.

assertions.text: Measured semaglutide purity in the delivered vials was 7.7–14.4% against the 99% claimed on the label.
assertions.quote: Furthermore, the measured semaglutide purity was significantly low, ranging between 7.7% and 14.37% and deviating from the 99% claimed on product labels by manufacturers.
assertions.note: Ashraf et al. found measured purity ranged from 7.7% to 14.37%, deviating from the 99% label claim.

assertions.text: Peptide content in the delivered semaglutide vials ran 29–39% above the labelled amount.
assertions.quote: The semaglutide content of samples substantially exceeded labeled amounts by 28.56%-38.69%, although no peptide-like impurities were identified.
assertions.note: Semaglutide content exceeded labeled amounts by 28.56% to 38.69% across the samples.

assertions.text: Bacterial endotoxin was detected in every delivered vial, although none grew viable microorganisms.
assertions.quote: The lyophilized peptide samples were devoid of viable microorganisms at the time of testing; however, endotoxin was detected in all samples with levels ranging between 2.1645 EU/mg and 8.9511 EU/mg.
assertions.note: Endotoxin was found in all samples despite all being devoid of viable microorganisms.

units.text:
What changes in practice
Research use only is a label, and never a route.
In the US, 'not for use in humans' labelling lets a supplier ship an investigational drug for laboratory or in-vitro research, and obliges the shipper to check that is how it will be used. FDA reads intended use from claims, marketing and the circumstances of sale, so the disclaimer changes nothing about a vial sold with injection instructions. A certificate cannot turn such a product into a pharmaceutical.
The label permits laboratory research only
Intended use is read from how a product is sold
A certificate cannot convert a research product
Narration: Research use only sounds like a category. In law it works as a shipping permission. The US rule lets a supplier send an investigational drug for laboratory or test-tube work if the label says it must stay out of people, and the shipper is meant to confirm that is h…
units.sourceNote: 21 CFR 312.160 · 21 CFR 201.128 · Aesthetic & Regenerative Endocrinology, ch. 3 · Peptide Pocket Guide, regulatory chapter

assertions.text: In the US, 'not for use in humans' labelling allows a supplier to ship an investigational drug intended solely for in vitro tests or laboratory research animals.
assertions.quote:
A person may ship a drug intended solely for tests in vitro or in animals used only for laboratory research purposes if it is labeled as follows:

CAUTION: Contains a new drug for investigational use only in laboratory research animals, or for tests in vitro. Not for use in humans.
assertions.note: 21 CFR 312.160 authorizes shipment of an investigational drug for in vitro tests or laboratory animals under this specific label.

assertions.text: The shipper of an investigational drug under 21 CFR 312.160 is required to use due diligence to verify that the recipient will actually use the drug for laboratory research or in vitro tests.
assertions.quote: A person shipping a drug under paragraph (a) of this section shall use due diligence to assure that the consignee is regularly engaged in conducting such tests and that the shipment of the new drug will actually be used for tests in vitro or in animals used only for laboratory research.
assertions.note: The regulation explicitly obliges the shipper to assure the consignee's engagement and actual research use.

assertions.text: FDA determines intended use objectively from labeling claims, advertising matter, and the circumstances surrounding distribution.
assertions.quote: The intent may be shown by such persons' expressions, the design or composition of the article, or by the circumstances surrounding the distribution of the article. This objective intent may, for example, be shown by labeling claims, advertising matter, or oral or written statements by such persons or their representatives.
assertions.note: 21 CFR 201.128 defines objective intent through expressions, advertising, and distribution circumstances.

assertions.text: An RUO disclaimer offers no legal protection where marketing or circumstances of sale establish intended human use.
assertions.quote: The RUO disclaimer provides no legal protection — the FDA regulates based on inferred intended use, not the label on the product.
assertions.note: The guide confirms that RUO disclaimers provide no protection because FDA regulates on inferred intended use.

assertions.text: A certificate of analysis cannot convert a research-use-only product into a pharmaceutical because sterility, GMP manufacturing standards, and a lawful clinical pathway remain absent.
assertions.quote: research-use-only material carries no GMP or quality guarantee and is not a lawful clinical pathway — impurity, dose, and contamination are real risks.
assertions.note: The guide states that research-use-only material lacks GMP and quality guarantees and is not a lawful clinical pathway.

units.text: In the EU, a product is a medicine by presentation (presented as treating or preventing disease) or by function (restoring, correcting or modifying physiological functions by a pharmacological, immunological or metabolic action), and where it could be both a medicine and another regulated product, medicines law applies (Directive 2001/83/EC, Articles 1(2) and 2(2)). The Directive's research exclusion covers medicinal products intended for research and development trials (Article 3(3)).

assertions.text: In the EU, a product is a medicine by presentation (presented as treating or preventing disease) or by function (restoring, correcting or modifying physiological functions by a pharmacological, immunological or metabolic action) (Directive 2001/83/EC, Article 1(2)).
assertions.quote:
(a) 

Any substance or combination of substances presented as having properties for treating or preventing disease in human beings; or

(b) 

Any substance or combination of substances which may be used in or administered to human beings either with a view to restoring, correcting or modifying physiological functions by exerting a pharmacological, immunological or metabolic action, or to making a medical diagnosis.
assertions.note: Directive 2001/83/EC Article 1(2) defines a medicinal product by presentation and by function.

assertions.text: Where a product could fall within both the definition of a medicine and another regulated product, medicines law applies (Directive 2001/83/EC, Article 2(2)).
assertions.quote: In cases of doubt, where, taking into account all its characteristics, a product may fall within the definition of a ‘medicinal product’ and within the definition of a product covered by other Community legislation the provisions of this Directive shall apply.
assertions.note: Article 2(2) specifies that where a product may fall within the definition of a medicinal product and other Community legislation, the Directive applies.

assertions.text: Directive 2001/83/EC's research exclusion covers medicinal products intended for research and development trials (Article 3(3)).
assertions.quote: Medicinal products intended for research and development trials, but without prejudice to the provisions of Directive 2001/20/EC of the European Parliament and of the Council of 4 April 2001 on the approximation of the laws, regulations and administrative provisions of the Member States relating to the implementation of good clinical practice in the conduct of clinical trials on medicinal products for human use
assertions.note: Article 3(3) excludes medicinal products intended for research and development trials from the scope of the Directive.

units.text: In Portugal, a medicine is any substance or combination of substances presented as having properties for treating or preventing disease in human beings or its symptoms, or which may be used in or administered to human beings to make a medical diagnosis or to restore, correct or modify physiological functions by exerting a pharmacological, immunological or metabolic action (Estatuto do Medicamento). Making, selling, supplying or administering medicines without the required authorisations or registrations is an administrative offence punishable by a fine from €2,000 up to 15% of turnover or €180,000, whichever is lower.

units.text: In the UAE, Federal Decree-Law 38 of 2024 has, since 2 January 2025, barred importing, distributing, possessing, selling, displaying or using any medical product without a marketing approval from the Emirates Drug Establishment (EDE), the federal regulator of medical products since Federal Decree-Law 28/2023. In Dubai, the DHA prohibits using any peptide product intended for research use on humans, or for therapeutic purposes outside an approved study or clinical trial, and bars facilities from buying peptide products from websites, social media or unverifiable suppliers (29 July 2026). In Abu Dhabi, the DoH's compounding standard (August 2026) prohibits compounding from unapproved or unknown-source substances, or from substances not on the DoH Registry for Compounded Substances, unless the DoH permits it.

units.text:
Regulatory status (outside the US)
Selling and advertising peptides outside the US.
Outside the US, whether a peptide is regulated as a medicine turns on what is claimed for it and on what it is and does, not on the category a seller chooses, and a medicine without a marketing authorisation may not be sold, supplied or advertised. Advertising a prescription-only medicine to the public is prohibited, or needs the regulator's prior approval.
Medicine or not: what is claimed, and what it is and does
No marketing authorisation: no sale, supply or advertising
Prescription-only: public advertising banned or approved first
Narration: Selling a peptide outside the United States starts with one question, whether the product is a medicine, and regulators answer it from the product itself. They look at what is claimed for it and at what it is and does, so a research-use label or a cosmetic box sett…

assertions.text: Outside the US, whether a peptide or product is regulated as a medicine turns on what is claimed for it and on what it is and does, rather than the category chosen by the seller.
assertions.quote: In broad terms, when classifying a product, the Agency looks at the way it is presented and its function, that is, its effects (when administered) on human physiology.
assertions.note: MHRA Guidance Note 8 confirms that classification depends on presentation and physiological function, and disclaimer statements are not conclusive.

assertions.text: A medicinal product without a marketing authorisation may not be sold, supplied, or advertised.
assertions.quote: It is an offence to sell or supply or to advertise a medicinal product which does not have authorisation.
assertions.note: Guidance Note 8 expressly confirms that selling, supplying, or advertising an unauthorized medicine is an offence under the regulations.

assertions.text: Advertising a prescription-only medicine to the public is prohibited or requires the regulator's prior approval.
assertions.quote: 284. —(1) A person may not publish an advertisement that is likely to lead to the use of a prescription only medicine.
assertions.note: Regulation 284 of HMR 2012 bars advertisements likely to lead to the use of prescription-only medicines.

assertions.text: The restriction on advertising prescription-only medicines to the public covers social media posts by clinics and influencers.
assertions.quote: The prohibition on advertising of prescription only medicines to the public applies to social networks such as facebook and twitter in the same way as for traditional media such as magazine advertisements or displays on clinic premises. Any mention of the availability of a named prescription only medicine from a clinic in social media is likely to be considered to be an advertisement which is prohibited.
assertions.note: The MHRA Blue Guide confirms that the ban on advertising prescription-only medicines applies to social media by clinics.

units.text: In the UK, MHRA decides whether a product is a medicine from its claims, including websites and social media, and from its form and the way it is used. A medicine with no UK marketing authorisation may not be sold, supplied or advertised. MHRA classes injectable melanotan products as medicines, and its largest seizure of unlicensed weight-loss medicines, in May 2026, included peptide products. Prescription-only medicines may not be advertised to the public at all: a clinic may promote 'treatment for lines and wrinkles' without naming the medicine, and in February 2026 the UK advertising regulator ruled that influencer posts tagging a weight-loss injection were adverts for a prescription-only medicine. GMC guidance requires doctors to examine a patient physically before prescribing an injectable cosmetic medicine.

units.text: In the EU, member states must prohibit any advertising of a medicine that has no marketing authorisation, and any advertising of prescription-only medicines to the general public, where advertising includes any inducement designed to promote prescription, supply, sale or consumption (Directive 2001/83/EC, Articles 86 to 88). EU audiovisual law also bans audiovisual commercial communications for prescription-only medicines and medical treatment, and video-sharing platforms must apply this to advertising on their services, including advertising they do not sell themselves (Directive 2010/13/EU).

assertions.text: In the EU, member states must prohibit advertising of prescription-only medicines to the general public.

assertions.text: Under EU rules, advertising of medicinal products includes any inducement designed to promote prescription, supply, sale or consumption.
assertions.quote: For the purposes of this Title, ‘advertising of medicinal products’ shall include any form of door-to-door information, canvassing activity or inducement designed to promote the prescription, supply, sale or consumption of medicinal products; it shall include in particular:

Health advertising practices fall under Decreto-Lei 238/2015, which bans false claims of guaranteed cure or results or of absence of side effects and is enforced by the Health Regulatory Authority (ERS).

units.text:
A patient shows you the certificate for a research-use-only peptide she injects: 99.1% purity by HPLC with a chromatogram, the correct mass by mass spectrometry, and a lot number that matches her vial. What does it establish?
Explanation: Read what each line tests, then name what no line can test.
Distractor (deliberately false, not a claim): That the vial is safe to inject.
Explanation: Identity and purity say nothing about sterility, endotoxin or storage, and research-use-only products are labelled not for use in humans.
Correct answer: That the supplier reports the right molecule at high purity for that lot, and nothing about sterility, storage since testing or a lawful route.
Explanation: Correct. A certificate describes a lot; it cannot make the product sterile, pharmaceutical or lawful.
Distractor (deliberately false, not a claim): Nothing at all, because certificates are always fo…

assertions.text: Identity and purity testing on a certificate of analysis do not establish sterility, endotoxin status, or the conditions under which the material was held since testing.
assertions.quote: What it cannot establish on its own is that a product is safe to inject — that turns on sterility, the dose and route, the conditions the material was held in since testing, and whether the lot tested is the lot in hand.
assertions.note: The guide notes that a certificate of analysis reporting identity and purity cannot establish sterility, storage conditions since testing, or safety for injection.

assertions.text: Investigational research-use-only products for animal or in vitro tests must be labeled 'Not for use in humans'.
assertions.quote: A person may ship a drug intended solely for tests in vitro or in animals used only for laboratory research purposes if it is labeled as follows: CAUTION: Contains a new drug for investigational use only in laboratory research animals, or for tests in vitro. Not for use in humans.
assertions.note: 21 CFR 312.160 mandates this specific labeling caution for investigational in vitro or animal laboratory research drugs.

assertions.text: A certificate of analysis is the supplier's own attestation describing a named lot and does not confer lawful authorization for use.
assertions.quote: A COA is the supplier's own quality attestation, not an independent certification. A serious COA tells you what the supplier found on a named lot: whether the mass matches the expected molecule, how pure the material was by HPLC, what counter-ion it carries, and what the endotoxin and microbial results were.
assertions.note: The source explains that a COA is merely the supplier's attestation of test findings for a lot and that RUO labeling provides no legal protection.

units.text:
Lesson 7.3 · Concept
Off-label needs a label.
Off-label prescribing means using an approved drug for a use its labelling does not cover, and FDA accepts it as clinical judgment. A never-approved peptide has no label to depart from, so prescribing it is use of an unapproved drug. Introducing an unapproved new drug into interstate commerce is a prohibited act under the FD&C Act, and FDA's 2020 warning letter to a compounding pharmacy named BPC-157 and GHK-Cu on exactly this basis.
Off-label applies only to approved drugs
Compounded is still unapproved
Narration: Off-label is the phrase to get right first. FDA uses it for an approved drug prescribed outside its labelling, which prescribers generally may do when they judge it medically appropriate. The idea assumes a label exists. A peptide that was never approved has none, so prescribing it counts as using an unapproved drug, and the Peptid…
units.sourceNote: FDA, unapproved use of approved drugs · 21 U.S.C. 331 · FDA warning letter, Tailor Made Compounding (2020) · Peptide Pocket Guide

assertions.text: Off-label prescribing means using an approved drug outside its labeling, which FDA recognizes providers may do based on clinical judgment.
assertions.quote: From the FDA perspective, once the FDA approves a drug, healthcare providers generally may prescribe the drug for an unapproved use when they judge that it is medically appropriate for their patient.
assertions.note: FDA states that providers generally may prescribe approved drugs for unapproved uses when clinically appropriate.

assertions.text: Off-label prescribing applies only to approved drugs, so prescribing a never-approved peptide constitutes using an unapproved drug.
assertions.quote: "Off-label" doesn't apply to unapproved drugs. Off-label use is a legal pathway only for drugs holding at least one FDA-approved indication. Prescribing BPC-157 or any never-approved peptide is use of an unapproved new drug — IND, Expanded Access, and Right-to-Try do not cover routine wellness use.
assertions.note: The Peptide Pocket Guide confirms that off-label use requires an approved drug and that prescribing never-approved peptides is using unapproved drugs.

assertions.text: Compounded drug products are unapproved by definition and lawful only when statutory exemption conditions are satisfied.
assertions.quote: Therefore, you compounded drug products that do not meet the conditions of section 503A and are not eligible for the exemptions in that section from the FDA approval requirement of section 505 of the FDCA, the requirement under section 502(f)(1) of the FDCA that labeling bear adequate directions for use, and the requirement of compliance with CGMP under section 501(a)(2)(B) of the FDCA.
assertions.note: The FDA warning letter explains that compounded drugs require meeting section 503A conditions to be exempt from new drug approval.

assertions.text: Introducing or delivering for introduction an unapproved new drug into interstate commerce is a prohibited act under federal law.
assertions.quote: Under sections 505(a) and 301(d) of the FDCA [21 U.S.C. § 331(d)], a new drug may not be introduced into or delivered for introduction into interstate commerce unless an application approved by FDA under section 505 of the FDCA is in effect for the drug.
assertions.note: The FDA warning letter cites the statutory prohibition against introducing new drugs into interstate commerce without an approved application.

assertions.text: FDA's 2020 warning letter to a compounding pharmacy cited its BPC-157 and GHK-Cu products as unapproved new drugs ineligible for compounding exemptions.
assertions.quote: For example, the investigators noted that your firm compounded drug products using Follistatin, GHRP-2, GHRP-6, Endurobal, AOD 9604, BPC 157, Bremelanotide (PT-141), Cerebrolysin, DSIP, Epitalon, GHK-Cu, IGF1-LR3, Ipamorelin, LL-37, Melanotan II, PEG-MGF, Selank, Semax, CJC 1295, SARMS, LGD-4033, and MK 677.
assertions.note: The 2020 warning letter specifically lists BPC 157 and GHK-Cu as ineligible bulk drug substances.

units.text: In the EU, no medicine may be placed on a member state's market without a national marketing authorisation or an EU-wide (central) authorisation (Directive 2001/83/EC, Article 6(1)). A member state may, under its own legislation, allow an unauthorised medicine for an individual patient on a bona fide unsolicited order from an authorised health professional, under that professional's direct personal responsibility (Article 5(1)).

assertions.text: In the EU, no medicine may be placed on a member state's market without a national marketing authorisation or an EU-wide (central) authorisation.
assertions.note: Article 6(1) provides that no medicinal product may be placed on a member state's market without national or EU marketing authorisation.

assertions.text: A member state may, under its own legislation, allow an unauthorised medicine for an individual patient on a bona fide unsolicited order from an authorised health professional, under that professional's direct personal responsibility.
assertions.quote: A Member State may, in accordance with legislation in force and to fulfil special needs, exclude from the provisions of this Directive medicinal products supplied in response to a bona fide unsolicited order, formulated in accordance with the specifications of an authorised health-care professional and for use by an individual patient under his direct personal responsibility.
assertions.note: Article 5(1) permits member states to exclude from the Directive medicines supplied on a bona fide unsolicited order under a health professional's direct responsibility.

units.text: In Portugal, marketing a medicine requires INFARMED's authorisation unless the law provides otherwise (Estatuto do Medicamento), and INFARMED may authorise exceptional use (AUE) of a medicine without a marketing authorisation, for example when it is clinically justified as indispensable and no authorised alternative exists.

assertions.text: In Portugal, marketing a medicine requires INFARMED's authorisation unless the law provides otherwise.
assertions.note: The cited statute (pt-dl176-2006) is unavailable and the provided Infarmed webpage does not state this general requirement.

assertions.text: INFARMED may authorise exceptional use (AUE) of a medicine without a marketing authorisation, for example when it is clinically justified as indispensable and no authorised alternative exists.
assertions.quote: A utilização excecional de medicamentos (AUE) reveste-se de carácter excecional e carece de autorização prévia a conceder pelo Infarmed, ao abrigo do disposto no artigo 92.º do Decreto-Lei n.º 176/2006, de 30 de agosto, na sua atual redação, observados os requisitos e condições definidas no regulamento aprovado pela Deliberação n.º 840/2023, de 31 de agosto..
assertions.note: The source confirms INFARMED grants AUE, but the provided page does not state the criteria that use must be clinically indispensable without authorised alternatives.

units.text: In Brazil, ANVISA stated in April 2025 that physicians keep the right to prescribe medicines off-label when they judge that, for a given patient, benefits outweigh risks, while no medicine may be manufactured, sold or supplied before it is registered (Law 6.360/1976, art. 12). ANVISA stated on 2 July 2026 that products presented as peptides including BPC-157 and GHK-Cu that promise aesthetic effects or improvement in health conditions are not registered with ANVISA, and that BPC-157 is not authorised for use as a food supplement.

assertions.text: ANVISA stated in April 2025 that physicians retain the right to prescribe medicines off-label when they judge that benefits outweigh risks for a given patient.
assertions.note: The provided text of the April 2025 ANVISA release does not mention off-label prescribing rights.

assertions.text: Under Brazilian Law 6.360/1976 (art. 12), no medicine may be manufactured, sold or supplied before registration.
assertions.note: The provided text for Law 6.360/1976 is a generic government portal homepage and does not contain the text of the statute.

assertions.text: ANVISA stated on 2 July 2026 that products presented as peptides including BPC-157 and GHK-Cu that promise aesthetic effects or health improvements are not registered with ANVISA.
assertions.quote: Os produtos que se apresentam como peptídeos denominados GHK-CU, BPC-157, TB500, CJC-1295 e Ipamorelina, que prometem efeitos estéticos ou melhora em quadros de saúde, também NÃO se encontram registrados na Anvisa.
assertions.note: The source explicitly states that products presented as peptides such as GHK-Cu and BPC-157 promising aesthetic or health effects are not registered with ANVISA.

assertions.text: ANVISA stated on 2 July 2026 that BPC-157 is not authorised for use as a food supplement.
assertions.quote: No Brasil, substâncias como BPC-157 e TB-500 não possuem autorização de uso como suplemento alimentar e, até o momento, não há solicitações de empresas ou estudos submetidos à Anvisa para a regularização dessas substâncias como suplementos alimentares .
assertions.note: The source explicitly confirms that BPC-157 lacks authorisation for use as a dietary supplement in Brazil.

units.text: In the UAE, Federal Decree-Law 38 of 2024 lets a physician prescribe a medical product for a use not in its leaflet, or one never submitted to the Emirates Drug Establishment (EDE, the federal regulator of medical products since Federal Decree-Law 28/2023) for marketing approval, only when necessary, when no equivalent alternative is available and with the patient's approval (Art. 42(1)). In Dubai, the DHA prohibits any peptide product that is not registered or licensed with the EDE and requires registered peptide products to be used strictly within their approved indications (29 July 2026). In Abu Dhabi, the DoH allows peptide therapies only for clinical indications supported by available scientific evidence, after a documented eligibility assessment and with informed consent that covers the product's regulatory approval status (31 July 2026).

assertions.text: Federal Decree-Law 38 of 2024 permits a physician to prescribe a medical product for an unapproved indication or one not submitted to the Emirates Drug Establishment only when necessary, when no equivalent alternative exists, and with patient consent.
assertions.note: Federal Decree-Law 38 of 2024 and Federal Decree-Law 28 of 2023 are unavailable in the provided sources.

assertions.text: The Dubai Health Authority prohibits any peptide product not registered or licensed with the Emirates Drug Establishment and requires registered peptide products to be used strictly within approved indications.
assertions.quote: It is prohibited to circulate, prescribe, dispense, administer, or use any peptide product unless it is duly registered or licensed with the Emirates Drug Establishment, and authorized for use within the scope of its license.
assertions.note: The DHA circular explicitly bans peptide products not registered or licensed with the EDE and mandates strict adherence to approved indications.

assertions.text: The Department of Health in Abu Dhabi permits peptide therapies only for clinical indications supported by available scientific evidence, requiring documented eligibility assessment and informed consent specifying regulatory approval status.
assertions.quote: Accordingly, all physicians are required to prescribe peptide therapies only for the appropriate clinical indications supported by available scientific evidence, and shall adhere to the following: 1. Conduct and document patient eligibility assessment and clinical evaluation prior to initiation of therapy; 2. Obtain documented patient informed consent specific to peptide therapy, including expected benefits, uncertainties, potential risks, available alternatives, and the product’s regulatory approval status
assertions.note: The DoH circular mandates prescribing peptides only for indications supported by scientific evidence, preceded by documented eligibility assessment and informed consent detailing regulatory status.

units.text:
Classification (US)
Same molecule, different rulebooks.
Route and claim decide the regime, whatever the molecule. Here is how each one treats a skin peptide in the US, as checked in September 2026.
Cosmetic
Appearance claims only
No premarket approval. A claim to affect structure or function, such as 'regenerates cells', makes it a drug; 'cosmeceutical' has no legal meaning.
Dietary supplement
Oral, no disease claims
The maker is responsible for safety and labelling before sale; FDA acts after products reach the market.
Approved drug
Labelled indications
Off-label use of an approved drug is lawful clinical judgment; document the reasoning.
Compounded (503A or 503B)
Unapproved, conditionally lawful
Only when the substance qualifies and the pharmacy meets the statute. Non-injectable GHK-Cu is in Category 1; BPC-157 and TB-500 have no route.
Investigational or research use only
Trials, or n…
units.sourceNote: FDA: cosmetic or drug; dietary supplements; off-label use · FDA 503A categories (14 May 2026) · 21 CFR 312.160 · Hormonaly guides

assertions.text: Cosmetics do not require FDA premarket approval.
assertions.quote: Under the FD&C Act, cosmetic products and ingredients, with the exception of color additives, do not require FDA approval before they go on the market.
assertions.note: The FDA cosmetic or drug webpage confirms that cosmetic products and ingredients generally do not require FDA approval before entering the market.

assertions.text: A claim that a cosmetic affects structure or function, such as 'regenerates cells', legally classifies it as a drug.
assertions.quote: Such claims establish the product as a drug because the intended use is to treat or prevent disease or otherwise affect the structure or functions of the human body. Some examples are claims that products will restore hair growth, reduce cellulite, treat varicose veins, increase or decrease the production of melanin (pigment) in the skin, or regenerate cells.
assertions.note: FDA guidance explains that claims affecting bodily structure or functions, explicitly including cell regeneration, establish a product as a drug.

assertions.text: The term 'cosmeceutical' has no legal meaning under US law.
assertions.quote: The FD&C Act does not recognize any such category as "cosmeceuticals." A product can be a drug, a cosmetic, or a combination of both, but the term "cosmeceutical" has no meaning under the law.
assertions.note: The FDA explicitly confirms that the term 'cosmeceutical' is not recognized and has no meaning under the FD&C Act.

assertions.text: For dietary supplements, the manufacturer is responsible for evaluating safety and labelling before sale, and the FDA takes action after products reach the market.
assertions.quote: That means that these firms are responsible for evaluating the safety and labeling of their products before marketing to ensure that they meet all the requirements of the Federal Food, Drug, and Cosmetic Act as amended by DSHEA and FDA regulations. FDA has the authority to take action against any adulterated or misbranded dietary supplement product after it reaches the market.
assertions.note: The FDA dietary supplements overview explains that manufacturers must evaluate safety and labeling prior to marketing, while the FDA acts post-market.

assertions.text: Off-label prescribing of an approved drug falls within lawful clinical judgment.
assertions.quote: From the FDA perspective, once the FDA approves a drug, healthcare providers generally may prescribe the drug for an unapproved use when they judge that it is medically appropriate for their patient.
assertions.note: The FDA off-label guidance states that healthcare providers generally may prescribe an approved drug for an unapproved use based on clinical judgment.

assertions.text: Non-injectable GHK-Cu is categorized under Category 1 for 503A bulk drug substances.
assertions.quote: On May 5, 2026, one of those nominators clarified that it intended to withdraw only its nomination of the injectable route of administration with respect to GHK-Cu and would like to retain its nomination for GHK-Cu for non-injectable routes of administration. GHK-Cu (except for injectable routes of administration) will be added back to category 1.
assertions.note: The May 14, 2026 FDA 503A update confirms GHK-Cu for non-injectable routes of administration is placed in Category 1.

assertions.text: BPC-157 and TB-500 have no lawful clinical compounding route under 503A.
assertions.quote: BPC-157, TB-500, CJC-1295/ipamorelin, epitalon, and thymalin have plausible mechanisms but only anecdotal human data (C); seven peptides go before the FDA's PCAC in July 2026 — but review is not approval, and there is no clear lawful compounding route yet.
assertions.note: The Hormonaly guides note that neither BPC-157 nor TB-500 has a clear lawful route to compounding.

assertions.text: A 'research use only' vial is outside any lawful clinical route and is not authorized for human use.
assertions.quote: CAUTION: Contains a new drug for investigational use only in laboratory research animals, or for tests in vitro. Not for use in humans.
assertions.note: 21 CFR 312.160 mandates that research-only investigational drugs must be labeled not for use in humans, and clinical guides corroborate that RUO is not a clinical pathway.

units.text: The UK sorts products the same way, by claim, form and use, into cosmetics, food and medicines; lesson 7.2 set out its route for unlicensed medicines.

assertions.text: The UK sorts products by claim, form and use into cosmetics, food and medicines.
assertions.quote: Depending on the product’s composition, presentation and intended use  they may meet the  definition of other consumer products and therefore must meet the safety regulations for those  categories of products, including medicines, medical devices, cosmetics, foods, food additives  or flavourings.
assertions.note: MHRA guidance notes that products are classified into categories including medicines, cosmetics, and foods based on their composition, presentation, and intended use.

units.text: In the EU, a product is a medicine by presentation or by pharmacological, immunological or metabolic function, and where it could also fall under another product law, medicines law applies (Directive 2001/83/EC, Articles 1(2) and 2(2)); anything intended to be ingested, inhaled, injected or implanted is not a cosmetic (Regulation (EC) No 1223/2009, Article 2(2)). Food supplements are foods, and a health claim on a food is prohibited unless it is authorised and on the EU lists of authorised claims (Directive 2002/46/EC; Regulation (EC) No 1924/2006, Article 10(1)).

assertions.text: In the EU, a product is a medicine by presentation or by pharmacological, immunological or metabolic function.
assertions.quote:
(a) 

Any substance or combination of substances presented as having properties for treating or preventing disease in human beings; or

(b) 

Any substance or combination of substances which may be used in or administered to human beings either with a view to restoring, correcting or modifying physiological functions by exerting a pharmacological, immunological or metabolic action, or to making a medical diagnosis.
assertions.note: Directive 2001/83/EC defines a medicinal product by presentation for treating/preventing disease or by function via pharmacological, immunological, or metabolic action.

assertions.text: Where a product could also fall under another product law, EU medicines law applies.
assertions.quote: In cases of doubt, where, taking into account all its characteristics, a product may fall within the definition of a ‘medicinal product’ and within the definition of a product covered by other Community legislation the provisions of this Directive shall apply.
assertions.note: Article 2(2) of Directive 2001/83/EC specifies that in cases of doubt where a product may fall under both medicinal and other Community product legislation, medicines law applies.

assertions.text: In the EU, anything intended to be ingested, inhaled, injected or implanted is not a cosmetic.
assertions.quote: For the purposes of point (a) of paragraph 1, a substance or mixture intended to be ingested, inhaled, injected or implanted into the human body shall not be considered to be a cosmetic product.
assertions.note: Article 2(2) of Regulation (EC) No 1223/2009 expressly excludes substances or mixtures intended to be ingested, inhaled, injected, or implanted from the definition of cosmetic products.

assertions.text: Food supplements are classified as foods under EU law.
assertions.quote: This Directive concerns food supplements marketed as foodstuffs and presented as such.
assertions.note: Directive 2002/46/EC confirms that food supplements are marketed and regulated as foodstuffs.

assertions.text: A health claim on a food is prohibited in the EU unless it is authorised and on the EU lists of authorised claims.
assertions.quote: Health claims shall be prohibited unless they comply with the general requirements in Chapter II and the specific requirements in this Chapter and are authorised in accordance with this Regulation and included in the lists of authorised claims provided for in Articles 13 and 14.
assertions.note: Article 10(1) of Regulation (EC) No 1924/2006 states that health claims are prohibited unless authorised and included in the lists of authorised claims.

units.text: In Portugal, INFARMED is the competent authority for cosmetics and states that products administered by ingestion, inhalation, injection or implantation into the body are not cosmetics (read 25 September 2026). Food supplements are meant to maintain the body's homeostasis, not to prevent, treat or cure disease, and must be notified to DGAV before sale; DGAV warns that notification does not mean a supplement is authorised or compliant.

assertions.text: In Portugal, INFARMED is the competent authority for cosmetics.
assertions.quote: De acordo com o disposto no número 1 do artigo 2º do Decreto-Lei n.º 23/2025, de 19 de março, o INFARMED - Autoridade Nacional do Medicamento e Produtos de Saúde, I. P. (INFARMED, I. P.), é a autoridade nacional competente para os produtos cosméticos.
assertions.note: INFARMED is designated under Portuguese law as the competent national authority for cosmetic products.

assertions.text: INFARMED states that products administered by ingestion, inhalation, injection or implantation into the body are not cosmetics.
assertions.quote: Não são considerados cosméticos produtos cuja administração se faça por ingestão, inalação, injeção ou implantação no corpo.
assertions.note: INFARMED explicitly clarifies in its FAQ that products administered via these routes are not considered cosmetics.

assertions.text: Food supplements are meant to maintain the body's homeostasis, not to prevent, treat or cure disease.
assertions.quote: Os suplementos alimentares destinam-se a manter a homeostasia do organismo e não à prevenção, tratamento ou cura de doenças.
assertions.note: DGAV states that food supplements are intended to maintain homeostasis rather than treat, cure, or prevent disease.

assertions.text: Food supplements must be notified to DGAV before sale.
assertions.quote: Os Suplementos Alimentares têm de ser notificados à DGAV , antes de serem colocados no mercado nacional, mesmo os que já se encontram comercializados noutro Estado-Membro da UE, de acordo com o “ Procedimento de notificação de suplementos alimentares “.
assertions.note: DGAV guidance notes that food supplements must be notified prior to marketing.

assertions.text: DGAV warns that notification does not mean a supplement is authorised or compliant.
assertions.quote: A inexistência de resposta significa que a DGAV aceitou a submissão do processo, mas não significa que tenham sido verificados os requisitos legais, pelo que, em caso algum, o operador poderá concluir que o produto se encontra autorizado ou que se encontra conforme.
assertions.note: DGAV explicitly states that submitting a notification does not imply authorization or verified legal compliance.

units.text: In Brazil, cosmetic labelling may not carry therapeutic claims for the product or its ingredients (RDC 907/2024, art. 12), and ANVISA stated on 2 July 2026 that injectable cosmetics do not exist and that, if a product is offered in this form, it is an irregular cosmetic. A food supplement is by definition a product for oral ingestion by healthy people (RDC 243/2018), and it may use only constituents on ANVISA's authorised list (IN 28/2018).

assertions.text: In Brazil, cosmetic labelling may not carry therapeutic claims for the product or its ingredients (RDC 907/2024, art. 12).
assertions.quote: II - representem alegações terapêuticas atribuídas ao uso do produto ou de seus ingredientes, como, por exemplo, prevenção ou tratamento de hematomas, feridas, rachaduras, dores, inflamações, câimbras, varizes, pediculose, incluindo ação de eliminação, redução, morte ou tombamento de piolho e lêndeas ou proteção completa contra eles;
assertions.note: RDC 907/2024, art. 12, II specifies that cosmetic labelling may not contain therapeutic claims attributed to the product or its ingredients.

assertions.text: ANVISA stated on 2 July 2026 that injectable cosmetics do not exist and that, if a product is offered in this form, it is an irregular cosmetic.
assertions.quote: Não existem cosméticos injetáveis e, se o produto é oferecido desta forma, trata-se de cosmético irregular.
assertions.note: ANVISA's 2 July 2026 release states that injectable cosmetics do not exist and any such product is irregular.

assertions.text: A food supplement is by definition a product for oral ingestion by healthy people (RDC 243/2018).
assertions.quote: VII - suplemento alimentar: produto para ingestão oral, apresentado em formas farmacêuticas, destinado a suplementar a alimentação de indivíduos saudáveis com nutrientes, substâncias bioativas, enzimas ou probióticos, isolados ou combinados.
assertions.note: RDC 243/2018 defines food supplements as products for oral ingestion intended to supplement the nutrition of healthy individuals.

assertions.text: A food supplement may use only constituents on ANVISA's authorised list (IN 28/2018).
assertions.quote: Art. 4° Os constituintes autorizados para uso na composição de suplementos alimentares restringem-se àqueles previstos nos Anexos I e II da Instrução Normativa n° 28, de 26 de julho de 2018, que estabelece as listas de constituintes, de limites de uso, de alegações e de rotulagem complementar dos suplementos alimentares.
assertions.note: RDC 243/2018 restricts constituents authorised in food supplements to those listed in IN 28/2018.

units.text: In the UAE, Federal Decree-Law 38 of 2024 makes cosmetics with a medical effect on the skin, hair or nails, and food supplements, medical products regulated by the Emirates Drug Establishment (EDE, the federal regulator of medical products since Federal Decree-Law 28/2023), while ordinary cosmetics need a MoIAT conformity certificate (Cabinet Resolution 18/2014); an EDE classification letter settles whether a product needs EDE marketing authorisation and in which regulatory category. In Abu Dhabi, the DoH keeps topical cosmetic peptides with no systemic effect on existing pathways as low-risk products, while systemic, regenerative or weakly evidenced peptides face enhanced controls (31 July 2026).

Practice
Six lines from a serum page.

units.sourceNote: Fictional product page · FDA, cosmetic or drug · Balshem 2011 · Core GRADE 5 (BMJ 2025) · Miller 2006 · Hormonaly guides

units.text:
Which lines overclaim?
Find each line that claims more than the evidence or the US rules support.
Flagged line (the learner flags it; the course's claim is only that the evidence does not support it): "GHK-Cu serum: a true cosmeceutical."
Explanation: 'Cosmeceutical' has no legal meaning. Route and claim decide the regime, whatever the molecule.
Flagged line (the learner flags it; the course's claim is only that the evidence does not support it): "It regenerates skin cells."
Explanation: A claim to affect structure or function, such as 'regenerates cells', makes it a drug.
Sound line: Tested in a trial of skin healing after laser resurfacing.
Explanation: Accurate as stated: topical GHK-Cu's only indexed trial measured healing after laser resurfacing. It is a real trial, of a different outcome.
Flagged line (the learner flags it; the course's claim is only that the evidence does not supp…

assertions.text: Under US law, the term 'cosmeceutical' has no legal meaning.
assertions.quote: The FD&C Act does not recognize any such category as "cosmeceuticals." A product can be a drug, a cosmetic, or a combination of both, but the term "cosmeceutical" has no meaning under the law.
assertions.note: The FDA page states that the FD&C Act does not recognize cosmeceuticals and the term has no legal meaning.

assertions.text: Under US regulatory standards, a claim that a product 'regenerates cells' classifies it as a drug.
assertions.quote: Certain claims may cause a product to be considered a drug, even if the product is marketed as if it were a cosmetic. Such claims establish the product as a drug because the intended use is to treat or prevent disease or otherwise affect the structure or functions of the human body. Some examples are claims that products will restore hair growth, reduce cellulite, treat varicose veins, increase or decrease the production of melanin (pigment) in the skin, or regenerate cells.
assertions.note: The FDA states that claims to regenerate cells establish a product as a drug.

assertions.text: Topical GHK-Cu was evaluated in a clinical trial assessing skin healing following carbon dioxide laser resurfacing.
assertions.quote: To evaluate the role of skin care products that contain a copper tripeptide complex, glycyl-l-histidyl-l-lysine-Cu(2+) (GHK-Cu), in treating carbon dioxide (CO(2)) laser-resurfaced skin.
assertions.note: The trial evaluated GHK-Cu in treating carbon dioxide laser-resurfaced skin.

assertions.text: Topical GHK-Cu is not supported as having a GRADE A rating, carrying a GRADE C evidence rating instead.
assertions.quote: GHK-Cu, a copper-binding tripeptide, has a long mechanistic record for collagen and matrix synthesis and modest clinical support in topical use GRADE C.[1]
assertions.note: Topical GHK-Cu is rated GRADE C based on modest clinical support and small trials.

assertions.text: A plausible biological mechanism alone does not prove clinical efficacy or elevate an evidence grade.
assertions.quote: Mechanistic appeal alone never raises a grade.
assertions.note: The guide explicitly notes that mechanistic appeal alone never raises an evidence grade.

assertions.text: A peptide certificate of analysis documents identity by reporting the expected mass alongside the observed mass.
assertions.quote: Mass spectrometry confirms the molecular weight matches the expected peptide. The theoretical monoisotopic mass should be reported alongside the observed mass.
assertions.note: The guide specifies reporting the theoretical mass alongside the observed mass to verify identity.

units.text:
Fictional case
'Just prescribe it off-label.'
A 52-year-old patient, three weeks after a fractional laser treatment, asks you to prescribe compounded BPC-157 injections 'off-label' to speed healing. She has found a pharmacy willing to make it and shows you its certificate of analysis. This is a fictional case built from the module's sources, and one response is clearly best.
BPC-157 has no approval, so there is no label to go off
It has no 503A route; FDA staff advised against listing it
A certificate describes a lot and creates no route
Role version (prescriber): You decline, explain, and document the request, the product's status in those words, the evidence you quoted and the alternatives you offered.
Role version (clinical-staff): If a patient asks you to arrange or give a compounded or research peptide, record the request and the product details and pass it to the prescriber; do not…
units.sourceNote: Fictional case · FDA BPC-157 briefing (July 2026) · FDA warning letter (2020) · Peptide Pocket Guide, prescriber exposure

assertions.text: BPC-157 has never received FDA approval, so it cannot be prescribed off-label because off-label prescribing applies only to approved drugs.
assertions.quote: Off-label doesn't apply to unapproved drugs. Off-label use is a legal pathway only for drugs holding at least one FDA-approved indication. Prescribing BPC-157 or any never-approved peptide is use of an unapproved new drug — IND, Expanded Access, and Right-to-Try do not cover routine wellness use.
assertions.note: Hannah-Shmouni affirms that off-label use applies only to FDA-approved drugs and does not apply to never-approved peptides like BPC-157.

assertions.text: BPC-157 has no 503A route, its nominations were withdrawn, and FDA reviewers advised against listing it in July 2026 citing insufficient evidence of effectiveness.
assertions.quote: Accordingly, we propose not adding BPC-157 (free base) or BPC-157 acetate to the 503A Bulks List.
assertions.note: The FDA briefing document notes withdrawn nominations and recommends against adding BPC-157 to the 503A Bulks List.

assertions.text: A certificate of analysis describes a batch or lot and does not establish a lawful compounding route under Section 503A.
assertions.quote: Under 503A the three routes to bulk eligibility are hierarchical, not alternative. A substance must comply with an applicable USP or NF monograph where one exists. Only if no monograph exists may it qualify as a component of an FDA-approved drug. Only if neither is true does the third route open — appearance on the 503A bulks list.
assertions.note: Hannah-Shmouni notes that bulk eligibility requires a monograph, approved component status, or 503A Bulks listing, which a CoA does not create.

assertions.text: Prescribers must decline unapproved peptide requests and document the request, the regulatory status of the product in those terms, the evidence quoted, and alternatives offered.
assertions.quote: 1. Document the identity of the article and its regulatory status in the chart, in those terms — not as off-label use of an approved drug.
assertions.note: Hannah-Shmouni instructs documenting the regulatory status of the article in the chart rather than charting it as off-label use.

assertions.text: Clinical staff asked to arrange or administer a compounded or research peptide must record the request and pass it to the prescriber rather than agreeing to administer it.
assertions.note: The provided sources do not discuss clinical staff protocols or handoffs for patient peptide requests.

recheck.note: None of the provided sources discuss protocols for clinical staff when asked to arrange or administer compounded or research peptides.

units.text:
What do you do?
Distractor (deliberately false, not a claim): Prescribe it as off-label use and file the certificate in her chart.
Explanation: Off-label presupposes an approved drug. BPC-157 has no approval and no 503A route, FDA has warned a compounder about it, and a certificate changes neither fact.
Correct answer: Decline to prescribe it. Explain the evidence and the US status in plain terms, return to the aftercare plan her treating clinician set, and record her request, what you explained and her decision.
Explanation: Right. You keep the conversation, give her the real category and the grade, and leave a chart note a reviewer can follow.
Distractor (deliberately false, not a claim): Suggest she buy research-grade BPC-157 with a good certificate and come back for monitoring.

assertions.note: The Peptide Pocket Guide confirms that off-label prescribing presupposes an approved product.

assertions.note: The FDA briefing document confirms that BPC-157 has no approved drug status, no compendial monograph, and is not approved on the 503A bulks list.

assertions.text: The FDA has warned a compounding pharmacy regarding compounding BPC-157.
assertions.quote: During the inspection, the FDA investigators noted that drug products produced by your firm failed to meet the conditions of section 503A. For example, the investigators noted that your firm compounded drug products using Follistatin, GHRP-2, GHRP-6, Endurobal, AOD 9604, BPC 157, Bremelanotide (PT-141), Cerebrolysin, DSIP, Epitalon, GHK-Cu, IGF1-LR3, Ipamorelin, LL-37, Melanotan II, PEG-MGF, Selank, Semax, CJC 1295, SARMS, LGD-4033, and MK 677.

assertions.quote: The drug-side analogue, 21 C.F.R. 312.160, permits shipping an investigational drug without an IND for laboratory animal or in vitro use if the label reads "Not for use in humans" — and obliges the shipper to confirm the consignee runs such tests.
assertions.note: The guide notes that regulations permit investigational shipments for animal or in vitro use if labelled not for use in humans.

assertions.text: The Peptide Pocket Guide considers directing a patient to research-grade peptides as practicing medicine with accompanying liability.
assertions.quote: "Recommending" is not a liability shield: directing patients to source research-grade peptides for self-administration is practicing medicine; liability and board jurisdiction attach regardless of whether the practitioner handled the product, and most malpractice policies exclude unapproved-drug claims.
assertions.note: The guide warns that directing patients to source research-grade peptides constitutes practicing medicine.

units.text:
From the vial to the note
Decide what you tell her, what FDA's record shows and what you write down.
What do you tell her?

Correct answer: Decline to supervise, supply or recommend it: a research-use-only product stays outside clinical care.
Explanation: Right. FDA reads intended use from claims, marketing and the circumstances of sale, so the 'not for use in humans' disclaimer changes nothing about a vial sold with injection instructions.

Explanation: A certificate of analysis, however clean, cannot convert that vial into a pharmaceutical: sterility, manufac…

assertions.text: FDA determines intended use from claims, marketing, and the circumstances surrounding distribution, meaning that a research-use disclaimer does not alter the regulatory status of a vial marketed or sold for injection.
assertions.quote: The words intended uses or words of similar import in §§ 201.5 , 201.115 , 201.117 , 201.119 , 201.120 , 201.122 , and 1100.5 of this chapter refer to the objective intent of the persons legally responsible for the labeling of an article (or their representatives). The intent may be shown by such persons' expressions, the design or composition of the article, or by the circumstances surrounding the distribution of the article.
assertions.note: 21 CFR 201.128 establishes that objective intended use is shown by expressions, advertising, and distribution circumstances.

assertions.text: Under FDA's 503A interim compounding lists as of May 2026, Category 1 covers only non-injectable GHK-Cu, while the nomination for injectable GHK-Cu was withdrawn.
assertions.quote: On May 5, 2026, one of those nominators clarified that it intended to withdraw only its nomination of the injectable route of administration with respect to GHK-Cu and would like to retain its nomination for GHK-Cu for non-injectable routes of administration. GHK-Cu (except for injectable routes of administration) will be added back to category 1.
assertions.note: The May 14, 2026 update confirms that only non-injectable GHK-Cu is in Category 1, following nominator withdrawal of the injectable route.

assertions.text: FDA 503A categories represent interim enforcement discretion postures while nominations are evaluated, rather than drug approvals.
assertions.quote: Categories 1, 2 and 3 are something else: enforcement-discretion postures described in FDA guidance while nominations are evaluated. Category 1 means FDA does not intend to act against a compounder using the substance if guidance conditions are met.
assertions.note: The Peptide Pocket Guide explains that 503A categories reflect FDA's interim enforcement policy, not statutory approval.

assertions.text: GHK-Cu moved twice on FDA's 503A category rosters between April and May 2026.
assertions.quote: GHK-Cu (except for injectable routes of administration) was removed from c ategory 1 on April 22, 2026, because the nominations for GHK-Cu were withdrawn by the nominators.
assertions.note: FDA's document details that GHK-Cu was removed on April 22, 2026, and reinstated for non-injectable routes following a May 5 clarification.

assertions.text: Off-label prescribing applies only to FDA-approved drugs; prescribing a never-approved peptide constitutes use of an unapproved new drug.
assertions.quote: Off-label prescribing presupposes an approved product to be off the label of; for a never-approved peptide the marketing prohibition is unrelieved and the adequate-directions exemption is unavailable.
assertions.note: The text confirms that off-label use presupposes an approved drug and does not apply to never-approved peptides.

assertions.text: When documenting clinical encounters involving unapproved peptides, clinicians should record the article, plain-language regulatory status, and the date the status was verified.
assertions.quote: 1. Document the identity of the article and its regulatory status in the chart, in those terms — not as off-label use of an approved drug.
assertions.note: The guide recommends charting the exact identity and regulatory status rather than calling it off-label use.

units.text:
GHK-Cu appears in three products: a cream sold 'for the look of fine lines', the same cream sold 'to regenerate skin cells', and an injectable vial labelled research use only. In the US, which statement is right?
Explanation: Name the claim and the route, then the regime.
Distractor (deliberately false, not a claim): All three are cosmetics, because the molecule is the same.
Explanation: The regime follows the claim and the route. A structure-or-function claim makes the second cream a drug, and the vial is no cosmetic at all.
Correct answer: The first is a cosmetic; the second makes a drug claim, so it is an unapproved drug; the vial is outside any clinical route.
Explanation: Correct. Claim and route decide the rulebook, whatever the molecule.
Distractor (deliberately false, not a claim): All three are lawful, because GHK-Cu is in Category 1.
Explanation: Category 1 covers 503A compound…

assertions.text: A structure-or-function claim, such as a claim to regenerate cells, establishes a cosmetic-type product as a drug under US FDA regulations.
assertions.quote: Such claims establish the product as a drug because the intended use is to treat or prevent disease or otherwise affect the structure or functions of the human body. Some examples are claims that products will restore hair growth, reduce cellulite, treat varicose veins, increase or decrease the production of melanin (pigment) in the skin, or regenerate cells.
assertions.note: FDA explicitly notes that claims to affect structure/function, such as regenerating cells, establish a product as a drug.

assertions.text: An investigational drug labeled for laboratory research or in vitro use is restricted from use in humans.
assertions.quote: A person may ship a drug intended solely for tests in vitro or in animals used only for laboratory research purposes if it is labeled as follows: CAUTION: Contains a new drug for investigational use only in laboratory research animals, or for tests in vitro. Not for use in humans.
assertions.note: 21 CFR 312.160 requires drugs for research animals or in vitro tests to be labeled not for use in humans.

assertions.text: Under Section 503A compounding categories, GHK-Cu is listed in Category 1 except for injectable routes of administration.
assertions.quote: GHK-Cu (except for injectable routes of administration) will be added back to category 1.
assertions.note: FDA's Category 1 listing specifically covers GHK-Cu except for injectable routes of administration.

Closing and commitment
My practice, from the next conversation.
This is the last step of the course. Build the commitment you will actually keep; it is saved in My notes, in the Library. The course is designed toward future CME accreditation and does not award credit at this time.
Choose what you will do in every peptide or hormone conversation from now on
Takeaway: Next: the course quiz, then your capstone, where you appraise a simulated certificate and marketing sheet and hold the patient conversation that follows.
Role version (prescriber): Your commitment ends with the chart: the regime, the grade, the consent and a dated status check.
Role version (clinical-staff): Your commitment ends with escalation: anything unapproved, compounded or research-use-only goes to the prescriber the same day, with the product details recorded.
Role version (advisor): Your commitment ends with referral…
